He studied at universities whose names, frankly, I had never heard of. Yet he had built an AI module for a cooperative in Palangkaraya, for its supply chain, written by himself in Python without asking AI to write his code. Many people today build AI using AI. He didn’t." "" "Ahmad Maulid Ridwan, a vice director, worked while continuing his education, through polytechnic, S1 and S2. He demonstrated the automation he had built for the institution using n8n. " "" "Dr. Yudhistira Adityawardhana took another path: ITS, Masters in UI and a PhD in Taiwan. He showed us machine learning, not just an LLM, built as the backbone of the AI he plans to develop." In Cikarang, I thought I may have arrived at the place where I can fulfill that dream." "" "People love titles, university names and exclusivity. Convenient gatekeepers into elite industry. There is a human behind the AI. Is that person a critical thinker? What has that person actually learned?" "" "For me it starts with Iqra, read. A corpus of knowledge takes years to build. "" "We will bring our strength: PMR and turning knowledge of paying customers into value in rupiah or dollars. Thirty percent theory, seventy percent hands-on." "" "Mens et Manus, in PolMind." I first remember Rosyid as a baby being breastfed beside his mother’s tahu goreng cart. He is now in primary school." "" "I have passed this family for years during my walks and jogging in Jakarta. But I have just learned something I did not know: Mama Rosyid has been selling at this corner in Menteng since 2003. Twenty-three years." "" "She told me she used to shop at Pasar Cikini and somehow received permission to sell here. When asked how she could have this spot, her answer was simple: “sudah rezekinya.”" "" "I would see Mama Rosyid and her 2nd husband (the first one has passed away) pushing the cart from where they kept it around the Cimandiri area to Menteng. I also recognized her husband from seeing him at night in the green jacket commonly worn by motorcycle ride-hailing and delivery drivers." "" "Mama Rosyid sells tahu goreng. Over time, I noticed coffee sachets hanging from the cart too. She makes cups of instant coffee for customers. I am always happy to see people stopping to buy from her." "" "They have four children. Two are already working, the third is in senior high school, and Rosyid is the youngest. The family lives in Cawang." "" "Now I finally understand why I see Rosyid there so often. There is nobody at home to look after him after school. His father picks him up after school and brings him to his mother in Menteng." "" "I have watched him grow from being breastfed beside the cart to spending hours absorbed in a tablet. I see him with it very often. For some reason, the screen cannot rotate and remains in portrait mode. His mother says he studies and can go to the mosque only 20 or 30 metres away." "" "There is a tarpaulin when it rains. One of my photographs was taken at around 21:00. " "" "Indonesia is 81 years into independence. Indonesia call themselves prosper. Economic growth is reported at 5.81 percent, along with other good macroeconomic numbers. I am not disputing those numbers." "" "Mama Rosyid has occupied this small corner of that economy since 2003." "" "All this happens in Menteng, perhaps two or three kilometres from the Palace, the symbolic centre of the Republic. And I have walked enough around Jakarta to know that this family is hardly alone." "" "My other photograph was taken at around 23:30. Mama Rosyid and her youngest son were asleep on the pavement beside the cart." "" "Finding the Remaining Goods of Indonesia, #31.
2026-08-27 The first thing I saw after entering the directors’ building at SMK Mitra Industri MM2100 was a pair of chairs on my left, bearing the names Naruhito and Masako.
The first thing I saw after entering the directors’ building at SMK Mitra Industri MM2100 was a pair of chairs on my left, bearing the names Naruhito and Masako. Rope stanchions kept visitors at a distance. They were arranged almost like a shrine. I had barely entered an SMK in Cikarang and was already asking why the Emperor and Empress of Japan had chosen to visit this place." "" "Outside, students walked on a dedicated green pedestrian lane. Motorcycles stayed in their designated parking area. The public toilet was spotless. Students wore blazers, kept their hair short, greeted older people properly, and answered questions sharply. They were not isinan. In the workshops, the teaching factory and Paint School made me wonder whether I was inside a school or a manufacturing plant." "" "The school was built by people from industry after confronting a practical problem: local young people wanted factory jobs, but some left after a week, several weeks, or a month. The founders decided to intervene earlier." "" "Students now follow different pathways according to where they intend to go: work, university, entrepreneurship, Japan, and other international routes. Some wear pins stating their dreams. One wanted a restaurant. Another wanted to become a teacher." "" "Then I went to the student-run café. I was told it generates around Rp50 million a month. The coffee failed my test because I prefer robusta, but something else caught my attention. I asked the students about their families." "" "Some told me their parents own PT companies. They still chose an SMK." "" "That matters to my research. Too many government SMKs I have studied remain second or third options. Here I found vocational education that families with alternatives were willing to choose." "" "Indonesian ministers and officials responsible for vocational education have also visited this school. They have seen the workshops, the discipline, the pathway system, the Japan program, the clean toilets, and students who can state where they want to go." "" "Yet very few government SMKs I have studied come close to this standard." "" "Artifacts are easy to copy. Paint the lane green. Buy screens. Build a café. Purchase equipment. Launch another program. Government already knows how to organize visits, ceremonies, ribbon cutting, photographs, and impressive titles." "" "What is harder to copy are the shared values and underlying assumptions that keep those artifacts working every ordinary day." "" "A clean toilet means little if it becomes clean only before a visit. A teaching factory means little if the machines become a backdrop. A dream pin is decoration if nobody changes learning around the future written on it." "" "The ontology is different." "" "" "Once a teacher, always a teacher. Unfortunately, once a maling, always a maling." "The chairs of Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako are still there behind the rope stanchions. Indonesian officials have stood in the same school and seen what works. I am still looking for what they brought home.

2026-08-27 Apri finished high school, sells gemblong, and adds flower buckets when there is demand. I met him in Blok M while he was attending to flowers.
Apri finished high school, sells gemblong, and adds flower buckets when there is demand." "" "I met him in Blok M while he was attending to flowers. I was actually interested in the gemblong beside him. When I asked who owned the business, he pointed to himself. It carried the name Gemblong Ibu Juju, sold from a thin blue round container that I later began noticing elsewhere in Jakarta." "" "Apri is in his early thirties, from a Minangkabau and Sundanese family. He had sold other things before gemblong. He told me this one was easier. The name helped him sell, he only needed to carry one container, and he had entered a larger network selling the same product. On a good day, he said sales could reach Rp1 million, leaving him around Rp300,000 to Rp350,000 in commission." "" "I have not verified the history he told me about Ibu Juju or how the network is organized. Apri described sellers living together, leaving in the morning for different parts of Jakarta, and sometimes recognizing other sellers through the same product even when they did not know one another. I could not identify an organization behind it that resembled a conventional franchise." "" "My PhD research examined why Indonesians often hesitate to become entrepreneurs. One variable was particularly strong: preference for stable employment, with an important cultural component. I am carrying that question into another piece of research I call “Finding the Remaining Good.”" "" "I have been meeting cobblers, barbers, jamu and gudeg sellers, tailors, vegetable-cart sellers, and bajaj drivers. Some learned the work from parents. Some continued what the family already knew. Some appear to have entered because there were few alternatives." "" "There are several entrepreneurship taxonomies that might help me think about them. I have put the three I am considering in the first comment." "" "Apri had already sold other products. He moved to gemblong because it paid better, was easier to sell, required less to carry, and connected him to an existing name and network." "" "His Minangkabau background also made me curious whether trading was something he had encountered in his family. Minang people are often associated with trading. I do not know whether that has anything to do with Apri. I did not ask whether selling was learned at home or whether someone in his family had done similar work." "" "When I asked why he had not gone to university, Apri said he was happy doing this because, after graduating, he might still have to work anyway. I do not completely share his conclusion about education." "" "Later I noticed flower sellers in many corners of Blok M. Apri was selling gemblong and taking care of flowers at the same time." "" "When I began “Finding the Remaining Good,” I expected to meet people who entered these trades because they had few alternatives. I have." "" "I would like to meet Apri again and ask where selling began for him.

2026-08-23 Eight expressions now form a troubling vocabulary around President Prabowo Subianto’s public communication: rakyat jelata, antek asing, ndeso, bajingan, a suggestion that citizens who...
Eight expressions now form a troubling vocabulary around President Prabowo Subianto’s public communication: rakyat jelata, antek asing, ndeso, bajingan, a suggestion that citizens who found Indonesia’s future bleak could seek another country, londo ireng, rasain sendiri, and a remark about when a 10-year-old girl might be allowed to date. The expressions are not identical. " "" "They arose from seven occasions because bajingan and cari negara lain came from the same speech. They were directed toward different people and used with different intentions claimed on their behalf. Two of them, rakyat jelata and ndeso, were not spoken by Prabowo himself, but by officials within his presidential apparatus. The remark to the child was neither a curse nor an insult in the ordinary sense. It was a different kind of breach: an unsolicited, gendered and paternalistic diversion from a girl’s educational and athletic achievement to her future romantic life." "" "These differences matter. An argument about the ethics of presidential communication should begin by refusing the very imprecision it criticizes. Yet the differences do not dissolve the pattern. They reveal its institutional breadth." "" "The article below 👇 examines that concern through Javanese principles of speech and power, reinterpreted within a constitutional republic." "" "The presidency is not a private microphone." "" "The deeper problem is that presidential speech is institutional action. From the highest office, a joke can become a cue, a label can become a classification, and an insinuation can tell ministers, supporters and bureaucrats which citizens may safely be treated as backward, disloyal, contemptible or unserious." "" "Several Javanese courtly principles can illuminate this thoroughly republican problem. They include sabda pandhita ratu, ajining diri saka lathi, empan papan, tepa selira, angon rasa and unggah-ungguh. They should not be used to turn the president into a king. Indonesia is not a court, citizens are not kawula, and political legitimacy does not descend from aristocratic tradition. These principles are valuable only after being democratically reinterpreted." "" "In a court, the king’s word bound subjects. In a republic, the president’s word is bound by the Constitution and responsibility to citizens.

2026-08-21 On 16 August 2026, I whispered to my former supervisor calmly: “I quit anthropology because of you”. I also told him: “I fell in love with ethnography because of you”.
On 16 August 2026, I whispered to my former supervisor calmly: “I quit anthropology because of you”. I also told him: “I fell in love with ethnography because of you”." "" "My first class with him was on 15 February 2023, during my first attempt at a PhD. I came from industry with expectations shaped by other educational experiences. I expected to understudy someone, to have access and conversation, and to build rapport with my supervisor. Perhaps I expected too much. He was also the head of the department, and I could not adjust to the distance and hierarchy between us." "" "My resignation document is quite specific: meeting requests rejected or unanswered, emails unanswered, and repeated attempts to establish contact that went nowhere. Yet his class was making me want to become an anthropologist. I became mesmerized by ethnography while becoming increasingly unhappy with the relationship through which I was supposed to learn it." "" "So I withdrew. I wrote then that my decision would revolve around “Happiness in Pursuing.” Health had priority. I also examined my own assumptions. Perhaps I thought too highly of my previous experience and expected an academic relationship similar to those I had experienced elsewhere." "" "I did not abandon the doctorate. I moved to a School of Business in a different city, within the country’s leading engineering school, something like MIT’s place in the United States. I completed my PhD there in the minimum time, with a 4.0 GPA, summa cum laude, and five Scopus-indexed Q1 and Q2 publications." "" "Three and a half years later, we were both invited to the VIP room of a wedding. I saw him sitting with two other guests. I went around the VIP section shaking hands and saying hello to familiar faces who recognized me and interested in my story. I felt blessed." "" "As I was leaving, an hour into the party, I approached him. I introduced myself as the student who had briefly studied with him in 2023, then kneeled beside him to talk." "" "He said he had recognised me, then joked about how handsome I looked. To be fair, I was unusually well behaved sartorially: Canali suit, Ermenegildo Zegna T-shirt, Hermès tie and Christian Louboutin shoes. I normally go almost everywhere in shorts and running shoes." "" "I told him why I had left, how hard I had tried to approach him, and how much the distance had hurt me. I also told him the other half: his teaching was the reason I had fallen in love with ethnography." "" "He smiled throughout. He congratulated me, said he was happy for me and proud of me. “Sometimes life is like this. We don’t always get what we want.”" "" "He did not say sorry - he must not. But I am no longer sure he ever knew how angry I had been. He seemed simply happy for his former student." "" "I felt peace. Proverbs 16:7 came immediately to mind:" "" "“When a man’s ways please the Lord, he makes even his enemies be at peace with him.”" "" "Then we shook hands and took this photograph. I pray for him and his family that God bestow him peace and makarios.

2026-08-20 MBG: Prof. Laksono, who studied anthropology in the 70s and was shaped by senior Indonesian anthropologists including Masri Singarimbun and the intellectual tradition established by...
MBG: Prof. Laksono, who studied anthropology in the 70s and was shaped by senior Indonesian anthropologists including Masri Singarimbun and the intellectual tradition established by Koentjaraningrat, still remembers his mother dividing one egg into six pieces for her children in Pakualaman in the 1960s." "" "When we spoke in Yogyakarta on 16 August about MBG, he returned to that childhood memory. Laksono grew up in a family of twelve children, with two civil-servant parents, and food had to be managed carefully. His mother also provided other nutritious food, so the memory should not be read as evidence of nutritional deprivation. More than sixty years later, he remembers the act because he remembers his mother through it." "" ""What happens when part of feeding moves from the household to the state, not only for mothers, but for how children experience and remember maternal care?", he asked. " "" "I had already written two Jakarta Post articles on MBG and ran a system-dynamics simulation to examine the program. Obviously, my model is not complete, I missed this basic question." "" "Viegas (2003) and Cook (2009) show that food provision can carry relational meaning and participate in maternal caring practices. Brenton (2017), Elliott and Bowen (2018), and Neuman et al. (2019) caution against reducing good motherhood to maternal foodwork and show that feeding and care can extend beyond mothers. Research on caregiving and attachment establishes the developmental importance of stable, responsive care (Zeanah et al., 2005; McGoron et al., 2012; Mountain et al., 2017; Fox et al., 2017). " "" "The one-sixth egg therefore has a very narrow value. It does not prove nutritional adequacy. It does not prove that scarcity shaped Laksono’s later life. It does not prove that mothers must personally prepare food. It shows that, in one child’s memory, an ordinary act of feeding became part of how he remembers his mother." "" "MBG is usually discussed through things governments can count: portions, nutrients, children reached, procurement and expenditure. In the field, even its nutritional premise is contested, with reports of food poisoning, sub-standard meals, and parents discarding food they considered unfit for their children. Laksono’s question sits outside those usual measures: when the state takes over part of the daily act of feeding children, are we also changing how care is given, received and remembered?" "" "From the mother’s side, that is a question about motherhood and food provision as part of maternal care. From the child’s side, it is a question about the experience and memory of being cared for through food. The literature does not tell us what MBG does to either. It tells us only that these are legitimate things to examine." "" "I have been writing around a theme I call “finding the remaining goods of Indonesia.” In Bulaksumur, I found one in a memory that survived more than sixty years: one egg, divided six ways, and a son who still remembers the mother who divided it.

"" "She studied until Madrasah Tsanawiyah and did not continue because, she said, she had no passion for studying. An old man, often dismissed as “overqualified” and quietly tagged as “irrelevant,” built an app to solve a problem in managing the corpus behind his research and writing." "" "I have more than 3,000 original physical books at home, not copies or HVS printouts, that I have been reading and collecting since junior high." "" "The friction appeared in a small technical place: ISBN metadata." "" "Many older Indonesian books have valid ISBNs, but Zotero and the usual international lookup systems often do not recognize them. WorldCat does not always solve it either. The ISBN exists, but the record does not return. The printed book is real, the identifier is real, yet the digital infrastructure treats it as if it is only half-present." "" "For a book without an ISBN, manual entry is part of the work. I can accept that. But for Indonesian books that do have ISBNs, starting from zero felt unnecessary, especially when the problem was repeated across shelves, not isolated to one title." "" "So I built a small ISBN-to-Zotero app for myself." "" "It scans a barcode with a phone camera. It also accepts manual ISBN entry, because many older books do not have barcodes. It accepts ISBN-10 numbers ending in X. It searches multiple bibliographic sources, compares possible records, and warns when sources disagree, which Zotero itself does not do. Zotero may choose one source and accept it without confirming that the record matches the book I physically have. Then the app checks for possible duplicates in Zotero and adds the selected record to my Zotero cloud library." "" "For many younger people, this may look ordinary. For me, it is not." "" "I grew up with physical books, handwritten notes, paper handouts, card catalogs, and libraries where finding one source could take days. Now I can connect a printed Indonesian book on my shelf to a searchable digital knowledge base with a small tool I would have wanted decades ago, when finding one source could still consume several afternoons." "" "Now I am happy to encounter a physical Indonesian book with a valid ISBN that the usual systems could not find. My app solves the problem. Now the book can sit inside my Zotero digital library because I refused to enter it from zero." "" "And I have very little patience left for people who treat age as evidence that the mind has stopped working.

Rice that had been perfectly good became part of their territory." "" "I dismantled the dispenser, cleaned it thoroughly with high-pressure water, dried it under the sun and left it empty for four months before using it again." "" "Everything was back to normal until last year. A friend gave me five kilograms of mixed red-and-white organic rice from her field in Subang. Again, kutu. "" "The dispenser did not produce the second infestation. A new batch apparently brought it in. Once inside, the kutu found conditions to multiply and spread into rice that had arrived clean." "" "Government institutions and SOEs also receive their next batch from society. There is no recruitment test that can tell us who may participate in corruption years later. What the institution controls is the environment they enter: whether corrupt behavior becomes difficult and costly, or finds enough protected space to multiply." "" "This morning my dispenser was empty, dry and clean." "" "Then I flushed almost 250 grams of what the infestation had left behind from places I could not see.

" "" "For almost a year, he occupied a position none of his classmates had. 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐭𝐥𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐰𝐚𝐲 𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐭." "" "Recently, I recommended several graduates from the class to a friend in my professional network. I did not give anyone my friend’s phone number because I had not asked his permission to share it. I left it to him to decide whom he wished to contact. He later called one graduate to follow up his application on that job opportunity." "" "The graduate working at my company then asked me for my friend’s phone number so he could also be called by my friend. There was nothing wrong with wanting the opportunity. What troubled me was how quickly he expected access to a privilege that someone else had received. For almost a year, he had enjoyed a different privilege. He worked alongside me in a growing AI company and gained experience unavailable to his classmates, yet he rarely shared the parts of that experience that were his to share." "" "I had seen a version of this before. During my years as an executive in the energy industry, only one among several Indonesian supervisors actively supported my promotion. Supervisors from other countries were more willing to sponsor me and introduce me to opportunities that would otherwise have remained out of reach. "" "The classroom episode is not evidence of a theory, nor was the theory developed to explain this one graduate. It reminded me of a phenomenon examined in my doctoral research. 2026-07-29 Just now, an LLM generated the wrong thumbnail for one of my posts. The mistake was obvious.
Just now, an LLM generated the wrong thumbnail for one of my posts." "" "The mistake was obvious. " "" "The instruction was explicit: "Never use “Modern AI.”"" "The generated thumbnail still said: "READING MODERN AI"" "" "At first, I called this a hallucination. The explanation is more interesting." "" "A transformer is trained by minimizing the next-token prediction loss." "" "L(θ) = −Σₜ log Pθ(xₜ | x₍<t₎)" "" "where " "" "x₍<t₎ is the previous context " "xₜ is the target token." "" "Notice what is missing. There is no term such as: " "" "Penalty(output contains “Modern AI”)" "" "The model is not trained to satisfy symbolic rules. It is trained to predict the most probable next token." "" "During inference, the model computes a contextual representation." "" "H = fθ(x₁:ₙ)" "" "and predicts the next token according to." "" "P(w | H) = softmax(WH + b)" "" "My instruction, " "" ""Never use “Modern AI,”" " "" "does not automatically become a logical constraint. It becomes one influence among many inside the hidden representation H." "" "The phrase “Modern AI” has a strong statistical association with discussions of Transformers, GPT, and recent AI research. If that learned association has greater influence at the point of generation than my instruction, the probability distribution can still favor the forbidden phrase. From the outside, it looks like the model ignored me. Mathematically, something else happened." "" "The instruction never became a theorem that had to be satisfied. It remained another feature in a probabilistic representation." "" "A symbolic system might encode the instruction as:" "" "Forbidden(“Modern AI”) " "" "making that output impossible." "" "A transformer has no equivalent hard constraint by default." "" "One way to enforce the instruction would be to introduce constrained decoding." "" "Let:" "" "C = {y : y contains “Modern AI”}" "" "where " "" "y is a complete candidate output." "" "The decoder could then use." "" "P′(y | H) = 0, if y ∈ C" "" "P′(y | H) = P(y | H) ÷ Σᵧ′∉C P(y′ | H), if y ∉ C" "" "Now every output containing the forbidden phrase has zero probability." "" "The thumbnail was wrong, but the mistake was informative. It illustrates the difference between symbolic constraints and probabilistic sequence prediction. " "" "An explicit instruction in a chat is not automatically a hard rule. It is another signal competing with everything the model has learned.

"" "Back in my Organizational Behavior class during my MBA in 2000, alongside Hersey and Blanchard’s Situational Leadership (1969), I had also encountered Bruce W. On 1 July, a WhatsApp message invited me to speak at a seminar on 15 July. Two days later, an 89-year-old lecturer at a prestigious institution sent a photograph of the handwritten programme. My name was absent. The uncertainty began there. I had been invited as a panelist, yet the programme gave me no role." "" "Out of respect for his age, standing, and the invitation, I did not withdraw. I reserved the date and continued preparing. Over the next twelve days, the assignment changed repeatedly. I would present, then I would not. Later I would present again, before another person was assigned the role. Four days before the seminar, I learned that the replacement speaker could not attend. By then, I had sent a letter declining the invitation. " "" "Organizational life rarely offers absolute certainty, but it depends on decisions becoming stable enough for people to act on them. Once someone has been formally assigned a speaking role, that decision creates a legitimate expectation. The speaker begins preparing, reserves the date, and rearranges other work around the commitment. Repeated reversals unsettle the basis on which that person has organized time and accepted responsibility." "" "Bounded rationality explains why decisions may need revision. Organizers work with incomplete information, limited time, and finite cognitive capacity. Circumstances change. Yet bounded rationality does not justify keeping a decision indefinitely unstable. A decision must eventually become sufficiently settled for affected people to act (Gigerenzer & Selten, 2001)." "" "Communication and uncertainty management theory distinguishes unavoidable uncertainty from uncertainty produced through communication. In this case, the organizer relied entirely on written WhatsApp messages and was unable or unwilling to discuss the changing arrangements by telephone. Each new message contradicted the previous one, while the absence of direct conversation prevented clarification. The communication process therefore increased the uncertainty rather than helping the invited speaker manage it (Brashers, 2001)." "" "High-reliability organizing does not require arrangements never to change. It requires close attention to changing conditions, clear coordination, and dependable communication when adjustments become necessary. Changing an assigned panel role repeatedly without first securing a stable replacement falls below that standard (Weick & Sutcliffe, 2007)." "" "The replacement speaker’s eventual unavailability matters because the transfer did not resolve the planning problem. It left the event without a dependable final arrangement while disrupting the person originally asked to prepare." "" "I prepare seriously for every speaking engagement, whether it is pro bono, modestly compensated, or professionally paid. The honorarium does not determine the respect owed to the speaker. That respect is shown through the stability of the invitation, the care taken before changing it, and the communication that follows.

Why are firms adopting AI faster than they can turn it into productivity, and what happens when every competitor gains access to the same technology?" "" "During an HBS-GMP alumni webinar on 10 July 2026, Prof. Felix Oberholzer-Gee presented a survey in which around 9 in 10 businesses reported no productivity impact from AI. Yet US private non-farm total factor productivity still grew by 0.8% in 2025, while the index rose from 100 in 2017 to 108.44. TFP measures performance across the economy, not the results of a few leading firms, so the problem is weak and uneven growth rather than no growth." "" "Felix then moved through four images: a light bulb, an old factory, a factory under reconstruction, and a production floor organised around electric power. Electricity entered factories in the late nineteenth century, but manufacturers first placed electric motors inside systems designed around steam. The machinery changed before the factory did; productivity improved after firms rebuilt layouts, supervision, and the sequence of work around distributed power." "" "After the webinar, I returned to the literature to test the analogy. Erik Brynjolfsson et al. describe this delay as the productivity J-curve: general-purpose technologies require investment in skills, software, data, management, and process redesign before measurable gains appear. Syverson adds that statistics miss some digital value, though not enough to explain the wider slowdown." "" "That separation now appears inside firms adopting AI. Firms can buy licenses and deploy copilots while retaining old approval layers, reporting routines, incentives, data structures, and decision rights. People carry old habits into a more powerful tool, so adoption advances quickly while organizational change may not begin or may proceed far more slowly." "" "Felix’s WTP and WTS framework shows how AI changes value creation inside the firm. AI can raise what customers are willing to pay through better products, faster service, or better decisions. It can also lower the effort and resources required to deliver them. Either change widens the gap between willingness to pay and willingness to sell." "" "The WTP-WTS gap can become a competitive advantage when a firm reorganises work around AI before most competitors do. Late movers may still improve productivity, but by then organizational redesign is less scarce and easier to copy. " "" "The delay economists observe is the period in which strategists compete, because the advantage created through organizational transformation may fade before the productivity gain becomes visible across the economy." "" "I kept thinking about Felix’s four slides. The light bulb began a process that took decades because the factory itself had to be redesigned. By the time electricity became standard, using it was no longer unique. Whether firms move more deliberately from AI adoption to organisational transformation remains uncertain. Electricity took decades to reshape factories. AI will spread faster.

"" "Most of my marathons here have used the East Coast Park stretch. The proverb sounds gentle until it is placed beside corrupted land policy, vanishing forests, and officials who speak about development while treating trees as disposable inventory." "" "I am not looking at these trees as a tourist. I first came here in 1988 as a high-school student representing my country, returned in 1999, and have lived here since 2008. I used to live in the East Coast area before moving near the Singapore Botanic Gardens. These routes have been close to my daily life for many years." At East Coast Park, the trees are still there, thick over the path.

I found him on the pedestrian path in front of the post office on Jalan Cibaduyut Raya, half an hour before Friday prayer. He sat on a low wooden box, bent over a shoe, with red scissors, knives, glue, spare soles, and two black boxes marked SOL around his feet. That patch of pavement was his workshop. At first, he told me to wait because he was about to close. Then he changed his mind and repaired two pairs before the adzan." "" "His wife sat and conversed with me in Basa Sunda while waiting. Forty-five minutes later, Asep returned in a clean shirt and continued with other three pairs of shoes. He had repaired shoes since 1987. He was born and raised in Cibaduyut. His father was also a shoe worker. Asep used to work in a shoe craft shop before it collapsed during COVID. Since then, his workplace has been the pedestrian path in a district still known for shoes." "" "When he needed spare parts, he walked two or three shops down, took what he needed, and would pay later. That part worked: no form, no app, only someone in the same trade allowing the repair to continue before the money came." "" "I knew his family had no bank account because I asked whether I could pay by transfer. I only had Rp195,000 in cash. His wife said they had no account. I asked how bantuan sosial reached them. She said a civil servant distributed it. I did not ask how much." "" "Somewhere in air-conditioned rooms with microphones, carpets, suits, ties, ceremony dresses, jewelry, and expensive watches, people discuss laws while monthly pay close to Rp100 million fills the news. They can sing and dance too, which is their right." "" "Asep repairs shoes on the pedestrian path, then goes home to a small rented house in the crowded kampung behind the main road. That Friday was a harvest day because I brought five pairs and paid Rp150,000 before tip, food, and drinks. On rainy days, his wife said, it can be two or three pairs, perhaps Rp60,000. After rent, his daughter’s vocational school, and daily food, motorcycle fuel, how much could be left? " "" "Before finding Asep, I had been taken to a repair shop behind a parking garage. "" "A tukang bakso stood almost in front of Asep’s spot. When I asked where else I could repair shoes, he pointed me back to the shop I had just left. Later, Asep’s wife told me she often bought bakso from him. I do not know why he did not point me to Asep." "" "I went to Cibaduyut to repair shoes. I returned with five repaired pairs, spare parts taken on trust, a husband and wife beside a polluted road, and a fellow citizen who, from what I saw, lives below the poverty line." "" "After 81 years of independence, people like Asep and his wife are still left to survive on their belief in the afterlife, neighbors, the pavement, pollution, and the lesser economy.
2026-06-23 This is another field note in my search for the remaining goods in Indonesia, a country that still photographs well...
This is another field note in my search for the remaining goods in Indonesia, a country that still photographs well from above while people below keep finding ways to stay alive." "" "I entered a slum “gang” (alley) about 100 meters from one of Indonesia’s richest residential areas to cut my hair. I had gone once before. The haircut was good, but I remembered the neck, shoulder, and head massage more." "" "It was two in the afternoon, but daylight barely entered. This was not a street. No sidewalk, no lane, no walking space. One strip of concrete was shared by house doors, small shops, wet-market activity, children, drains, walls, and motorcycles." "" "Then the barbershop came into view: glass front, sliding door, white tiles, one chair, mirror with television, aircon, sound system, neon light, purifier, and barber pole outside. Before I stepped inside, the barber, whom I will call akang Cecep, asked me to wait. He wanted to clean the floor from the previous customer’s hair. I think he remembered that I was particular about cleanliness." "" "From two visits, I learned that he has worked around that same gang for fifteen years. Before this shop, he lived in a small house twenty meters away and used the front room as his barber place. Later, he rented a small room nearby, about two by three-and-a-half meters." "" "He no longer lives inside the gang. He said it was not healthy for raising a family, and at night it became scarier. He now lives somewhere in North Jakarta. His daughter lives with her grandmother in Garut and has just finished junior high school." "" "He spoke about one MBG package his daughter once received: three ubi Cilembu, two lychees, two quail eggs, and a small carton of sweetened milk. She took only the lychees and sweet potatoes, then ate lunch cooked by her grandmother. “Would you feed your daughter with this? No parent with dignity would do that. I may look simple, but I will provide the best for my child.”" "" "I was careful not to turn the barber chair into a political stage. He did not need me to recruit his anger into my argument. I remembered Eugene Rogan’s history of the Arabs, where an Ottoman barber recorded public life from the conversations inside his shop." "" "Kang Cecep has regulars from Brazil, Germany, and Taiwan. I asked whether he charges foreigners more. He said no. A local adult may pay Rp30,000, a child less. A stranger like me pays Rp40,000. Even twenty customers at Rp30,000 is Rp600,000 in gross cash before costs. For many guru honorer, it is a monthly honorarium. " "" "This is what I call the lesser economy. People stay low, work legally, avoid spectacle, and produce daily cash through skill: rent, electricity, cleanliness, repeat customers, pricing, and trust. He is already producing the economy, one haircut, one shoulder massage, one swept floor at a time." "" "I found another remaining good. Again from the precarious, I mean a barber who keeps his floor clean, charges properly, and refuses to feed his child without dignity.

2026-06-22 Under a tree in Menteng, a man was roasting jadah (yakimochi in Japanese) on his cart. I sat with him...
Under a tree in Menteng, a man was roasting jadah (yakimochi in Japanese) on his cart. I sat with him for about half an hour, eating there and carrying some home. He spoke gently, greeted me easily, and talked about his village in Tasikmalaya without bitterness." "" "He described his daily route through the neighborhood, and from the places he named I estimated it at roughly ten kilometers, perhaps more on some days. His jadah, roasted rice cake, is sold for Rp4,000 a piece. If he sells one hundred pieces, that is already a good day. I do not know his exact margin, but the point is clear enough: many hours on the street, a long route, and a life carried by small transactions. Perhaps this is our most efficient laissez-faire policy, to leave precarious people alone until their survival becomes scenery." "" "Afterward, the photograph reminded me of old colonial-era images of peddlers: men carrying food through the street, selling mostly to pribumi buyers who were themselves living under colonial rule, working for employers, households, offices, or whoever controlled daily wages. The paying customer was there then, and is still there now. The flag changed, and so did the road, clothing, and buyers. Yet the method of earning a day still feels painfully familiar." "" "Later I saw a sign that said Budayakan 5S: Senyum, Salam, Sapa, Sopan, Santun. Smile, greet, say hello, be courteous, be polite. Indonesia prints this moral instruction on walls, in schools, in offices, and in public places. Under that tree, I saw it without the poster: a man who smiled, greeted, spoke gently, and still carried almost all the risk of his own livelihood." "" "This is where my search for Indonesia’s remaining goods becomes uncomfortable. The poor should not be used as symbols of national optimism. I do not worship poverty. Peddlers like him were materially poor under colonial rule, and many remain materially exposed eighty years after independence. The irony is not that they still survive. The irony is that we keep admiring their survival while asking too little about what independence has changed for this layer of people." "" "Then I asked about Indonesia’s pride and venerated 310 trillion rupiahs program, “MBG”. His criticism came as a father’s inspection of food. He said he was proud his children did not eat it. Food like that, he said, would be given to chicken at home. He could count the beans. The egg was partial. Milk, when present, was too sweet. He had heard the price was around Rp15,000, and he could not see Rp15,000 of nutrition in the box." "" "When I left, he was still roasting jadah and greeting the next buyer. That was the good I found: the discipline to keep earning, the courtesy to keep greeting, and the clarity to judge a meal for children by beans, egg, and milk. I do not know how to celebrate that without also asking why, eighty years after independence, so much of Indonesian life still depends on the same old method: walk, sell, smile, return tomorrow.

A friend in Menteng, one of Jakarta’s most expensive old residential neighborhoods, sent this story this morning." "" "Rp341,000, about US$19, bought him a week of groceries from a house-to-house vegetable seller: bean sprouts, mushrooms, cabbage, kangkung, eggplant, small eggplant, bitter gourd, corn, cucumber, carrot, tofu, fish, salted gabus fish, one kilogram of eggs, two pieces of tempeh, bawang putih, bawang merah, chili, ginger, daun bawang, celery leaves, lemon for vegetables, one packet of sayur asam, and several other items. He did not buy them in a supermarket. He bought them from Mudin, pushing his cart from house to house." "" "Three weeks ago, he wrote that something must still work in this country. "" "He is trying to find something good in Indonesia without pretending he is not worried." "" "The supermarket he uses has not raised prices this year, yet this vendor remains roughly one-third cheaper. After Eid al-Fitr, the vendor admitted tempeh had gone up about 10 percent. Even then, the basket disturbed his assumptions." "" "He asked whether the vendor charged more because he sells in an elite residential area. The vendor said no. The price was the same as in other neighborhoods. Jakarta contains several price worlds. People can choose to live here almost as expensively as in Singapore, and many do. Yet the same city also allows another choice: a wealthier household can buy Rp341,000 for the week from the cart, while a more modest household may buy Rp30,000 for the day from the same seller, at the same price, only in smaller volume. The cart is shared. The daily arithmetic is not." "" "This does not prove food is cheap everywhere. Remote areas face different costs: distance, logistics, distribution, and smaller transaction volume. Jakarta is the center, which is why a house-to-house vendor can still sell competitively even in one of the country’s most expensive areas." "" "There is a small laissez-faire in this scene: the seller comes, the household chooses, and the price is spoken directly at the gate, outside the lighting and packaging of high-end retail." "" "His story does not prove that Indonesia is fine. It only gives one sentence some evidence: yes, there is still something good in Indonesia, as long as people do not let fear become the only way they read the country.
2026-06-20 I brought Joshua Lumbantobing, Stefen Sutandi and Geraldus Lumi to meet Dr. Norman Yanuar yesterday because I wanted them to...
I brought Joshua Lumbantobing, Stefen Sutandi and Geraldus Lumi to meet Dr. Norman Yanuar yesterday because I wanted them to hear how transferable skill is formed: disciplined execution under field conditions, patience, and work repeated under consequence before anyone knows how to name it." "" "Many students now reach their first job with thirty or forty lines of “experience,” before they have carried one task with real consequence. On LinkedIn, experience is easy to declare. Volunteer roles, artificial internships, committee titles, short programs, and projects with impressive names can fill a profile before the first hard test of work. I do not blame the students entirely. Recruitment platforms reward early accumulation and mislead them into thinking more listed experience means stronger proof of readiness. But a job-matching platform is also a disqualification machine. Its first task is to cut a large pool before anyone has seen the work (see comment section). " "" "Norman and I were sitting at the same table, two engineers who entered SLB (Schlumberger) through the same kind of first gate. I joined in 1994. He joined in 2006. Different decades, same beginning: a detailed CV, screening, interviews, and an institution willing to accept us on paper before either of us had proven anything in the field. The paper opened the gate. It did not yet say whether we could execute." "" "Norman said, without ceremony, that almost none of the roles he held after Schlumberger came from an application he sent. People who had watched him work recommended him to other people who needed someone like him. My own record reads much the same. The people who hired me afterward had usually watched me work in the field themselves, or heard about it directly from someone who had. Most had been my bosses at Schlumberger Geco-Prakla segment first." "" "The transferable skill was the discipline of execution under field conditions. It meant dirty hands, incomplete data, equipment that did not wait for a perfect plan, and repetition under conditions where mistakes had consequences. Repetition did the work that no certificate, volunteer title, short program, or self-declared LinkedIn experience could do. It turned activity into judgment, and judgment into a story other people were willing to carry." "" "Only after the first real test of work does the field begin to separate participation from competence, and declared experience from a record other people are willing to stand behind. " "" "At the table yesterday, Norman was describing the years when the work had no profile line yet. It had supervisors, field operators, mechanics, field service managers, clients, and other witnesses who had seen him execute with discipline before anyone called it a transferable.
2026-06-20 A dear friend shared with me his concerns which is precise: BI-Rate up 25 bps again. 100 bps in a...
A dear friend shared with me his concerns which is precise: BI-Rate up 25 bps again. 100 bps in a month. Possibly 6.0 to 6.25 percent by year-end. Lending tightening. SMEs losing financing access. NPL risk building. Then came the line that mattered: this is not simply about whether USD/IDR is “safe.” The harder concern is how many middle-income households slide, and whether the government keeps doing what it is doing." "" "He is half right. The half he is missing is the part Indonesia keeps postponing." "" "However, he is still anchored to the rate itself, even while saying the rate is not the point. Basis points, trajectory, year-end forecast. Those numbers matter, but they are not where the signal begins. Rp18,000, Rp20,000, Rp22,000. The number tells less than the conditions underneath it. " "" "Household pressure and social strain may come later, but they are late-stage evidence of work that should have been done long before the exchange rate made everyone nervous." "" "Supply chains do not become important because the rupiah weakens. Export competitiveness does not become necessary because USD/IDR crosses a frightening number. Logistics, productive financing, and firm-level competitiveness are not emergency tasks. Indonesia needed them at Rp14,000, needed them at Rp16,000, and still needs them now. The weak rupiah does not create the homework. It exposes how much of it was left unfinished." "" "That is why the blaming culture is so dangerous. It gives the public a visible object to attack: BI-Rate, the rupiah, Bank Indonesia, the monthly decision. Public figures can frighten the lambs more easily by pointing to the alarm than by admitting how long the upstream work has been delayed. An alarm is uncomfortable because it makes noise. It is also useful because it tells you where something has already gone wrong." "" "BI can manage liquidity, defend stability, and respond to pressure. It cannot build export capacity, shorten logistics chains, make firms more competitive, or ensure financing reaches producers instead of being rationed by panic. Those tasks sit elsewhere in government and in the long discipline of economic management. When that distinction disappears, every rate decision becomes a national drama, and every structural failure gets renamed as a monetary crisis." "" "My friend’s forecast may still come true. More middle-income erosion. More SME stress. More visible strain in household budgets. But that would not prove that the rate was the main event. It would prove that Indonesia kept treating the alarm as the crisis while the unfinished work stayed in the same place." "" "Thanks Kak Iman Pribadi for inspiring me to write this post.

2026-06-16 After one semester, my EL-4062 co-learners no longer worship the product. That makes me proud. It also shows me what entrepreneurship education still cannot rush.
After one semester, my EL-4062 co-learners no longer worship the product. That makes me proud. It also shows me what entrepreneurship education still cannot rush." "" "They know the Primary Market Research doctrine. They interview, build personas, and ask about users, buyers, pains, and markets. They have moved beyond the old habit of starting with product specification and then looking for people to agree with it." "" "Still, I saw the same problem in several final decks. The workflow was already drawn. The buying unit was already named. The market number was already calculated. The high-level specification was already waiting on the slide. But the field evidence underneath still felt too thin. I still wanted to ask: who exactly had been interviewed? The persona, the buyer, the technical user, the approver, the budget holder, or someone who understood only one part of the workflow? Who confirmed the buying unit? Who confirmed the Target Addressable Market? Who said the pain was felt in this form?" "" "Another team heard something more tempting. A respondent asked, “When will you launch?” That sounds close to validation. But what did the sentence mean inside the customer’s world? Willingness to pay, permission to test, curiosity, politeness, internal urgency, budget ownership, or encouragement?" "" "An old ethnography note gave me the language for this discomfort. ETIC is the researcher’s view. EMIC is the respondent’s view. The note did not begin with asking. It began with entering the field, observing, and taking notes before asking anything - PMR! That order matters because it delays judgment." "" "For me, ETIC is sense-making. It is the helicopter view that allows a founder to understand the industry widely enough: who uses, who pays, who blocks adoption, what regulation shapes behavior, what budgets are real, and why a complaint does not automatically become a market. Without ETIC, students may collect interviews and still return with fragments." "" "EMIC is slower. In entrepreneurship language, people often say founders must see from the customer’s lens. Anthropology makes that instruction harder. EMIC is closer to seeing from behind the back of the customer’s neck, close enough to follow what they see, what they ignore, what they tolerate, and what they no longer explain because it has become ordinary." "" "For my fellow anthropologists and ethnographers, this may sound familiar. Entrepreneurship calls it Primary Market Research. The discipline underneath is older: stay with the respondent’s world long enough before converting it into category, market, specification, or evidence." "" "My students are already listening better than many product-first founders. The unfinished work is learning when not to translate too quickly." "" "Ria Yustitia Winartha Ivan Wirawan Poggy Macello Gultom Moh. 2026-06-08 The more I looked at a Ficus ecosystem at Singapore Botanic Gardens, the harder it was to accept the claim that a palm estate is a forest. From a distance, it looked like one old tree.
The more I looked at a Ficus ecosystem at Singapore Botanic Gardens, the harder it was to accept the claim that a palm estate is a forest." "" "From a distance, it looked like one old tree. A closer view was less tidy. Roots came down from above. Some had thickened into pillars. What looked like a trunk from the ground was actually a network of roots. Ferns grew around the base. Smaller plants lived in the shade. The lower part looked less like a trunk and more like a small forest standing on itself." "" "The living mass included Ficus kurzii, or Burmese Banyan, and Ficus kerkhoveni, or Johor Fig. A fig seed may be dropped by an animal high in another tree. The young fig begins there, sends roots downward, reaches the soil, then grows faster. The roots thicken. The canopy expands. The host tree first gives it height. Later, the host may be covered and weakened." "" "The fig fruit is a syconium, a hollow structure with tiny flowers inside. Ficus depends on specialised fig wasps for pollination. Birds feed on the ripe syconia. Around one tree, there are host trees, fig, animal-dropped seeds, aerial roots, wasps, birds, ferns, shade plants, old growth and new growth." "" "That is why the phrase “palm estate as forest” sounds careless. A palm estate may have rows of trees. But rows are not an ecosystem. Rows do not replace host trees, aerial roots, syconia, fig wasps, birds, ferns, shade, soil memory and age." "" "A short-termist country did not plant the old forests now being cut for estates. The damage is then passed to rivers, soil, wildlife, and the next generation." "" "From an anthropological point of view, the first task is not to insult culture. I found this faint inscription carved into a sundial at Singapore Botanic Gardens: “𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂 𝘀𝗲𝗲𝗸𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝗮 𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗱𝗼𝘄.” I had walked past that sundial many times without reading it properly, although my home is seven minutes away on foot." "" "The white-on-white carving was difficult to read. I had to circle around the sundial, taking video three or four times, before the sentence became clear. Only then did I begin to question what I had been seeking in life, and whether I had been chasing the thing itself, or only its shadow." "" "From there, I contemplated my own life. A humbling process of earning a PhD after two decades in energy, failing as an entrepreneur and investor, then becoming a teacher two years after leaving corporate life at 47. I am grateful, but these are merely shadows. That is epistemology for me." "" "Once I ask how I know, I cannot avoid asking what is real beneath the visible sign, especially among people still forming judgment. A junior writer may chase a polished paragraph without asking whether the content has depth. A student may chase the grade without asking whether the subject has changed his way of seeing. An early graduate may chase the first respectable title without asking what kind of work is forming him. A junior worker may chase approval from the room and mistake it for accomplishment. None of these are automatically wrong. But they may also be only shadows. Ontology is not abstract when a person needs to know why he is here, because knowing why you are here gives you an anchor in eternity." "" "Even knowing what is real does not settle the matter, because the way a person chases something reveals the value system already operating inside him. Axiology becomes uncomfortable here because it exposes moral struggle. A young writer who chases visibility may compromise the thinking itself, writing not because the content has become true enough, but because fame, influence, or paid instruction demands output. A student who chases only marks may outsource his brain to AI and still call it learning, although he no longer knows what he has understood. A worker who chases approval may become an apple polisher, losing integrity and dignity." "" "It is easier said than done to change a person’s axiology, because the seed of moral formation starts early. Perhaps from three to seven years old, a child already learns what gets praised, compared, hurried, and hidden. Later, when the child becomes a student, worker, or writer, the chase may look adult, but part of him still carries what was formed between the ages of three and seven. In my reading of neuroscience, as much as 45% of adult patterns may come from that early formation." "" "If the universe was formed across billions of years, and eternity is allowed into our imagination, meaning belongs to a longer horizon." "" "So, what are we chasing?" "" "A life that repairs the self and becomes useful beyond the self, or only its shadow?

"" "He may understand why this happens. Society is wired collectively, and status often functions as a practical shortcut. Understanding the mechanism does not make the conversation less lonely." " "" "The session was built on his 2025 HBR Prize wining article⁽*⁾ with Prof. Bharat Anand. I had read it last year. I thought I knew what was coming." "" "The first thing Wu did was place AI inside Porter’s five forces framework, not as a technology trend sitting alongside strategy, but as a force operating directly on market attractiveness and competitive position. I have taught Porter’s framework for years. Until that session, I had never heard anyone frame AI adoption as a Porter-level strategic commitment." "" "The second shift came from a diagram I recognized as soon as it appeared: worth to customer at the top, cost to supplier at the bottom, price between them, and value created as the span. What I had not seen before was AI mapped onto it with this precision. AI raises the top line and lowers the bottom line, so the span widens. But a wider span does not mean more capture. Capture depends on where price sits relative to both moving lines, and whether competitors are moving them faster." "" "The third recognition came when Wu turned to the organisation chart. Wu and Anand’s quadrant plots every organisational task on two axes: cost of errors and type of knowledge required. Where error cost is low and knowledge is explicit, deploy now. Where stakes are high and judgment is tacit, the human stays at the centre. Specific roles, specific quadrants, specific verdicts about who stays and who does not." "" "The fourth moment inverted something I had held for years. Most AI conversations I sit in are about outputs: better text, better summaries, better answers. Wu’s argument ran the other way. In the section on access, he argued that the deeper change is in how intelligence is accessed. Gen AI changes the input to software more than the output from software. More people can now use more computing power for more specialised purposes. That is not just a productivity shift. It changes who can ask questions, who can use tools, and who gets to turn knowledge into action." "" "The fifth was confirmation of something I have believed for a long time, now inside a rigorous framework. An excellent data pipeline matters. Every asset has to be understood as data. "" "From there, he shifted to the harder question of who holds technology: lithography, semiconductors, Fairchild, Taiwan, chip production, and the strategic exposure seen around current war fronts, including Ukraine and Iran." "" "That was not a random tour of world affairs. It was a demonstration of how a senior industry leader reads power before reading markets." 2026-03-24 Failure in professional communication is not just a missed opportunity; it is...
Failure in professional communication is not just a missed opportunity; it is a fundamental strategic risk. Patrick Winston famously asserted that success is determined by the ability to speak, the ability to write, and the quality of ideas, in that order. The blunt reality is that nobody cares what ideas you have if you cannot articulate them. To enter the modern workforce without these skills is analogous to a soldier entering battle without a weapon (Winston in Tambun, 2024)." "" "The Week 6 Class Storytelling Challenge is the bridge we have engineered to move students from conscious incompetence to conscious competence. In the Indonesian context, this is a vital intervention for navigating cultural barriers such as isin, wedi, and sungkan—shame, fear, and the hesitation to speak out (Geertz, 1961 in Tambun, 2024). We use the Disciplined Storytelling framework to help students move beyond the myth of simple authenticity and toward rigorous, structured mastery (Tambun, 2024)." "" "We explicitly apply the What, But, Then framework from The Undying Art of Storytelling to navigate this transition:" "" "The What defines the universality of storytelling. It is built into the human plan, serving as the foundational compass of civilization. Long before stories were codified into text, they were shared around bonfires in the desert to guide moral and social landscapes (Tambun, 2023)." "" "The But represents the modern eclipse of this art. Our analytical minds and digital hoards of empirical data have created a tyranny of information overload. We are voracious collectors of facts, yet we often lose the human connection and wisdom that only narrative can provide (Tambun, 2023)." "" "The Then is the resolution. Our students are the ones reviving this ancient art on the digital stage. Through disciplined practice, they are adapting storytelling to ensure wisdom is not lost in a world of data (Tambun, 2023)." "" "The strategic linchpin here is the connection between academic value and lived experience. Larry McEnerney argues that professional writing is not about communicating ideas, but about fundamentally changing the reader’s ideas (McEnerney, 2014 in Tambun, 2024). To achieve this, we use Thick Description—a concept from Clifford Geertz—as the specific tool to capture detailed, nuanced meanings that make the unseen palpable." "" "This practice is more than a soft skill; it is a mechanism for cognitive resilience. " "" "Engaging in the creative complexity of Thick Description stimulates the prefrontal cortex and promotes neuroplasticity, strengthening the neural pathways required for higher-order reasoning and problem-solving. In a data-driven world, narrative is a survival necessity. Mastery of these skills is what allows a professional to define, confirm, and convey meaning with authority." "" "Asyendita Dyah Desi Utami PhD; Prof. Y Andi Trisyono PhD PNU20242206 UGM" "https://lnkd.in/gH7a2-7i

I used to think the question was whether one posts too much. Now I think THE Question instead is “What is one asking from the reader?”" "" "I post often because writing helps me think. A five-star hotel breakfast in Singapore gave me an ethnographic lesson before 8 a.m." "" "The hot-food station looked elegant. Heavy glass lids. Curved wooden handles. Clean design." Hold the heavy lid with one hand, scoop food with the other, then close it again awkwardly." "" "Then a chef stepped in and said, firmly, “Let me teach you.”" "" "That sentence caught my attention, not because it was shocking, but because it revealed so much in one moment." "" "The chef may not have meant disrespect. In many Chinese Singaporean settings, people can sound sharp, loud, or stern without actually being angry. Directness can be normal. "" "𝐈𝐟 𝐚 𝐟𝐢𝐯𝐞-𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫 𝐛𝐮𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐭 𝐫𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐥𝐢𝐝 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲, 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐦 𝐢𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐠𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭. 𝐈𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧" "" "And once design fails, tone matters even more." People have asked why I still prefer Parahyangan and why I do not enjoy taking the newer fast train from Halim." "" "The answer is personal and based on experience. It is not a blanket judgment. This post is not about travel options. It is about whether a product is designed as a whole journey, or only as a spectacle." "" "On paper, the newer high-speed option should feel superior. "" "What stood out from the feedback of a few friends who accompanied me to Bandung, including foreigners with experience using trains in Japan, China, and Europe, was how fragmented the journey felt in both directions. The return from Bandung to Jakarta simply made that weakness more visible." "" "The promised half-hour logic began to blur the moment the real sequence started. Even on the way from Jakarta to Bandung, the journey already felt broken by transfer points, platform movement, and weak continuity. But from Bandung to Jakarta, it became harder to ignore: long waiting in a packed hall, then the platform bridge, then security screening, then more waiting, then another platform, then waiting again before the fast-train leg itself." "" "In Bandung, the waiting could take 20 minutes, 40 minutes, sometimes close to an hour, depending on when the passenger arrived at the station. The hall was often packed, with little real distinction in the waiting experience between first-class passengers and the rest. For some of them, it felt less like a premium intercity journey and more like sitting in an overcrowded 1970s hospital waiting room." "" "From the entrepreneurship framework I teach, the question is whether, for the chosen segment, we deliver the whole product. Here, the answer is no. Fast first, then long waiting, then a super slow commuter leg, then more waiting, is not the whole product. It is a broken end-to-end experience." "" "That is why this feels larger than transport." "" "My doctoral research examines performative culture in Indonesia, the habit of celebrating what looks advanced, what photographs well, and what signals prestige, even when the substance underneath remains weak. "" "Parahyangan by PT Kereta Api Indonesia (Persero) gives me the opposite feeling. It is slower, but it is whole product. it also lets me feel something that still gives hope in Indonesia: institutional improvement that can actually be experienced." "" "This is no longer just about one train versus another." "" "For some of my friends, this fast train reflects the culture of yang penting ada, yang penting keren, not a culture that seriously solves the real problem from start to finish. And history has shown for centuries that this kind of mindset does not help a country progress in a serious and lasting way.

"" "Not PMR as a ritual. Not PMR as a checkbox. Not PMR as students asking polite questions and then rushing back to their slides. PMR is inquiry mode. It is disciplined listening. It is ethnographic immersion. It is entering the field without trying to look smart too early." "" "If we put garbage PMR in, we get garbage results out. That is why PMR is not small talk, and not selling. It is inquiry mode, collecting data points to be analyzed, and it is learned by doing." "" "So this year I changed one thing. I helped bring them into direct contact with a real operator, so the framework would not remain abstract. " "" "I did not only ask them to go into the field. I helped bring the field closer to them. "" "We also brought in alumni and startup founders working in bank-related and AI-related spaces." "" "The students did not stop at broad answers. They asked for sequence, clarification, and consequence. When risk management was discussed, they pinned it down into four handling steps: identify, measure, monitor, and mitigate." "" "The session also surfaced eight major risks discussed in the conversation: credit, operational, reputational, market, liquidity, compliance, legal, and external risk." "" "A professional lesson, observed up close." "" "Late last year, a senior practitioner was approached by a professional contact with a request. The task was to design an AI module to accelerate sustainability analysis, hundreds companies, 7 dozens of criteria, producing a composite score. Historically, the same work had been done manually for years, involving large teams and long cycles." "" "An NDA was signed. Work began." "" "On 16 December 2025, the question of commercial terms was explicitly raised. The response was that there would be none. The engagement was described as trust-based. A handshake. An NDA. That was considered sufficient." "" "Despite discomfort, the work continued." "" "In January, urgency escalated. Messages arrived asking to speed up, to expedite, to prioritize. Instructions came directly from the requesting party. Over the following month, the delivery team worked extended hours to complete the module. On 24 February 2026, the system was delivered and demonstrated. The feedback was positive. The team on the receiving side expressed satisfaction." "" "Only after delivery did the discussion return to compensation. The response was unexpected. Payment could not be made. Governance would not allow it. One justification offered was that payment had never been explicitly requested. Another was that the engagement was framed as a “test,” and tests, by definition, were unpaid." "" "This raised a basic question. Who commissions months of professional work, under time pressure, with repeated instructions to expedite, while assuming there is no compensation? The assumption on the delivery side had always been that the work would be paid, given the scope, the hours, and the energy involved, especially after commercial terms had been raised earlier." "" "There was no confrontation. What remained was unease. Not mainly about money, but about responsibility toward the team who worked in good faith, trusting that normal professional norms still applied." "" "This is not a story about intent or character. It is about structure." "" "NDAs protect information, not labor." "Urgency does not replace agreement." "Calling something a “test” after delivery does not retroactively change the nature of the work." "" "The lesson is old, obvious, and still regularly ignored." "Commercial terms must be declared upfront, clearly, and in writing. Not to protect egos, but to protect the people whose time and effort are being committed." "" "Anything else leaves too much to assumption. And assumption is not governance.

AI Citation Tools, ChatGPT, and the Discipline of Theory-Tiered Review" "" "A generic email offering a 50% discount made me think again about scite.ai. I had subscribed once, during my first semester, and later chose to stop. The decision was not because the tool failed, but because I changed how I wanted to work. I deliberately chose a theory-tiered literature review. Grand theories first, then middle-range theories, then low-range and empirical extensions. Fewer papers, read fully and slowly. Not keyword expansion. Not citation-density chasing." "" "There was also a more uncomfortable reason. I noticed that the convenience of the tool made it possible to cite faster than I could read. The citations were real, but my understanding was thinner than my own standard. That felt like betraying myself. So I stopped." "" "The discount brings the question back. Not whether scite.ai is useful, but what kind of “AI” it actually is, how it differs from large language models in general, and whether such tools belong in the workflow at all." "" "scite.ai is not a single intelligence. It is a layered pipeline. Retrieval widens the search space. Citation context extraction pulls the actual citing sentences. Classification labels citations as supporting, contradicting, or mentioning. This is its real strength, because it breaks the lazy habit of equating citation count with consensus. A synthesis layer now sits on top, producing paragraphs dense with citations using an LLM. That layer rewrites and compresses. It does not judge quality, resolve disagreement, or assess applicability." "" "General-purpose language models, including ChatGPT developed by OpenAI, fail differently. Their characteristic failure mode is fluent fabrication. Hallucination exists inherently, even at their best. The language can sound careful, nuanced, and persuasive while being weakly grounded or not grounded at all. The confidence comes from fluency, not evidence." "" "Citation-driven systems fail through fluent legitimacy. The prose feels solid because the citations are real. Yet weak studies, context mismatches, unresolved disagreements, and unread material can be smoothed into summaries that look authoritative. Claims are not mistaken for discoveries simply because they appear frequently." "" "Neither replaces the actual work. Reading papers end-to-end. Evaluating methods and assumptions. Knowing whether findings travel across contexts. Synthesising positions rather than assembling references. That work stays human." "" "If scite.ai is used after theory is fixed and after papers are genuinely read, as a mapping tool, it can help. If it is used as a shortcut to citation-dense prose, it recreates the same problem that made me stop before." "" "Tambun, A. R. Y. T., Yudoko, G., & Aldianto, L. (2024). "" "A decision can be expressed as:" "D = g(P, J)" "and a firm minimizes the cost of achieving decision quality:" "C = pP·P + pJ·J" "" "When pP ↓, the optimal mix shifts: more prediction is used; substitutes fall; complementary inputs rise. This aligns with standard comparative statics. It mirrors earlier economic shocks—when computing or storage became cheap, firms redesigned production around the new cost structure." "" "Prediction (P) and judgment (J) act as complementary inputs when:" "∂²g / (∂P ∂J) > 0" "" "When prediction improves, the marginal value of judgment rises. When judgment is clearer, the payoff from prediction rises. AI does not replace judgment; both inputs complement each other inside the decision loop." "" "Cheap prediction reshapes unit economics. Forecast-driven processes—inventory, underwriting, triage, routing—must be rebuilt. As prediction becomes abundant, the constraint moves to setting thresholds, acceptable risk, escalation rules, and defining “good enough.” Errors also scale because automated prediction repeats its mistake across the system. Without explicit judgment policies, automation amplifies ambiguity." "" "The value of complementary inputs rises: clean data, domain expertise, situational awareness, intervention capability, and oversight. "" "So when students choose stability, the question is not “Why don’t they dare?” A more honest question is: “What did history teach their families about where security comes from?” If an office with a tiny salary but wide informal privileges was the safest livelihood for generations, then the hesitation toward entrepreneurship today makes sense." Published in SSRN (thanks) my first autoethnography paper “We Built It Anyway: Autoethnographic Reflections on Innovation, Risk, and Institutional Apathy” (September 28, 2024). Available at : https://lnkd.in/g-Xq_zpE or https://lnkd.in/gzFwJqk4" "" "" "Abstract" "The aim of this article is to examine what occurs when a practitioner-academic launches an innovation and entrepreneurship program within a Southeast Asian university that neither requested nor rewarded such work. Despite widespread promotion of entrepreneurial education, this study shows that institutional transformation depends not on imported models but on cultural fit. The importance of this inquiry lies in exposing how postcolonial institutional culturesrooted in hierarchy, compliance, and certification-undermine pedagogies built on autonomy, experimentation, and risk. Although policy discourse frames innovation as universally desirable, its deployment into unreceptive environments produces contradiction rather than change. The urgency of this intervention arises from intensifying regional pressure on universities to "entrepreneurialize" without confronting the logics that structure rejection. Using critical autoethnography, the author reflects on seven years of program-building in a system where innovation was tolerated but not absorbed. Still, student engagement surged when given space to practice rather than perform. Yet the institution's immune response-through bureaucratic friction and evaluative silence-revealed what remains unspeakable in metrics-driven reform. Culture, in this context, does not merely constrain; it adjudicates what counts as knowledge, initiative, and legitimacy. Whereas many studies locate innovation failure in flawed design or weak leadership, this article argues that culture is the decisive mechanism shaping whether innovation can take root. By rendering this mechanism visible, the article contributes to autoethnographic scholarship on entrepreneurship education, critical pedagogy, and higher education reform in postcolonial contexts." "" "Keywords: Autoethnography, Institutional Culture, Entrepreneurship Education, Postcolonial Higher Education, Innovation Resistance" "" "https://lnkd.in/gKpHuDT6

"" "Born in 1981, he passed sixth grade but couldn’t get his certificate because his dues were unpaid. So he left Jatinom, took a bus to Prambanan, then a yellow KUBOTA to Terban Terminal. "" "He was only a boy, too small to reach the pedals, but he worked a few weeks and earned enough to pay the debt. He got his certificate and kept working, proud to earn his own way." "" "In the sleeper train carrying me back to Jakarta tonight, I think of him." "" "People like him keep this nation standing. They work, survive, and take pride in what they do. Dignity comes from effort, not titles — and never from “gratis.”" "" "It is a pity, and I cannot celebrate it. " "" "However, record shows that punishment often comes before guidance. The law does protects, but its practice too often destroys. "" "In 2016, a television assembler in Karanganyar was sentenced for producing non-SNI units under Law No. 3/2014 on Industry [1]. "" "In 2019, a village head in Aceh Utara distributing the high-yield rice seed “IF8” was detained under Law No. 12/1992 on Crop Cultivation [2] and freed only after public protest." "" "Between 2016 and 2025, jamu producers in Cilacap were raided for lacking BPOM permits under Law No. 36/2009 on Health [3]; many were later invited into the state “Jamu Aman” coaching program." "" "In 2025, Alsintan, an agricultural-machine firm in Madiun built hundreds of combine harvesters after a political promise that never became a contract. Unable to pay, it was declared in arrears; its equipment was seized and auctioned by the tax office."
