Entrepreneurship, Innovation, & Growth Journal, Vol. 20, No. 117: October 24, 2025 https://lnkd.in/gbnwcksx or https://lnkd.in/gBnRkt4j" "" "Abstract" "Retention in entrepreneurship education is often undermined by reliance on passive instructional strategies, resulting in rapid knowledge decay. The aim of this research is to quantitatively demonstrate that one model of pedagogical intervention achieves significantly higher retention than others within university-based entrepreneurship accelerators. This research is important because institutions often adopt instructional approaches without rigorous evidence of their long-term effectiveness. A simulation model grounded in Ebbinghaus’ Forgetting Curve was developed to compare seven pedagogical interventions over a 14-week semester. The model’s structure was informed by insights drawn from extensive instructional experience across 17 course executions since 2019. Results reveal that interventions integrating bootcamps, weekly experiential assignments, mentoring, and customer engagement sustain retention rates up to 49.29%, while passive methods such as quizzes and midterms result in only 2.48%. These findings offer a practical foundation for designing entrepreneurship curricula that prioritize long-term knowledge retention." 2025-10-13 Theory-Tiered Literature Review: A Pragmatist Method for Structuring Research Design in En...
Theory-Tiered Literature Review: A Pragmatist Method for Structuring Research Design in Entrepreneurial Ecosystem Studies (July 22, 2024). Available at SSRN: https://lnkd.in/ggnm4r8f or https://lnkd.in/gQAj6mni" "" "Abstract" "This article aims to address a persistent limitation in management literature reviews: despite becoming more transparent and structured, they remain constrained in their ability to advance theory. Systematic reviews enhance reproducibility but often privilege completeness over conceptual clarity. State-of-the-art reviews highlight novelty yet neglect continuity with foundational theories. Narrative reviews allow interpretive breadth although they lack replicability and analytic integration. This limitation is important because it leaves the field with descriptive catalogues rather than theoretical architectures that enable cumulative knowledge. To overcome this gap, the article introduces the Theory-Tiered Literature Review (TTLR) as a methodological response. TTLR explicitly organizes theories across three levels of abstractiongrand, middle-range, and low-range-and embeds this tiering within a transparent five-stage pipeline: scoping, selection, tiered categorization, cross-theory synthesis, and framework development. In doing so, TTLR combines decision rules, audit loops, and reliability checks to preserve procedural discipline while ensuring vertical coherence across theoretical levels. The contribution of TTLR lies in what it enables reviews to deliver. Instead of descriptive taxonomies, reviews can generate design-ready frameworks that connect constructs genealogically and clarify how theories interact across tiers. Illustrated through entrepreneurship research, TTLR demonstrates how fragmented literatures can be transformed into integrative theoretical architectures. Thus, TTLR provides a reproducible, theory-informed approach that complements existing methodologies, directly answers calls for evaluative and agenda-setting synthesis, and strengthens the capacity of management research to build cumulative knowledge. " "Keywords: Theory-Tiered Literature Review (TTLR), Review Methodology, Tiered Theorizing, Theoretical Integration, Management Research Synthesis, Entrepreneurial Ecosystems
2025-10-13 Strategy and Innovation in AI Oversight: Fiduciary Duties of Banking Boards (August 24, 20...
Strategy and Innovation in AI Oversight: Fiduciary Duties of Banking Boards (August 24, 2025). Available at SSRN: https://lnkd.in/ghuE4WHs or https://lnkd.in/ggBNxuUZ" "Abstract" "Artificial intelligence is transforming Indonesian banking, yet rapid adoption without mature oversight exposes boards to fiduciary and strategic risk. The aims of this study are to clarify how independent commissioners can discharge fiduciary duties over AI and to provide a governance architecture that links statutory obligations to practical oversight mechanisms. The importance lies in preserving compliance, legitimacy, and trust in a sector where algorithmic opacity and fragmented guidance have left oversight ambiguous. This question is particularly important now, with the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (2024) and the Otoritas Jasa Keuangan AI Governance Roadmap (2025) raising expectations for board accountability. The method applies a literature review as methodology, combining a semi-systematic search (2011–2025) with doctrinal legal analysis of Indonesian statutes and international standards. The findings present a five-dimensional fiduciary oversight framework: (i) human judgment and transparency, (ii) legal and fiduciary duties, (iii) accountability and enforcement, (iv) societal and cultural fairness, and (v) institutional trust and legitimacy. Although AI is often framed as a source of competitive advantage, governance gaps erode fiduciary confidence and expose directors to liability. By contrast, the framework consolidates fragmented guidance into a diagnostic tool that connects duties with decision rights, assurance, and escalation. This study contributes by reframing AI supervision in Indonesian banking as a non-delegable fiduciary responsibility of the board, equipping commissioners with an actionable oversight model and outlining a research agenda on board capabilities and assurance effectiveness." "Keywords: AI Governance, Fiduciary Duty, Board Oversight, Indonesian Banking, Accountability, Fairness, Trust" "" "https://lnkd.in/gN_9akXY

Cognitive-coherence Dynamics and the Formal Modeling of Consciousness Resonance: A Theoretical Integration (December 02, 2023). Available at SSRN: https://lnkd.in/giCgnShS or https://lnkd.in/gYhSMj-J" "" "Abstract" "Cognitive science has long emphasized coherence in neural activity for attention and integration. However, despite this recognition, current frameworks do not explain how coherence scales into resonance—the patterned stability that marks conscious experience. The aim of this article is to develop a formal theoretical model that addresses this gap by framing resonance as structured coherence operating against multidimensional internal noise. Its importance lies in clarifying how attentional stability and conscious integration can be understood within a single framework, rather than through fragmented neural or contemplative accounts. Specifically, the model introduces a symbolic formalism in which resonance emerges as coherence is challenged by diverse internal fluctuations. Yet existing approaches remain siloed, either privileging neural synchrony without phenomenological grounding or emphasizing contemplative practices without formalization. By contrast, this model synthesizes cognitive neuroscience, information theory, and systems logic to represent resonance as an emergent process of clarity-driven dynamics amid cognitive, sensory, and emotional interference. Although conceptual, its consequences are concrete: without such a framework, attempts to link neural synchronization, attentional modulation, and conscious integration remain incomplete. This contribution is timely, as debates on neural coherence, contemplative practice, and consciousness are intensifying, creating an urgent need for a unifying framework to guide both empirical and philosophical inquiry." "" "Keywords: Spiritual Resonance, Cognitive-Spiritual Coherence, Internal Interference Modeling, Theoretical Consciousness Model, Neuro-philosophy of Meditation
2025-10-13 The Insult Cascade: Elite Contempt, Neural Fragility, and Collective Disorder (September 1...
The Insult Cascade: Elite Contempt, Neural Fragility, and Collective Disorder (September 10, 2025). " "" "published in SSRN POLITICAL BEHAVIOR: COGNITION, PSYCHOLOGY, & BEHAVIOR eJOURNAL Vol. 18, No.74: Oct 8, 2025 Available at SSRN: https://lnkd.in/gus3cfnM or https://lnkd.in/gX27Fwxs" "" "Abstract" "This article aims to develop the Insult Cascade Framework to explain how contempt expressed by elites can ignite disorder through interconnected neuro-social processes. The importance of this framework lies in its capacity to show that legitimacy does not only erode through long-term institutional decline but may collapse suddenly when publics are denied recognition. Yet existing theories of legitimacy, humiliation, and protest have remained siloed, rarely integrating neural mechanisms with structural deprivation. This article addresses that gap. Methodologically, it advances a conceptual synthesis that couples insights from neuroscience with theories of recognition, affect, and collective action. The framework specifies six layers through which insults escalate: contemptuous speech, neural disruption, emotional contagion, legitimacy collapse, the emergence of a nothing-to-lose mindset, and anarchic unrest. Two long-term vulnerabilities—deprivation of critical thinking and socio-economic deprivation—are identified as amplifiers that condition publics to be fragile and reactive. The findings show that what appears to be irrational protest is in fact a predictable outcome of impaired regulation interacting with systemic deprivation. The contribution of the Insult Cascade Framework is to clarify how words can trigger disorder with disproportionate speed, thereby linking neuroscience, protest psychology, and social theory in a unified account." "Keywords: Legitimacy, Humiliation, Contempt, Neuroscience, Emotional Contagion, Protest Dynamics

Constructing Entrepreneurial Identity in Indonesia: Cultural Constraints, Hybrid Pathways, and the Challenge for Multicultural Education  (March 04, 2025). " "" "Published in SSRN Entrepreneurship, Innovation, & Growth eJournal Vol 20, No. 112: Oct 13, 2025 Available at SSRN: https://lnkd.in/gR3V3Qft or https://lnkd.in/gYijjwYz" "" "Abstract" "Purpose – The aim of this study is to investigate how Indonesian undergraduates construct entrepreneurial identity through experiential entrepreneurship education. A critical gap was found: while canonical models of entrepreneurial intention presume universal applicability, they mispredict behavior in high uncertainty-avoidant and short-termist contexts. It must be now, since global entrepreneurship education is rapidly expanding into emerging economies, yet little is known about how cultural and familial obligations reshape identity work. Why important? Without accounting for these dynamics, curricula risk misreading hybrid or deferred careers as failure rather than culturally rational strategies." "Design/methodology/approach – A qualitative, interpretivist design was applied to three course-stage datasets: (1) pre-course entrepreneurial exposure survey; (2) mid-course career aspirations survey (n = 44); and (3) post-bootcamp reflections (n = 19 essays/LinkedIn posts). Six phases thematic analysis six phases, reinforced by triangulation, reflexivity, and peer debriefing. Evidence was structured in a Gioia framework." "Findings – Four identity layers emerged: (1) Identity formation (family obligations and cultural expectations); (2) Exposure & motivation (incubators, competitions, coursework); (3) Competency confidence (hands-on self-efficacy); and (4) Perceived integration (dual-track or delayed careers). Students consistently preferred hybrid or deferred pathways. Experiential learning raised capability, yet cultural obligations and risk norms redirected action into culturally coherent forms." "Practical implications – By specifying culture and family as moderators, the study explains why students rationally select dual-track or deferred pathways. Programs should design explicitly for such careers, equipping students with tools for staged commitments and identity-sensitive negotiation." "Originality/value –This study offers Four-Layer Entrepreneurial Identity Model." " "" "Published in Entrepreneurship, Innovation, & Growth eJournal by SSRN Vol. 20, No. 111: Oct 10, 2025 Available at SSRN: https://lnkd.in/gtekC83s or https://lnkd.in/g9hhBnXW" "" "This study aims to develop and validate a policy-relevant faculty evaluation model that aligns institutional assessment practices with differentiated academic roles and motivational factors, particularly for entrepreneurship-oriented educators in Indonesian higher education. The problem addressed is the persistent reliance on the uniform Tri Dharma framework, which fails to recognize and reward diverse academic contributions outside traditional teaching, research, and service, leading to demotivation among entrepreneurial faculty and misalignment with national innovation policies. The study employs Monte Carlo simulations to compare three evaluative approaches: equal-weighted roles, the existing Tri Dharma criteria, and a proposed model incorporating motivational theories (Vroom, Herzberg, Ryan & Deci) and vocational fit (Holland’s RIASEC typology). In an attempt to understand what happened in late August 2025 in Indonesia," "" "Tambun, A.R.Y. Toronata and Gatot Yudoko and Leo Aldianto, The Insult Cascade: Elite Contempt, Neural Fragility, and Collective Disorder (September 10, 2025). Journal for the Theory of Social Behaviour, Forthcoming, Available at SSRN: https://lnkd.in/ghnVsSHs or https://lnkd.in/g2s7aSU5" "" "Abstract" "This article aims to develop the Insult Cascade Framework to explain how contempt expressed by elites can ignite disorder through interconnected neuro-social processes. The importance of this framework lies in its capacity to show that legitimacy does not only erode through long-term institutional decline but may collapse suddenly when publics are denied recognition. Yet existing theories of legitimacy, humiliation, and protest have remained siloed, rarely integrating neural mechanisms with structural deprivation. This article addresses that gap. Methodologically, it advances a conceptual synthesis that couples insights from neuroscience with theories of recognition, affect, and collective action. The framework specifies six layers through which insults escalate: contemptuous speech, neural disruption, emotional contagion, legitimacy collapse, the emergence of a nothing-to-lose mindset, and anarchic unrest. Two long-term vulnerabilities—deprivation of critical thinking and socio-economic deprivation—are identified as amplifiers that condition publics to be fragile and reactive. The findings show that what appears to be irrational protest is in fact a predictable outcome of impaired regulation interacting with systemic deprivation. The contribution of the Insult Cascade Framework is to clarify how words can trigger disorder with disproportionate speed, thereby linking neuroscience, protest psychology, and social theory in a unified account." "" "Keywords: Legitimacy, Humiliation, Contempt, Neuroscience, Emotional Contagion, Protest Dynamics" "" "https://lnkd.in/gcaVmecX
2025-10-05 Early Chilhood topics: Teaching Children to Think in Systems"
Early Chilhood topics: Teaching Children to Think in Systems" "" "I’ve always wished children could learn early that life is not linear — that everything connects, that cause and effect take time, and that blaming anyone or anything never really helps. If kids could grow up seeing the world as a system — where every action loops back into something larger — they might learn patience, empathy, and responsibility in a deeper way." "" "I came to system dynamics late. I was 46 when I first learned it from Prof. John Sterman at MIT Sloan. But it changed how I think, how I teach, and how I understand frustration and hope. Most of us were trained from childhood to think linearly and to assign blame — that’s why learning this discipline feels like seeing the world through a clearer lens." "" "The truth is, nobody has yet cracked the code on teaching system dynamics to children. There are fragments — simulations, causal loop exercises, and stock-and-flow “bathtub” activities — but they’re designed for older students. The real challenge is helping children see feedback, delay, and interconnection without math or jargon¹." "" "Maybe it starts as a board game. Maybe later it becomes digital. Either way, this is the next frontier: helping children see loops, not lines." "" "These two books — System Dynamics Modelling with Vensim²  by Juan Martín García and Systems 1: An Introduction to Systems Thinking³ by Draper Kauffman — are helpful resources to convey the philosophy of system dynamics in a way that even children might one day grasp." "" "Notes: " "" "¹ There have been solid foundations to build on: Fishbanks and En-ROADS from the MIT group, The Systems Thinking Playbook by Sweeney and Meadows, and Habits of a Systems Thinker cards. For younger ages, these lessons can hide inside stories or toys — the same way Lego teaches engineering without calling it engineering. Imagine a simple game where marbles or tokens move through time, showing how small choices accumulate, and how cooperation matters more than competition." The influencer in the clip spoke about ethanol fuel blends, with a disclaimer that she only reads from Google and isn’t an expert. Her intent was to spark curiosity, but the mix of non-expert status + public reach risks turning fragments into false certainty — the precise danger Mark Twain described: “It ain’t what you don’t know that gets you into trouble. It’s what you know for sure that just ain’t so.” This analysis applies to me too. " "" "𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹? 𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 3 𝗼𝗳 𝟲." "" "Analysis (why Level 3):" "•The influencer acknowledged not being an expert, which shows some honesty. But posting anyway, without stronger caveats, still prioritizes appearing helpful and gaining approval (Stage 3 🤞 Approval) over accuracy." "•A Stage 4 👍 Duty approach would require checking facts, citing standards, or pointing to expert sources." "•A Stage 5–6 approach would both encourage critical thinking and stress humility: “Quick reading gives a starting point, but it does not make anyone an expert. Always take early knowledge with grain and salt.”" "•The Twain insight applies: Not yet knowing keeps a person searching, but half-knowing with confidence makes them stop searching and mislead others." "" "𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘁’𝘀 𝟰 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗯𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻:" "👆 Moral Sensitivity – See it: Saw people’s curiosity about fuel and science." "☝ Moral Judgment – Decide it: Judged that a disclaimer (“not an expert, just Google”) made it safe to share." "🤲 Moral Motivation – Want it: Wanted to appear encouraging and helpful, but without full responsibility." "✊ Moral Character – Do it: Shared anyway, without the key humility caveat that online reading must be taken “with grain and salt.”" "" "Neuroscience note: 🧠 Social approval strengthens the brain’s link between confidence and truth. Once rewarded with likes, a person feels “I must be right,” even if their knowledge is shallow." "" "𝗞𝗼𝗵𝗹𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗴’𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀:" "1️⃣ 👎 𝗣𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝗿 – “Wrong because I’ll get punished.”" "2️⃣ 👈 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁 – “What’s in it for me?”" "3️⃣ 🤞 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗮𝗹 – “I want to be liked.”" "4️⃣ 👍 𝗗𝘂𝘁𝘆 – “Follow the rules to keep order.”" "5️⃣ 🫱 𝗥𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 – “Protect rights, even if they belong to a minority — and be willing to change laws to do so.”" "6️⃣ ✋ 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀 – “Justice, truth, conscience.”" "" "Disclaimer: The face of the influencer has been blurred intentionally to avoid ad hominem focus. 2025-09-24 Someone I deeply respect often prefers to engage in serious, even heavy discussions—throug...
Someone I deeply respect often prefers to engage in serious, even heavy discussions—through WhatsApp. As much as I admire him, I’ve found that this mode sometimes leads to misunderstanding. Not out of ill will, but because written messages, especially on complex topics, can strip away tone, rhythm, and intent." "" "That’s when I remembered Albert Mehrabian’s Silent Messages (1971). He showed that when emotions or intentions are involved, only 7% of meaning comes from the words. 38% is carried by tone. And 55% by presence—facial cues, gestures, even pauses. WhatsApp, for all its convenience, simply can’t carry that full signal." "" "I don’t say this to push for a call or a meeting out of preference. I say this because I want to learn clearly, not just respectfully. Some messages deserve to travel in full—not clipped, flattened, or misread between taps." "" "Reference" "Mehrabian, A. (1971). Silent messages. Wadsworth Publishing Company." "" "https://lnkd.in/gJ4diCTz

2025-09-09 Tacit Mastery vs. Know-It-All Students: The biggest trap in learning isn’t ignorance — it’...
𝗧𝗮𝗰𝗶𝘁 𝗠𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘃𝘀. 𝗞𝗻𝗼𝘄-𝗜𝘁-𝗔𝗹𝗹 𝗦𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀: The biggest trap in learning isn’t ignorance — it’s thinking you already know. This is where confidence runs far ahead of competence, and why so many fall flat." "" "Here’s the quadrant that maps the journey (often linked to Dunning–Kruger):" "" "① 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗕𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗿 – low competence, high perceived. False confidence. The “wannabe entrepreneur” who thinks ego is competence and frameworks are beneath them. Or the PhD in entrepreneurship who has never built a business but acts superior to those who have. As Mark Twain warned: 𝘐𝘵 𝘢𝘪𝘯’𝘵 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘥𝘰𝘯’𝘵 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘨𝘦𝘵𝘴 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘣𝘭𝘦. 𝘐𝘵’𝘴 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘴𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘫𝘶𝘴𝘵 𝘢𝘪𝘯’𝘵 𝘴𝘰." "② 𝗛𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 – low competence, low perceived. They now know they don’t know." "③ 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗰𝗶𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘁 – high competence, high perceived. They combine tacit + explicit knowledge and can teach it." "④ 𝗧𝗮𝗰𝗶𝘁 𝗠𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘆 – high competence, low perceived. Silent mastery: “I just do it.”" "👉 Tacit knowledge fits especially in Quadrant ④." "" "Students usually follow ① → ② → ③ → ⑤." "Entrepreneurs often follow ② → ④." "Here’s the hard truth: Stage ⑤ is the ideal peak — but very few ever get there." "" "Tacit knowledge itself is powerful. It cannot be earned from degrees or diplomas; it comes from doing. The habits, instincts, and judgment built through repeated practice, trial and error, and lived experience are what shape it. A street entrepreneur may negotiate, time decisions, and manage risk better than a PhD who has only studied theory (she/he is good at research though). " "" "A fisherman can sense a storm by the smell of the sea. A mechanic can diagnose an engine by sound. A seasoned salesman knows the deal is lost or won by a subtle pause in the buyer’s voice. These things are not in textbooks — they are embodied, often unconscious, and passed on informally. Most entrepreneurs remain in Quadrant ④. " "" "Discipline in execution is embedded, the frameworks are in their head, unspoken, hence outsiders — investors, policymakers, academics — often undervalue them as “unstructured.”" "" "My job is not to hand out illusions. It is to break their overconfidence, guide awareness & help learners grow toward competence: through frameworks or/and direct experience." "" "📌𝗶𝗳 𝘀𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝘀 𝗶𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗱𝗼𝗻’𝘁 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗳𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀, 𝗮𝘀 𝗶𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 “𝗯𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘂𝗿𝘀” 𝗯𝘆 𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗲, 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗴𝗿𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀: 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁’𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘆, 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁’𝘀 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 ① — 𝘁𝗵𝗲 “𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄-𝗶𝘁-𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴.”" "" "Wishing luck to Richard Mote Nicholas Sidharta Joshua Lumbantobing you’ve moved from Stage ② (Humbled Realization) to Stage ③ (Framework Learners). 2025-08-27 Billions, Fame, Like and Emptiness "
Billions, Fame, Like and Emptiness " "" "At Harvard Business School I learned from professors who, unlike many who chase symbolic capital late in life, were already content and blessed. They pointed back to purpose. Clayton Christensen taught that the true metrics of a life are the people whose self-esteem we strengthen, whose faith we reinforce, and whose discomfort we help ease. Dr. Arthur Brooks taught that joy does not come from endless striving, but from service, relationships, and what he calls the “second curve of life”—moving from chasing success to cultivating wisdom and meaning." "" "Against this backdrop, Barry L. Rowan stands out. An HBS alumnus and frequent invited speaker, I met him at dinner with fellow alumni. That evening he was simply one of us—just one seat away. He has scaled companies from millions into billions, yet what lingers is his rhythm: one disciplined hour of prayer each morning, steady giving to the poor in Honduras and Brazil, and faith lived day to day, not just on Sundays." "" "When I introduced myself, I closed with Psalm 90:10: “If we have the strength, yet their pride is but toil and sorrow, for they quickly pass and we fly away.” Learning from failures was the topic of the night. " "" "And this is where his own book matters: The Spiritual Art of Business: Connecting the Daily with the Divine. It’s a 40-day, field-tested guide to integrating prayer, character, and commercial decision-making. The themes are practical: begin the day in quiet, listen before acting, keep integrity in small choices, steward power and money wisely, give consistently, and measure outcomes not only by P&L but by people and character. His morning hour of prayer is not piety on the side; it is the operating system for how he runs companies and serves communities." "" "We also shared common ground in book I read in 1995 “Experiencing God”. Barry not only knows the authors but live the content: know Him, enter into non transactional relationship - obedience." "" "Other traditions echo the same truth. Thich Nhat Hanh showed how every breath and act can be prayer. Barry Nobel revealed mindfulness in the Bible (hence not necessarily from eastern teaching). Teresa of Ávila described the soul as an interior castle. John Shelby Spong wrote that God’s call is to be fully human—to live, to love, and to be." "" "Science also points here. Loretta Breuning, PhD reminds us happiness comes from balance among the brain’s “happy chemicals.” Barry lives that balance: dopamine in worthy goals, serotonin when exercising leadership, endorphins in setbacks, and oxytocin in compassion. Together, they form harmony." "" "The lesson is simple but not easy: prayer shapes priorities, generosity shapes decisions, discipline shapes results. Whatever the tradition—Buddhist, Jewish, Catholic, Protestant—the test is not performance but daily practice. In the boardroom and in the barrio alike." "" "🙏HCI Audrey Utoyo Felicia Hanitio I Ketut Adi Putra Kusnadi Zenin Adrian

2025-08-22 Moral Moment – Episode 10 🛒 Fifty-Year Cycle of Stalls and Signs"
𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 – 𝗘𝗽𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝟭𝟬 🛒 𝗙𝗶𝗳𝘁𝘆-𝗬𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗖𝘆𝗰𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗦𝗶𝗴𝗻𝘀" "" "For more than half a century of lived memory, a paradox repeats: public signs declare “DILARANG BERJUALAN DI SEPANJANG JALAN INI” (“It is forbidden to sell along this road”), yet food stalls and vendors crowd the same space. Authorities raid, stalls vanish, sometimes for a few days. Then, inevitably, they return. This cycle persists across decades, across governments, across generations. The deeper point: it is not only the poor. Even the wealthy bend or break laws when enforcement is weak. Across classes, morality anchored only in punishment fear collapses without enforcement." "" "𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹? 𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 𝟭️⃣ 𝗼𝗳 𝟲." "𝗞𝗼𝗵𝗹𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗴’𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀:" "1️⃣ 👎 𝗣𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝗿 – “Wrong because I’ll get punished.”" "2️⃣ 👈 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁 – “What’s in it for me?”" "3️⃣ 🤞 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗮𝗹 – “I want to be liked.”" "4️⃣ 👍 𝗗𝘂𝘁𝘆 – “Follow the rules to keep order.”" "5️⃣ 🫱 𝗥𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 – “Protect rights, even if they belong to a minority — and be willing to change laws to do so.”" "6️⃣ ✋ 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀 – “Justice, truth, conscience.”" "" "The conduct aligns with Stage 1️⃣ 👎 Punishment fear. Rules are followed only when authorities are near, regardless of wealth or poverty. Compliance depends on external threat, not internal duty." "" "𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘁’𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗯𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻:" "👆 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗶𝘁𝘆 – Signs and raids make the rule visible to all." "☝ 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗝𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 – “Wrong” is defined only by presence of punishment." "🤲 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗼𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 – Gain, survival, or profit outweigh law or order." "✊ 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗿 – Action repeats: disperse when pressured, return when safe." "" "🧠 Neuroscience note: When generations witness that rules “only count if police show up,” the brain wires morality at Stage 1. This is not about poverty — it is about the persistence of externalized morality. Wealth does not guarantee higher stages; many affluent actors break laws when enforcement is absent." "" "𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 👎 𝘁𝗼 ✋ — 𝘄𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝗿, 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗮𝗹, 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝘂𝘁𝘆, 𝘁𝗼 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀." "𝗘𝘆𝗲𝘀, 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱, 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘁, 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱 — 𝘀𝗲𝗲 𝗶𝘁, 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗶𝘁, 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝘁, 𝗱𝗼 𝗶𝘁." "" "(Kohlberg, 1971, 1981, 1984; Rest, 1986; Pascual et al., 2013; Kapogiannis et al., 2009; Moll et al., 2005)" "" "Reflective question: If both poor and rich break the rules when punishment is absent, what truly moves a society beyond fear — toward duty and principles?

𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 – 𝗘𝗽𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝟵 🚦 𝗝𝗮𝗸𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗮 𝗬𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗭𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗕𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸" "" "This photo from a central Jakarta intersection shows cars and motorcycles occupying the yellow cross-hatched “no-stop” zone. Despite its clear marking, meant to remain free for traffic flow, private vehicles entered and waited inside the box. As a result, Transjakarta buses were obstructed, unable to proceed smoothly through the intersection. The behavior reflects self-centered decision-making: short-term personal convenience outweighing public order and collective efficiency." "" "This action violates Minister of Transportation Regulation No. 34/2014 on Road Markings (revised by No. 67/2018), which explicitly prohibits stopping in yellow-box areas. The regulation’s purpose is simple: keeping intersections clear ensures buses and other vehicles can move without gridlock. When individuals ignore this, the system breaks down — the very congestion the rule was designed to prevent is amplified." "" "⸻" "" "𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹? 𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 2️⃣ 𝗼𝗳 𝟲." "☝ 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗝𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 – They reasoned that entering was acceptable if it provided a personal time advantage." "🤲 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗼𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 – The priority was individual convenience, not collective efficiency." 2025-08-09 Moral Moment – Episode 6 🚲 Bike Lane or Car Lot?"
𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 – 𝗘𝗽𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝟲 🚲 𝗕𝗶𝗸𝗲 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗲 𝗼𝗿 𝗖𝗮𝗿 𝗟𝗼𝘁?" "In a city where cycling is not treated friendly during working hours, a narrow two-lane street has one lane painted green for bicycles. Car owners use this bike lane for parking convenience, aided by informal parking attendants. Building owners either are not legally required to provide parking or build only the minimum needed for permits. The government maintains the lane markings to meet policy checklists despite the cultural dominance of private cars." "" "𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹? 𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 𝟮 𝗼𝗳 𝟲 (with city office elements of Levels 2–4)." "𝗞𝗼𝗵𝗹𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗴’𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀:" "" "𝗞𝗼𝗵𝗹𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗴’𝘀 𝟲 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀 (exact wording and emojis):" "1️⃣ 👎 𝗣𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝗿 – “Wrong because I’ll get punished.”" "2️⃣ 👈 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁 – “What’s in it for me?”" "3️⃣ 🤞 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗮𝗹 – “I want to be liked.”" "4️⃣ 👍 𝗗𝘂𝘁𝘆 – “Follow the rules to keep order.”" "5️⃣ 🫱 𝗥𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 – “Protect rights, even if they belong to a minority — and be willing to change laws to do so.”" "6️⃣ ✋ 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀 – “Justice, truth, conscience.”" "" "Car owners and parking attendants align with Stage 2 👈 Self-Interest, prioritizing convenience or income over cyclist access. Building owners appear to act within Stage 4 👍 Duty when meeting only the minimum legal requirements, but without progressing toward rights-based or principled reasoning. The city office blends Stage 2 👈 Self-Interest, Stage 3 🤞 Approval, and Stage 4 👍 Duty in implementing the bike lane as a compliance measure without addressing underlying use or enforcement." "" "𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘁’𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗯𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻:" "👆 Moral Sensitivity – The bike lane is frequently blocked by parked cars, limiting safety and use for cyclists." "☝ Moral Judgment – Decisions prioritize immediate gain, minimal compliance, or visible policy completion over protecting vulnerable road users." "🤲 Moral Motivation – Convenience, income, and checklist satisfaction outweigh equitable road sharing." "✊ Moral Character – These repeated behaviors normalize the lane’s de facto repurposing." "" "🧠 Early childhood “spark moments” where rule-bending is tolerated or rewarded can lock reasoning into self-interest stages; religiosity alone does not shift it toward principled reasoning." "" "𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 👎 𝘁𝗼 ✋ — 𝘄𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝗿, 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗮𝗹, 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝘂𝘁𝘆, 𝘁𝗼 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀." "𝗘𝘆𝗲𝘀, 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱, 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘁, 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱 — 𝘀𝗲𝗲 𝗶𝘁, 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗶𝘁, 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝘁, 𝗱𝗼 𝗶𝘁." 2025-08-09 Moral Moment – Episode 5 🚧 Peak-Hour Roadwork"
𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 – 𝗘𝗽𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝟱 🚧 𝗣𝗲𝗮𝗸-𝗛𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗥𝗼𝗮𝗱𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸" "A major three-lane road was reduced to a single lane for approximately 2 km due to daytime construction work, causing severe traffic congestion. While the fencing was orderly, the choice to work during peak hours prioritized project speed over public convenience, a practice often avoided in more developed cities by scheduling such work at night despite higher costs." "" "𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹? 𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 𝟮 𝗼𝗳 𝟲." "𝗞𝗼𝗵𝗹𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗴’𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀:" "1️⃣ 👎 𝗣𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝗿 – “Wrong because I’ll get punished.”" "2️⃣ 👈 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁 – “What’s in it for me?”" "3️⃣ 🤞 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗮𝗹 – “I want to be liked.”" "4️⃣ 👍 𝗗𝘂𝘁𝘆 – “Follow the rules to keep order.”" "5️⃣ 🫱 𝗥𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 – “Protect rights, even if they belong to a minority — and be willing to change laws to do so.”" "6️⃣ ✋ 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀 – “Justice, truth, conscience.”" "" "Reasoning: Based on the scenario — a decision to conduct roadwork during peak hours despite knowing it causes massive congestion — here’s how the levels fit from our reference:" "• Level 1️⃣ 👎 Punishment fear would apply if the choice was purely to avoid penalties (e.g., finishing quickly to avoid fines)." "• Level 2️⃣ 👈 Self-Interest would fit if the main driver was minimizing project costs and time for the contractor’s benefit, without considering broader public impact." "• Level 4️⃣ 👍 Duty would apply if they truly believed “the rules say work can be done anytime” and followed that to maintain formal compliance, even if public interest suffered." "Given the context described — possible prioritization of speed/cost over congestion relief, and no clear evidence they acted out of fear of punishment or to uphold societal order — Level 2️⃣ 👈 Self-Interest seems the best match." "" "𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘁’𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗯𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻:" "👆 Saw that construction blocked two out of three lanes for an extended stretch during busy hours." "☝ Judged that completing the work quickly in daytime would minimize project duration and cost." "🤲 Wanted to avoid overtime wages and extended schedules, even at the cost of public congestion." "✊ Carried out the project in peak hours, causing major delays." "" "🧠 Early childhood “spark moments” where rule-bending is tolerated or rewarded shape later reasoning. The brain’s moral reasoning circuit is separate from religiosity, so belief alone does not automatically move reasoning to the principled stages." "" "𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 👎 𝘁𝗼 ✋ — 𝘄𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝗿, 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗮𝗹, 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝘂𝘁𝘆, 𝘁𝗼 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀." "𝗘𝘆𝗲𝘀, 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱, 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘁, 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱 — 𝘀𝗲𝗲 𝗶𝘁, 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗶𝘁, 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝘁, 𝗱𝗼 𝗶𝘁." "" "(Kohlberg, 1971, 1981, 1984; Rest, 1986; Pascual et al., 2013; Kapogiannis et al., 2009; Moll et al., 2005)
2025-08-09 Moral Moment – Episode 4 🚫🚶‍♂️ Pedestrian Blockers"
𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 – 𝗘𝗽𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝟰 🚫🚶‍♂️ 𝗣𝗲𝗱𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗕𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝗿𝘀" "In Central Jakarta, some vehicle owners — including certain cars with official or government plates — park on pedestrian walkways despite having ample garage space. This blocks and endangers pedestrians, including those with visual impairments, and disturbs neighbors, yet few confront it due to fear of perceived authority." "" "𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹? 𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 𝟮 𝗼𝗳 𝟲." "𝗞𝗼𝗵𝗹𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗴’𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀:" "1️⃣ 👎 𝗣𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝗿 – “Wrong because I’ll get punished.”" "2️⃣ 👈 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁 – “What’s in it for me?”" "3️⃣ 🤞 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗮𝗹 – “I want to be liked.”" "4️⃣ 👍 𝗗𝘂𝘁𝘆 – “Follow the rules to keep order.”" "5️⃣ 🫱 𝗥𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 – “Protect rights, even if they belong to a minority — and be willing to change laws to do so.”" "6️⃣ ✋ 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀 – “Justice, truth, conscience.”" "" "This behavior aligns with 👈 Self-Interest, as vehicle owners prioritize convenience and personal comfort over public safety and accessibility. The choice reflects a calculation of personal benefit with low perceived risk, ignoring legal and ethical duties to protect pedestrians." "" "𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘁’𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗯𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻:" "👆 Moral Sensitivity – Saw the walkway as a parking space, not as vital pedestrian infrastructure." "☝ Moral Judgment – Decided it was acceptable because it was more convenient and unlikely to be punished." "🤲 Moral Motivation – Wanted quick access and personal ease over public accessibility." "✊ Moral Character – Parked in a way that blocked and endangered pedestrians." "" "🧠 Early childhood “spark moments” where rule-bending is tolerated or rewarded can normalize self-serving decisions. The brain’s moral reasoning circuit is separate from religiosity, so belief or official duty alone does not guarantee principled behavior." "" "𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 👎 𝘁𝗼 ✋ — 𝘄𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝗿, 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗮𝗹, 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝘂𝘁𝘆, 𝘁𝗼 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀." "𝗘𝘆𝗲𝘀, 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱, 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘁, 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱 — 𝘀𝗲𝗲 𝗶𝘁, 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗶𝘁, 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝘁, 𝗱𝗼 𝗶𝘁." 2025-08-09 Moral Moment – Episode 3 🚗 Entitled Parking"
𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 – 𝗘𝗽𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝟯 🚗 𝗘𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘁𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴" "In a luxury condominium, many tenants — mostly affluent residents and high-ranking officials — routinely ignore the “No Parking” and fire hydrant zone in front of the lobby, despite having their own assigned parking lots. When gently reminded by security staff or the front office, they often reply, “only for a short while,” yet vehicles have been observed remaining in place for over five hours — for example, one car parked from 13:30 until at least 18:42. These actions repeatedly block the narrow passage, creating avoidable congestion. This car does this every Sunday at least. " "" "This moral lapse is not linked to economic hardship; if anything, it appears more common among those with greater wealth and status." "" "𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹? 𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 𝟮 𝗼𝗳 𝟲." Over dinner with fellow alumni in Indonesia Jessica H. Laihad, Surya Tri Harto, Prof. Nugroho Budisatrio Sukamdani, Ali Kusno Fusin, Nur Munir and guest Charles Fuad , our conversation on moral reasoning didn’t stop at Kohlberg’s six stages (Kohlberg, 1981). Someone asked, “Once you know what’s right, what makes you actually do it?”" "That’s when we turned to psychologist James Rest’s Four-Component Model (Rest, 1986): a framework that focuses not on how you reason, but on how you act." "" "✋ Rest’s 4 Moral Steps :" "" "1️⃣ 👁️Moral Sensitivity – See it" "“First, you’ve got to notice the moral issue.”" "2️⃣ 🧠Moral Judgment – Decide it" "“Then, figure out what’s the right thing to do.”" "3️⃣ 🫀Moral Motivation – Want it" "“You have to care enough to choose the moral option.”" "4️⃣ 🏃🏻‍➡️Moral Character – Do it" "“Finally, have the courage and persistence to act.”" "" "Eyes, head, heart, hand: see it, decide it, want it, do it." "" "Just like moral reasoning, the capacity to follow through is shaped early: those repeated exposures in childhood that fire neurons and form the circuits for noticing, deciding, caring, and acting (Pascual et al., 2013)." "" "The wiring for each of these steps often begins side-by-side in early life:" "" "What we saw the adults around us notice." "The way they decided between easy and right." "Whether they cared for others." "And whether they had the courage to act." "" "Those early sparks set the circuitry then influencing how we live our values as adults." "" "References" "" "Kohlberg, L. (1981). The philosophy of moral development: Moral stages and the idea of justice. Harper & Row." "" "Pascual, L., Rodrigues, P., & Gallardo-Pujol, D. (2013). How does morality work in the brain? A functional and structural perspective of moral behavior. Frontiers in Integrative Neuroscience, 7, 65. https://lnkd.in/gduGTHJr" "" "Rest, J. R. (1986). Moral development: Advances in research and theory. Praeger.

Over dinner with fellow alumni in Indonesia Prof. Nugroho Budisatrio Sukamdani, Nur Munir, Jessica H. Laihad, Surya Tri Harto and Ali Kusno Fusin, the talk turned from casual updates to a spirited discussion on moral frameworks — and why we think the way we do about right and wrong." "" "𝗡𝗲𝘂𝗿𝗼𝘀𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘄𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗮 𝗴𝘂𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘀 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗶𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘆 (Moll et al., 2005; Pascual et al., 2013)." "" "𝗥𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗶𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗳 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗷𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗰𝗶𝗿𝗰𝘂𝗶𝘁 (Kapogiannis et al., 2009; Tambun, 2025)." "" "The moral pathway is built early — when repeated exposures fire neurons, creating mental models that guide decisions for life. In early childhood, every meaningful exposure and spark — those moments that fire neurons repeatedly — shapes the mental model we carry into adulthood." "" "Psychologist Lawrence Kohlberg (1981) found that moral reasoning develops through three levels, six stages: " "" "𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 𝟭 – 𝗣𝗿𝗲-𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹" "1️⃣ 👎 𝗣𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝗿 – “Wrong because I’ll get punished.”" "2️⃣ 👈 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁 – “What’s in it for me?”" "" "𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 𝟮 – 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹" "3️⃣ 🤞 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗮𝗹 – “I want to be liked.”" "4️⃣ 👍 𝗗𝘂𝘁𝘆 – “Follow the rules to keep order.”" "" "𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 𝟯 – 𝗣𝗼𝘀𝘁-𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹" "5️⃣ 🫱 𝗥𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 – “Protect rights, even if they belong to a minority — and be willing to change laws to do so.” (legal/contractual equality)" "6️⃣ ✋ 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀 – “Justice, truth, conscience.” (moral equality above the law)" "" "The higher stages — where justice, fairness, and human dignity take priority — don’t appear out of nowhere. They grow from repeated exposures in childhood:" "" "The stories told at home." "The fairness (or unfairness) seen in school." "The justice (or injustice) observed in society." "" "These experiences often happen side-by-side, and together they wire the brain — setting the pathways for how we reason about right and wrong as adults." "" "⸻" "" "✅ WHAT" "Indonesia is accelerating its EV transition." "Factories are rising. Battery output is growing. Jobs are being created. Regulation 79/2023 is structured and enforced. These efforts are not cosmetic. They are intended to move Indonesia into a higher position in the global supply chain." "" "⚠️ BUT" "Indonesia still doesn’t control what matters." "Kits, tools, manuals, designs, technology standards, battery patents—all come from abroad. Sovereignty is being measured in location, not in authority. The country hosts the work, but does not direct it. After decades of assembling cars, Indonesia still isn’t in the global car supply chain. With EVs, the risk is repeating the same pattern on a new platform." "" "🔁 THEN" "If the strategy stops at assembling what others design, Indonesia will reach its 100th year still dependent." "This article argues: unless Indonesia gains supply chain control, builds technical expertise, and stops measuring progress by volume alone, it will inherit factories but not power." 2025-07-30 Honored to attend the MIT graduates’ send-off at His Excellency Minister Dr. Agus Harimurt...
Honored to attend the MIT graduates’ send-off at His Excellency Minister Dr. Agus Harimurti Yudhoyono’s office—an inspiring moment anchored in substance and sincerity. 🇮🇩" "" "Minister AHY reminded the departing students: “Hati dan pikiran kita untuk Indonesia. Tidak pernah saya menanyakan borders.” To love this country is not about where the feet stand—but where the heart and mind commit. Patriotism is not about place. It’s about purpose." "" "He speaks not just as a minister, but as someone shaped by quiet discipline. Grandson of General Sarwo Edhie Wibowo. Son of President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono—who never dreamed of becoming president, but lived as a loyal soldier. SBY served with obedience, not ambition. That ethos shaped AHY from the beginning." "" "AHY grew up under that value system. Educated at Taruna Nusantara, he topped his class. At the Military Academy, he earned the Adhi Makayasa. He served with honor in Aceh, in Lebanon, and led elite forces—not as “the son of the president,” but as a soldier bound by rank, law, and humility." "" "He resigned from the military as a Major in 2016 when asked to lead his party—despite being eligible to pursue 1-star or 2-star general rank. He could have changed the rules. He didn’t. He walked away clean." "" "He holds three master’s degrees (NTU, Harvard, Webster) and earned his doctorate from Universitas Airlangga. He reads. He thinks. He acts with deliberation." "" "And he has suffered. When his father-in-law faced sentencing during his father’s presidency, AHY submitted to the process. He could have intervened. He didn’t. He stood still—beneath the law, not above it. That silence, that choice to let justice run its course, became his deepest teacher." "" "Now, as Coordinating Minister of Infrastructure and Regional Development, he shows that principled matters. Law matters. Reading matters. And Indonesia deserves leaders who do not bypass process just to gain power." "" "Wishing Dr. AHY strength in the years ahead. Indonesia needs leaders who build, not bypass. Who listen, not posture. Who suffer quietly when tested—and come out cleaner, not louder." "" "To the incoming MIT students: Carry that spirit. You are global, but your soul is anchored. Patriotism is not where you stand. It’s who you serve—even when no one is watching (Diandra Riando, Nadia Assegaf, Imam Sefriyadi et al)" "" "Thanks Bpk. Deputy Minister Rachmat Kaimuddin, Special Staff jovan latuconsina ; Kreiton Sitorus and Daniar Masita Nadya for making this event happened. "*Scale – problems that are large in scope (temporal, spatial, institutional, or demographic)." "*Policy resistance – when well-intentioned interventions produce counterintuitive or ineffective results due to underlying feedback structures." "*Dynamic behavior over time – when the problem unfolds gradually or has delayed effects (e.g., unintended consequences, time lags)." "*Circular causality – when cause and effect are not linear but recursive, often forming feedback loops." "*Mental model misalignment – when different stakeholders interpret the same problem differently or act based on conflicting assumptions." Many of us were surprised—or even disheartened—when we saw the RI² red and yellow flags¹. " "" "According to national media coverage, 5 major institutions were reported under yellow flag (moderate risk) and 8 others under red flag (high risk). "" "This article published in The Jakarta Post “𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗜² 𝗙𝗹𝗮𝗴𝘀 𝗠𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗕𝗲 𝗧𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗨𝘀” July 12,2025 What the RI² flags might really be telling us https://lnkd.in/g4eEPcA2 does not assign blame. "" "Rather than using a linear cause-blame narrative, I applied system dynamics thinking—to map how feedback loops and institutional saturation may be driving what RI² is capturing." "" "The article surfaces five reinforcing loops:" "𝗥𝟭: Publication Pressure" "𝗥𝟮𝗮: Faculty Shortcut Loop" "𝗥𝟮𝗯: Graduate Student Pressure Loop" "𝗥𝟰: External Validation Loop" "𝗥𝟱: Shortcut Normalization Loop" "And one balancing loop:" "𝗕𝟭: Integrity Response Loop (flags, audits, reputational signals)" "" "Beneath them are two stock variables:" "𝗜𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗣𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁 and 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗙𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗲" "" "𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗰𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲𝘀:" "" "➊ Stop assuming compliance means health." "Even formal systems can produce unhealthy outcomes when loop pressures exceed absorption. Risk is structural, not moral." "" "➋ Reform incentives, not just procedures." "This includes slowing KPI cycles (weakens R1), adjusting promotion dynamics (weakens R4), and pacing supervision (dampens R2b). These are not separate loops—but targeted interventions inside existing feedback structures." "" "➌ Use RI² not as punishment, but as diagnosis." "" "Flags are not verdicts. They are stress signals in the loop network. The call is not to tighten every rule—but to redesign pressure at its source." "" "Let’s not waste the signal. Let’s read it structurally—before our best quietly disengage." "" "¹ Flag color classifications and institutional names have been widely reported in national media. 2025-07-10 Why Indonesia Plans the Way It Does ?"
𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐚 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐖𝐚𝐲 𝐈𝐭 𝐃𝐨𝐞𝐬 ?" "" "Indonesia’s obsession with planning didn’t emerge on its own. It was introduced—taught—exported. And today, I finally understand where the doctrine came from." "" "In the 1950s, economists introduced a model of national planning to governments—first in Pakistan, then South Korea. It wasn’t neutral advice. It was Cold War strategy." "" "At the center was W.W. Rostow, whose theories shaped how developing nations were meant to grow:" " " "𝟭. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐓𝐚𝐤𝐞-𝐎𝐟𝐟 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥: Countries pass through linear stages—traditional society, preconditions, take-off, maturity, mass consumption. The key was to sequence investment, infrastructure, and industrial priorities." "" "𝟮. 𝐀𝐧𝐭𝐢-𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐭 𝐃𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐨𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥: Planning wasn’t just about productivity—it was about preventing communism. Economic growth became a geopolitical tool. If capitalist systems could deliver prosperity, alternatives could be discredited." "" "Pakistan implemented five-year plans under external guidance. South Korea followed with export-led restructuring." "" "By the late 1960s, Indonesia applied both doctrines, launching REPELITA and embracing technocratic planning as a pillar of state legitimacy." "" "But these models were strong on production and weak on distribution." "" "Growth was assumed to be enough. Taxation and equity were afterthoughts." "" "The frameworks we absorbed weren’t just technical—they carried an entire belief system: about control, progress, and who gets to decide." "" "That’s why thinkers like Thomas Piketty matter now. They remind us: Even when growth succeeds, wealth concentrates—unless we build in redistribution." "" "Planning alone doesn’t guarantee justice. It only guarantees structure." 𝗕𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮 𝗥𝗲𝗯𝗲𝗹 𝗜𝘀𝗻’𝘁 𝗦𝗮𝗳𝗲. 𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗘𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗔𝗽𝗲𝘀." "" "In Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors, Carl Sagan and Ann Druyan describe the daily politics of chimpanzee life—not through language, but through power." "" "Chimpanzees don’t survive by speaking truth. They survive by reading the room." "" "They watch power." "They flatter it." "They mimic the group." "They suppress pain." "They fake strength." "They perform submission—not out of weakness, but as a survival skill." "" "“𝐀𝐬𝐬-𝐤𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐬 𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐦𝐢𝐜. 𝐂𝐨𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐝. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐫𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐨𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐧 𝐝𝐢𝐞 ” (p. 293)" "" "Even dominance is ritualized. A lower-ranking male will crouch and “present” his rump to a higher-ranking one—inviting a simulated mounting act. There’s no orgasm. No penetration. It’s not sex. It’s theatre." "" "A symbolic way of saying:" "“I submit. You win.”" "" "And here’s the deeper point:" "This act is not that far—structurally—from certain rituals of submission in human institutions. In some corporate cultures, political environments, or group dynamics, gestures of symbolic deference—or even verbal aggression like “fxxx you”—aren’t about offense. They’re about asserting status. They say:" "“I’m above you.”" "“You yield.”" "“You stay in your lane.”" "" "It’s not about sex. It’s about dominance—performed, signaled, and enforced." "" "Sagan and Druyan even write:" "" "“In chimpish, ‘Let’s fxxx’ sounds almost exactly like ‘I’m gonna kill you.’” (p. 303)" "" "That’s what dominance rituals are: threats disguised as gestures." "" "So yes—being a rebel is dangerous. In the ape world and in ours." "Truth-tellers rarely rise. Compliance often does." "" "Those who thrive are not those who confront power—but those who mirror it." "Those who flatter it." "Those who submit, symbolically or silently." "" "And we ask:" "" "How much of what we call professionalism, diplomacy, or strategic silence—" "is actually just learned submission with better clothes?" "" "📘 Sagan, C., & Druyan, A. (1993). Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors: A Search for Who We Are. Ballantine Books." "" "🦍 Based on chapter 16, pp. 293–304." "" "https://lnkd.in/gGNtJZTi

These are not more important—they’re just the most recent. And they reminded me of how far this story stretches." "" "Before those two, other updates came quietly from many corners—different years, different lives, but the same spirit." "" "Some also pursued further study - Levina Kerensa and Tjia, Alphani Putri in Columbia University, Richard Mote in Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Wifal Inola in National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Yessika Natalia Chelsie in (UST) University of Science and Technology, Korea, Muhammad Daffa Rasyid in Inha University in Incheon, Ghozy Abror in University of South Wales, Aisyah Adlina Ghassani in HEC Paris, Dzaky Rahman in The University of Edinburgh, Bartolomeus Delphito in Carnegie Mellon University, Barra Alfarisi Abadi in UCL " "" "Others entered the O&G service sector, as I once did - Muhammad Adnan and Martinus William Hartono joined SLB, Shelma Mayolaika in Weatherford et al" "" "Yumna Dzakiyyah Irfandi Sarana Michael Fransiscus Munthe Nikolas Notohardjo Muhammad Syafiq Fauzan Dedek Adrian pursue their career into global FMCG firms, consulting companies, IT or communication firms." "" "Some work in state-owned companies (Ar Ryan Shifa Izzati) and others in national companies (Priskilla Buna et al Muhammad Ridlo)" "" "Some became civil servants—taking up public roles in quiet, persistent ways - Tamash" "" "Some started their own ventures—not always innovation-driven, not always scalable, but chosen with pride and purpose (Yahya Aqrom)" "" "And some are still searching—between jobs, between roles, between certainties." "" "Each of these paths matters. In different seasons, each of them had a place in my classroom—or more truthfully, in my home, because that’s what I try to offer. I’m honored—not because I made their journey—but because I was allowed to walk beside them, however briefly." "" "They are not “former students.” They are my 𝐜𝐨-𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐬—and they still teach me." "" "What they’ve chosen teaches us: that success is not one shape. It is a life lived with integrity, wherever they are planted.
2025-07-08 How Many Times Can You Say the Same Thing Before It Means Nothing?"
𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗧𝗶𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗖𝗮𝗻 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗦𝗮𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗕𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗜𝘁 𝗠𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗡𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴?" "" "For four years, a student kept sending me the same message — word for word. It was polite. Respectful. Carefully worded." "" "But always came the delay excuse — always apologetic, always centered on his own situation. " "" "Then came the “let’s meet” gestures — warm but never followed through." "" "The emojis. The default phrases. The pattern." "" "That’s when I realized: this was neither rudeness nor politeness." "𝗜𝘁 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲." "𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗺 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘁𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁." "" "I’ve seen this pattern more than once — and I know others have too. The overly polite but disengaged junior. Always apologizing. Always asking to meet. Never following through." "" "I wrote this piece to name something many of us have felt but haven’t said out loud. It puts into words what mentors, team leads, and educators often recognize but can’t always explain." "" "It also pushed me to reflect — not just on others, but on myself." "Have I tolerated this too long?" "Have I done this in some other form?" "" "This isn’t about one person. It’s about how easily we confuse form for effort, politeness for presence." "That’s the reason I wrote it.

2025-07-02 In our new article, published by The Jakarta Post 3 July 2025 When the Loop Fails Before I...
In our new article, published by The Jakarta Post 3 July 2025 𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩 𝐅𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐬 𝐁𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐈𝐭 𝐁𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐬, Innovation paradox: When the loop fails before it begins https://lnkd.in/gf9XNYCf we explore why innovation systems stall—not because they lack components, but because the feedback loops never activate." "" "We often assume that if we build the right platform, design the right program, or launch the right course, innovation will follow. Especially in academic or government settings, this assumption feels safe—because it is formal, fundable, and familiar. But in many ecosystems, it simply isn’t true." "" "We show that innovation ecosystems aren’t powered by design alone. They are powered by circulation. And circulation depends on feedback. But feedback is not just a technical flow—it’s a cultural decision." "" "📊 We present two system dynamics models:" "🦩 A national ecosystem map based on research across 20 countries" "🦩A corporate–university lab that was fully funded, aligned—and yet launched zero pilots" "" "Across both, the pattern was the same:" "🦩The system was built." "🦩The actors were aligned." "🦩But the loop never ran." "🦩Not because the design was wrong—" "🦩But because the system didn’t allow itself to move." "" "🔁 What triggers innovation loops?" "🦩Market attractiveness, not research quality" "🦩Capital, not discovery" "🦩Visibility, not evidence" "🦩Universities are present in these loops—but they don’t trigger them. They amplify. They don’t ignite." "" "📉 What causes loops to stall?" "🦩Private capital can reduce openness: investment increases caution, sharing drops, co-development slows, and future funding weakens" "🦩Failed pilots lower expectations: trust collapses, pessimism rises, firms exit" "🦩Once momentum fades, no actor—not even the university—can restart the loop" "" "📌 What’s really blocking the loop?" "Culture." "In particular:" "🦩Short-term orientation: fast results are rewarded, long bets avoided" "🦩High uncertainty avoidance: systems favor predictability over deviance" "🦩Rebel minds are filtered out early—despite being the ones who could activate change" "🦩Performance systems reinforce delivery, not discovery" "The result isn’t failure—it’s controlled sameness." "" "One loop had a chance:" "➡️ Rebel talent integration" "But the system filtered for conformity. So the loop never spun." "This is our core claim:" "🦩Innovation doesn’t fail at the policy level." "🦩I t fails at the point of behavior." "Even a fully built system stays silent if it never gives itself permission to move." "Until institutions ask which behaviors are allowed—and which ones are quietly excluded—the loop will fail before it begins." "" "🙏 With appreciation to the editorial team of The Jakarta Post and my co-author / thesis supervisor Dr. Leo Aldianto from School of Business and Management ITB" "" "Sumantri Ishak Prof.Tirto Prakoso Prof. Zulfiadi Zulhan Prof. Endra Joelianto Prof. Yudi Darma " "" "https://lnkd.in/gCghbnQw

"" "But their mental model of business is often:" "𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝 𝐚 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭, 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐬." "Not:" "𝐅𝐢𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐚𝐢𝐧. 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐲 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐢𝐭. 𝐔𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐢𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐞𝐩𝐥𝐲." "" "This sermon wasn’t born from a book." "It came from watching students hit walls—again and again—and trying to make sense of why." "" "Later, I encountered a phrase from Uri Levine, founder of Waze, that gave language to what I had already been noticing:" "𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐢𝐧 𝐥𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐦, 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧." "That was it." "" "𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐚 𝐟𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤." "𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐚 𝐟𝐢𝐱." "But a 𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐨𝐰 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐟 𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐬𝐞𝐭 I wish more of us could hold—especially in our formative years." "" "So this message is for those who are still learning." "Still adjusting." "Still figuring out that 𝐟𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐬 𝐢𝐬𝐧’𝐭 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧—it’s 𝐟𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐨𝐦." "And that 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐫 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐦 isn’t delay—it’s 𝐰𝐢𝐬𝐝𝐨𝐦." "" "Here’s the full sermon:" "𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐢𝐧 𝐋𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐦, 𝐋𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐲 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡: 𝐁𝐢𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐑𝐨𝐨𝐭𝐬 𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐬?" "(Proverbs 18:13)" "" "𝐓𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐮𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐨 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐡𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐭𝐬—𝐲𝐨𝐮’𝐫𝐞 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐰𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠. 𝐘𝐨𝐮’𝐫𝐞 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲." My deep thanks to the editorial team at The Jakarta Post for publishing this 8th column in my nuclear energy series—released June 23, 2025: https://lnkd.in/gzY4RgfZ 𝑺𝒕𝒓𝒂𝒕𝒆𝒈𝒊𝒄 𝑻𝒆𝒎𝒑𝒐 𝒗𝒔. 𝑺𝒚𝒎𝒃𝒐𝒍𝒊𝒄 𝑨𝒍𝒊𝒈𝒏𝒎𝒆𝒏𝒕: 𝑾𝒉𝒂𝒕 𝑻𝒓𝒖𝒎𝒑’𝒔 𝑵𝒖𝒄𝒍𝒆𝒂𝒓 𝑶𝒓𝒅𝒆𝒓𝒔 𝑹𝒆𝒗𝒆𝒂𝒍 𝑨𝒃𝒐𝒖𝒕 𝑰𝒏𝒅𝒐𝒏𝒆𝒔𝒊𝒂’𝒔 𝑷𝒐𝒔𝒕𝒖𝒓𝒆" "" "This one is personal—for every nuclear student, engineer, researcher, and policymaker in Indonesia." "" "Here’s the hard question:" "𝑨𝒓𝒆 𝒘𝒆 𝒔𝒉𝒂𝒑𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒇𝒖𝒕𝒖𝒓𝒆 𝒐𝒇 𝒏𝒖𝒄𝒍𝒆𝒂𝒓 𝒆𝒏𝒆𝒓𝒈𝒚—𝒐𝒓 𝒋𝒖𝒔𝒕 𝒐𝒑𝒆𝒓𝒂𝒕𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒘𝒉𝒂𝒕 𝒐𝒕𝒉𝒆𝒓𝒔 𝒉𝒂𝒗𝒆 𝒅𝒆𝒄𝒊𝒅𝒆𝒅?" "" "In the U.S., nuclear is now being tied to defense strategy, AI infrastructure, and fuel sovereignty—with clear deadlines and clear authority. In Indonesia, we announce 250 MW reactors—but rely on vendors who’ve never built one." "" "And when the system treats nuclear as a special project, not a long-cycle discipline—what role is left for the nuclear PhD, the regulator, the researcher? Are we training world-class engineers to supervise paperwork? Or are we designing a future that actually needs them?" "" "This article explores:" "– Why Indonesia risks becoming a testing site, not a strategic actor" "– What it means when the U.S. adopts SMRs for AI data centers—a use case I proposed last year" "– And how our nuclear professionals will be sidelined unless the governance structure is rewritten" "" "𝑰𝒇 𝒚𝒐𝒖'𝒓𝒆 𝒊𝒏 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒏𝒖𝒄𝒍𝒆𝒂𝒓 𝒇𝒊𝒆𝒍𝒅—𝒕𝒉𝒊𝒔 𝒊𝒔 𝒏𝒐𝒕 𝒂𝒃𝒐𝒖𝒕 𝒑𝒐𝒍𝒊𝒄𝒚. 𝑰𝒕’𝒔 𝒂𝒃𝒐𝒖𝒕 𝒚𝒐𝒖𝒓 𝒄𝒂𝒓𝒆𝒆𝒓. 𝑼𝒏𝒍𝒆𝒔𝒔, 𝒐𝒇 𝒄𝒐𝒖𝒓𝒔𝒆, 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒂𝒗𝒆𝒓𝒔𝒆 𝒄𝒖𝒍𝒕𝒖𝒓𝒆 𝒊𝒔 𝒔𝒐 𝒆𝒎𝒃𝒆𝒅𝒅𝒆𝒅 𝒕𝒉𝒂𝒕 𝒚𝒐𝒖 𝒕𝒂𝒌𝒆 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒋𝒐𝒃 𝒄𝒉𝒆𝒆𝒓𝒇𝒖𝒍𝒍𝒚—𝒂𝒔 𝒍𝒐𝒏𝒈 𝒂𝒔 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒔𝒂𝒍𝒂𝒓𝒚 𝒌𝒆𝒆𝒑𝒔 𝒄𝒐𝒎𝒊𝒏𝒈." "" "𝑻𝒉𝒆𝒓𝒆𝒇𝒐𝒓𝒆, 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒓𝒆𝒊𝒏𝒇𝒐𝒓𝒄𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒍𝒐𝒐𝒑 𝒕𝒂𝒌𝒆𝒔 𝒉𝒐𝒍𝒅: 𝒓𝒊𝒔𝒌-𝒂𝒗𝒆𝒓𝒔𝒆 𝒄𝒖𝒍𝒕𝒖𝒓𝒆 𝒃𝒆𝒄𝒐𝒎𝒆𝒔 𝒅𝒆𝒆𝒑𝒆𝒓, 𝒊𝒏𝒏𝒐𝒗𝒂𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏 𝒇𝒖𝒓𝒕𝒉𝒆𝒓 𝒇𝒓𝒂𝒈𝒊𝒍𝒆, 𝒂𝒏𝒅 𝒘𝒆 𝒔𝒍𝒊𝒑 𝒇𝒖𝒓𝒕𝒉𝒆𝒓 𝒊𝒏𝒕𝒐 𝒑𝒆𝒓𝒊𝒑𝒉𝒆𝒓𝒂𝒍 𝒔𝒕𝒂𝒕𝒖𝒔—𝒏𝒐𝒕 𝒇𝒐𝒓 𝒍𝒂𝒄𝒌 𝒐𝒇 𝒔𝒌𝒊𝒍𝒍, 𝒃𝒖𝒕 𝒇𝒐𝒓 𝒍𝒂𝒄𝒌 𝒐𝒇 𝒄𝒐𝒖𝒓𝒂𝒈𝒆." "" "" "https://lnkd.in/gnrW4UCF" "" "📣 New op-ed out in The Jakarta Post (thanks so much) "Social Media and the Quiet Return of Imperialism"  last weekend June 7, 2025 https://lnkd.in/grRXVcNf" "" "This reflection grew from years observing how Indonesia’s political industry exploits algorithmic logic—while public reasoning weakens." 2025-06-21 Breakfast with Prof. Jay Rosengard."
𝐁𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐤𝐟𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟. 𝐉𝐚𝐲 𝐑𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐚𝐫𝐝." "𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑖𝑛𝑔 ℎ𝑖𝑠 𝑏𝑜𝑜𝑘 𝑜𝑛 𝑡ℎ𝑒 𝑤𝑎𝑦 ℎ𝑜𝑚𝑒. 𝑆𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑙 𝑛𝑜𝑡 𝑓𝑖𝑛𝑖𝑠ℎ𝑒𝑑—𝑏𝑢𝑡 𝑎𝑙𝑟𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑦 𝑢𝑛𝑒𝑎𝑠𝑦." "" "He spoke briefly—mostly on Harvard’s institutional position on recent events. But what stayed with me wasn’t just the breakfast. It was the book I started reading after: Economics of the Public Sector, co-authored with Joseph Stiglitz." "" "It clarified something I’ve seen too often: 𝐰𝐞 𝐤𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐚𝐬𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐠𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐝𝐨 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐭 𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐝𝐨—𝐛𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐲𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐫 (expecting the government to act as both architect and investor). " "" "In a recent FGD organized by a leading institution, it became clear that in the context of industry collaboration and innovation ecosystems, many actors still demand the government to be both the playmaker and the source of fund. This expectation—though widespread—is structurally misaligned with how public finance operates. That may not what government is designed for. Its role is to be 𝐫𝐞𝐠𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐨𝐫 and 𝐟𝐚𝐜𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐨𝐫—not the 𝐬𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫." "" "That’s how public finance works:" "It’s not short-term. It’s 𝐠𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐝." "It doesn’t improvise. It 𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐨𝐧 𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐞." "It’s not chaotic. It’s 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞." "There’s no room for 𝐦𝐚𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐤 𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧." "" "The short-termist mindset isn’t in the public finance system. It’s in 𝐮𝐬—in how we think policy should move, how fast it should act, how flexible it should be." "" "So when people say “Let’s just build collaborative industry”, the better question is:" "𝐀𝐫𝐞 𝐰𝐞 𝐚𝐬𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐠𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐛𝐞 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐭’𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐬𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐛𝐞?" "" "This book lays that out—not as criticism, but as a mirror." "" "Still reading. But I already know this:" "" "𝐂𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐟𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐰𝐞𝐚𝐤, 𝐛𝐮𝐭 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐰𝐞 𝐤𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐬 𝐰𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐛𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝." E., & Rosengard, J. K. (2015). Economics of the public sector (4th ed.). W.W. Norton & Company." "" "https://lnkd.in/gbaqsz-9

Too often, officers, policymakers, and even educators continue to confuse 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 with 𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. The result? We keep rewarding novelty without outcomes. We celebrate patents that sit unused. We cite global rankings, yet wonder why our transformation stalls." "" "The issue is not lack of creativity. It’s the habit of calling progress what is, in truth, unfinished work." "" "This article lays out what 𝗦𝗰𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗽𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗿, 𝗘𝗱𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗕. 𝗥𝗼𝗯𝗲𝗿𝘁𝘀, 𝗕𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗔𝘂𝗹𝗲𝘁, and even 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗟𝗮𝘄 𝗡𝗼. 𝟭𝟮/𝟮𝟬𝟭𝟵 all affirm:" "" "𝗜𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 = 𝗜𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 × 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻⁽*⁾ " "" "If there’s no application—no economic or social benefit—then it’s not 𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. It’s just a good idea waiting forever." "" "𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀:" "• 𝗦𝗰𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗽𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗿 made commercialization the foundation of innovation—nearly a century ago." "• 𝗘.𝗕. 𝗥𝗼𝗯𝗲𝗿𝘁𝘀 distinguished invention from innovation through real-world application." "• 𝗕𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗔𝘂𝗹𝗲𝘁 framed it as a usable formula for entrepreneurs and institutions." "• 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗟𝗮𝘄 𝗡𝗼. 𝟭𝟮/𝟮𝟬𝟭𝟵 defines innovation as invention that produces benefit." "" "Dictionaries like Merriam-Webster are helpful for understanding how words are commonly used. But when it comes to defining 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘀 for policy, research, or national planning, we need more than usage—we need frameworks that reflect 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀." "" "𝗟𝗲𝘁’𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗯𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲. 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐨𝐧𝐬—𝐛𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐤𝐟𝐚𝐬𝐭, 𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐨, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭" "" "I first met Pak Trio Herlambang — General Manager of Four Points by Sheraton Bandung —during a difficult time in 2021. We were still under COVID restrictions, and I on behalf of Yayasan Mens et Manus needed a quiet space for my students to present their group projects. One department said no. But with his intervention, that “no” became a full-day access: from 7AM to 10PM. That’s when I first saw his leadership." "" "What stood out was not just the solution—but how he led the team. He didn’t offer the room because I was a Bonvoy Gold member. He helped because someone needed help. He didn’t micromanage. He empowered his operations manager, banquet team, finance, sales—all to move toward one goal: support." "" "Since then, I’ve held all my events in his hotel. And I keep coming back. Not out of habit—but because the leadership culture stays consistent. At breakfast, you don’t find a single “ambassador.” You find a whole team that acts like one. From the GM to the barista to the chef—they all represent the brand, the hotel, and his leadership." "" "Last week, I heard someone from a top institution say: “That professor doesn’t represent us. He’s not part of our organizational chart.” I was speechless. Because that mindset—exclusive, rigid—is the opposite of an innovation trait." "" "Meanwhile, in Pak Trio’s leadership, everyone represents. Everyone is empowered. And that’s why the guest experience becomes predictably excellent—yes, even down to my espresso, orange juice, and a chef-made egg every morning." "" "Congratulations, Pak Trio Herlambang. The brand is safe in your hands. And if God allows, when I visit Bandung, I’ll keep returning to the hotel —not just for events, but because of the culture you lead." "" "https://lnkd.in/gutNF3Fv

2025-06-15 Grateful to have been present on behalf of Aren Energy Investment at the recent Focus Gr...
Grateful to have been present on behalf of Aren Energy Investment at the recent Focus Group Discussion hosted by ITB’s Forum Guru Besar on “Kolaborasi Industri dan ITB.” I did not speak, but had the privilege of listening and exchanging thoughts informally at the table—with some of the country’s most thoughtful academic and industry leaders (Sumantri Ishak, Prof. Tirto Prakoso, Prof. Zulfiadi Zulhan, Hilmi Panigoro and Prof. Dwiwahju Sasongko) " "" "In the spirit of contribution, I’m sharing a keynote manuscript I had prepared for the occasion. Though not published by the organizers, the argument hopefully may still be relevant—especially given how persistent certain policy assumptions have become." "" "The manuscript challenges one of the most repeated but least examined beliefs in innovation policy: that universities, by collaborating structurally with industry, can activate innovation ecosystems. This assumption is not just flawed—it is misleading." "" "𝐔𝐧𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐬. 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭’𝐬 𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞." "" "And market attractiveness is not engineered through MOUs or pilot programs. It is revealed through the response of risk capital. If no investor believes the market is worth entering, no ecosystem emerges—regardless of how many centers, incubators, or partnerships are built." "This point is illustrated through two causal loop diagrams—one from Passi et al. (2023), based on 20 national systems, and another from my own Indonesian case study (Tambun, 2025). Both expose a missing layer in the current approach: culture." "" "𝐂𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐁𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞" "" "The manuscript argues that ecosystem loops often remain inactive not because of weak strategy or absent institutions, but because the underlying culture filters out deviance, risk-taking, and long-cycle thinking. Structural interventions fail when cultural conditions are not ready to support feedback loops." "" "Dominant frameworks such as the Triple Helix and National Systems of Innovation emphasize institutional design but neglect the cultural variables—like low uncertainty avoidance or tolerance for failure—that determine whether innovation behavior is even allowed to emerge. Without these, feedback loops collapse at the point of selection, long before any policy can be evaluated or pilot tested." "" "This manuscript calls for a shift: from structure-heavy design toward feedback-aware, culture-sensitive diagnostics—and market-informed policy logic." "" "Full draft follows in the article below.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐏𝐡𝐃 𝐉𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐲: 𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐒𝐜𝐨𝐩𝐮𝐬 𝐁𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐆𝐨𝐝" "It starts with conviction." "A good question. A meaningful cause." "The kind of research meant to matter." "Each day brings progress." "The charts align. The arguments sharpen." "The dream is alive." "" "Until one sentence knocks:" "“Has it been published in Scopus yet?”" "" "Not:" ""Is it true?"" ""Is it useful?"" ""Will it help someone?"" "" "But:" "𝐒𝐜𝐨𝐩𝐮𝐬." "" "The golden stamp. The modern altar." "Suddenly the question isn't about contribution," "but compliance." "Not value—" "but validation." "" "Then come the rejections." "Not for error," "but for “scope.”" "For “insufficient theoretical novelty.”" "For “lack of international interest.”" "" "The gods of the manuscript," "faceless, tasteless, shameless—" "decide worth through silence." 2025-06-09 When Internships Become a Detour Instead of a Bridge"
𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐬 𝐁𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐚 𝐃𝐞𝐭𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐈𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐨𝐟 𝐚 𝐁𝐫𝐢𝐝𝐠𝐞" "" "Some students now find themselves entering their fifth year of undergrad—not due to academic failure, but because of internship overload. From one brand to another, they keep chasing prestige. Many of these roles are paid—yes—but only at standard intern rates. Not illegal, just disproportionate when weighed against the long-term cost of delaying graduation." "" "What started as exposure turned into a loop. CVs stacked with logos. Deadlines postponed. Thesis neglected. Graduation delayed." "" "Many also list these internships under “Work Experience” on LinkedIn—sometimes without indicating the short-term or training nature of the role. " "" "Is that wrong? Not necessarily. " "" "It reflects how blurred the categories have become. When junior roles are scarce and signaling pressure is high, even a 6-week internship can be framed as a “position.” The issue isn’t dishonesty—it’s structural ambiguity. Platforms, universities, and employers have not agreed on where training ends and experience begins." "" "They’re not alone." "" "Across campuses, internship addiction is quietly normalizing. What looks like ambition may actually be anxiety—fuelled by unclear career signals, performative resume culture, and the shrinking of entry-level roles." "" "Here’s what recent research suggests:" "✔️ Internships act as social signals, not just skill builders (Spence, 1973)" "✔️ LinkedIn-style performance pressure inflates even short gigs into “roles” (Marwick & boyd, 2011)" "✔️ Full-time junior jobs are vanishing, replaced by unpaid cycles (Curiale, 2010)" "✔️ “Hustle capital” becomes currency, with no guardrails (Cabanas & Illouz, 2019)" "✔️ University career centers stay silent on what counts as real work" "✔️ Internships replace identity milestones, delaying diplomas (Arnett, 2000)" "" "Worse, it’s often system-driven, not student-driven." "" "When students start chasing brands more than building skills—or when collecting internships becomes more valued than completing school—then we have to ask:" "" "📌 What are we training them for?" "📌 What signals are we reinforcing?" "📌 Who’s responsible for helping them see the finish line?" "" "Internships are not the problem. But misframed internships are. The goal isn’t just to gain experience—it’s to advance with meaning, with clarity, with direction." "" "And we need to help them remember that. Having said that, many are helpless, are stubborn: think they know the answer all along! Disciplined they are not. An example of Dunning Krueger at its best!

Not because people resist change, but because pushing boundaries carries relational risk. Question a process, and you're called kurang ajar. Try to fix what isn’t yours, and you’re labeled ngototan. These aren’t just words. They’re cultural sanctions." "" "Across our universities, policy centers, and pilot programs, many so-called innovation models are not engines—they’re showroom pieces. Built to impress donors or fulfill KPIs. Chosen not because they work, but because they’re easy. They demand less change and give the illusion of progress through templates and shortcuts." "" "But innovation can’t be simulated. It must be built, stress-tested, and aligned with how people actually work and decide. " "" "Real innovation needs two things: discipline like Navy SEALs, and rebellion like pirates. Indonesia struggles with both.A student who questions is called “kurang ajar.” A junior who insists on improvement is labeled “ngototan.” These aren’t neutral—they are cultural sanctions. In a society where pushing boundaries is seen as arrogance, not initiative, how can innovation happen? Not through slogans. Not through imported frameworks. Only when the system stops punishing those who try differently will innovation stop hiding." "" "Meanwhile, Taiwan and China both deliver innovation—but through opposite logics. One runs on decentralized trust, soft coordination, and plural consensus. The other relies on top-down clarity, speed, and execution discipline. Both models work—because they match how their societies are structured to behave, not how they aspire to." "" "Indonesia often looks to China’s model. On paper, it fits: hierarchy, collectivism, strong state. But unlike China, Indonesia lacks the institutional backbone. Authority is personalized. Risk is negotiated. Innovation that pushes boundaries is often punished, not protected." "" "This is not a critique. It’s a cultural diagnosis." "" "I am deeply grateful to the esteemed editor of The Jakarta Post who publishes my humble op-ed "Innovation Isn’t Imported: What Indonesia Can Learn from Taiwan and China" https://lnkd.in/geRGGJzY" "" "Innovation isn’t a policy. " "It’s a cultural structure." "To reach Indonesia "Golden" 2045, " "we must stop importing frameworks " "and start asking:" ""What actually works here, with who we already are?"" "" "20250528

"" "I listed 20 in the article and here are some excerpts:" "" "1. Information Bias: to startups gathering a plethora of opinions without discerning which are truly beneficial." " 2. Diversification Bias: a startup might want mentors from various backgrounds even if not all those backgrounds are relevant to their domain." " 3. Wisdom of Crowds: Startups might seek multiple mentors believing that a collective advice might be more comprehensive." " 4. Naive Diversification: A startup might evenly distribute its attention among multiple mentors, regardless of each mentor's relevance or expertise." " 5. Network Effect: a startup might perceive a mentor as more valuable if they have a larger network or more affiliations." " 6. Feedback Loop:. Startups might believe that by having multiple mentors, they get more feedback, leading to better refinement of ideas." " 7. Scenario Planning: a startup might believe that diverse mentors can help them prepare for diverse business scenarios." " 8. Cultural Capital: Startups might seek mentors from diverse backgrounds to gain insights into various cultures." " 9. Best Practice Bias: A startup might want to implement practices from diverse industries believing they are universally effective." " 10. Halo Effect: A startup might perceive a mentor positively in all aspects due to one specific strength." " 11. Confirmation Bias: Startups might favor advice that aligns with their existing beliefs, leading to potential blind spots." " 12. Overconfidence Bias: Mentors might provide advice based on their own experiences without considering the startup's unique context." " 13. Analysis Paralysis: Startups with too many mentors might find it difficult to make decisions due to conflicting advice." " 14. Stereotyping: Making broad generalizations based on group characteristics." " 15. Cognitive Load: Managing relationships and advice from multiple mentors can be mentally taxing for startups." " 16. Choice Overload: Startups might feel overwhelmed if they receive a vast amount of diverse feedback." " 17. Status Quo Bias: Startups might resist changes suggested by mentors due to a comfort with their current strategies." " 18. Groupthink: A startup might conform to a popular viewpoint without critically analyzing it." " 19. Not Invented Here Syndrome: it’s from MIT! " " 20. Attribute Substitution: A startup might focus on the diversity of mentors as a marker of value instead of assessing the actual expertise each brings

"" "Ronnie never took to sports but walks daily. Disciplined. Never tolerated lateness in his team. But patient with slow thinkers—“People are different,” he said." "" "His work history reads like a timeline of Singapore’s hotel evolution:" "24 years at Shangri-La, Orange Grove Road. Then Tung Lok. Mandarin Orchard. Ritz-Carlton." "One son. One daughter. One granddaughter, 21." "One wife—who never worked outside the home. She prefers the house quiet now. So Ronnie goes out. Every day." "" "He takes three meals. Breakfast at work. Lunch. Then dinner—bought from the food centre, packed properly, respectfully—shared at home with his wife. A quiet evening ritual." "" "He receives CPF. Started at 55. Retirement payout at 65. But he doesn’t work out of necessity. He works because he still can. Still chooses to. Still contributes." "" "Only as I was about to leave, I learned:" "Ronnie is not a waiter." "" "He is the Allora Ristorante’s Breakfast Ambassador." "" "And he’s not alone." "There are 78-year-olds still teaching, guiding, thinking." "Not retired—but re-committed." "" "A country that honours its elders doesn’t fear the future—it learns from them." "What we need more of isn’t volume—but listening." "Because listening earns the right to speak." "" "“Listening is the skill of kings.”" "" "The exit isn’t speed or status: Still inspiring. Still kind. Still giving.

But this isn’t just about economics. It’s about how academia, across disciplines, outsources judgment to prestige." "" "Their finding?
