"" "This hurts not because I’m an economist (I’m not). It hurts because I recognize the pattern." "" "One of my articles has now been rejected thirteen times—by journals within the same publishing group. Each rejection says the same thing: “not aligned with our aims and scope.”" "" "But I did my homework. I studied the scope. Compared it line by line with accepted articles. Matched keywords. I even accepted their offer to transfer the paper—thirteen times. Same group. Same response." "" "What makes it worse is the illusion of process. Polite language masking exclusion. Praise for originality followed by silence. Again and again." "" "And I know I’m not alone. Many early-career researchers are told the problem is their writing. But what if it’s not?" "" "What if the system isn’t broken—but designed to protect sameness? What if cross-cultural, ethical, or interdisciplinary work is meant to be bounced around until we give up?" "" "Relevance is not measured by acceptance. Some of the most important work wasn’t accepted early. It was resisted, then remembered." "" "I don’t want to keep proving myself to systems built on performance and fake prestige. I’m not fighting to stay in the room." "" "Maybe I’ll step away—from the ivory towers, from the inflated egos industry, from the gatekeeping masquerading as feedback." "" "And maybe that’s not giving up. Maybe that’s just choosing peace." "" "Reference:" "Heckman, J. J., & Moktan, S. (2020). Publishing and promotion in economics: The tyranny of the top five. Journal of Economic Literature, 58(2), 419–470. https://lnkd.in/dGfAjcDh

"" "Pythagoras understood this danger long ago. The five-year silence required by Pythagoras is linked to the strict initiatory discipline of his philosophical school. New students—called akousmatikoi—were required to observe a five-year period of silence (ēchēn) as part of their training. This was not literal muteness at all times but a mandated refusal to speak in the classroom or ask questions. The purpose was:" "👁️ To cultivate deep listening before forming judgments." "👁️To train self-restraint as ethical and spiritual discipline." "👁️To test readiness for deeper understanding (mathēmatikoi stage)." "" "This practice reflects the Pythagorean belief: speech must follow understanding—not precede it." "" "Writing, for some, is not a tool to influence. Writing is a way of thinking." "It demands discipline, care, structure." "Speaking should be no less demanding." "" "References:" "" "Burkert, W. (1972). Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism." "Guthrie, W.K.C. (4 of 5) 𝖂𝖍𝖆𝖙 𝖎𝖋 𝖙𝖍𝖊 𝖑𝖆𝖗𝖌𝖊𝖘𝖙 𝖙𝖊𝖓𝖘𝖎𝖔𝖓 𝖎𝖓 𝖕𝖗𝖆𝖞𝖊𝖗 𝖎𝖘 𝖔𝖓𝖊 𝖘𝖊𝖓𝖙𝖊𝖓𝖈𝖊?" "𝘗𝘢𝘳𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘴: 𝘞𝘩𝘺 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘉𝘳𝘢𝘪𝘯 𝘙𝘦𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘯𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘙𝘪𝘵𝘶𝘢𝘭" "" "Because “who is in the heavens” creates a deliberate paradox. It follows Abba—a word of radical intimacy, relational closeness, and shared access—yet immediately introduces cosmic distance and transcendent authority." "" "The tension lies in what is held together:" "• Abba is familiar, personal, spoken in the vernacular." "• “Who is in the heavens” affirms that the one addressed is not local, not controllable, not humanlike—but sovereign, holy, and beyond comprehension." "" "Without that phrase, Abba risks being misread as casual or sentimental." "Without Abba, “who is in the heavens” reverts to distance, hierarchy, or fear." "" "Together, they form a structural tension that redefines how reverence and access can coexist. Nearness without presumption. Majesty without exclusion. That’s why it becomes the largest theological tension—in just one line." "" "In this installment of the series on ritual structure and mental architecture, I explore why this line is not a soft opening—but the load-bearing tension of the entire prayer. And why that structure matters now, in an era where every word is cheapened by noise." In a 2020 webinar hosted by the Indonesian Embassy in Moscow, led by His Excellency Azis Nurwahyudi (Deputy Chief of Mission), I stated that Indonesia would continue to rely on fossil energy in the foreseeable future¹. As I indicated during the presentation:" "" ""Russian energy sector players should view this as an opportunity to invest in Indonesia—not only in new and renewable energy, but also in the development of fossil energy using clean technology."¹" "" "Some will argue that hydrocarbons must remain in the ground. But reality imposes constraints. The shift to renewables cannot happen instantly—nor can it happen without structure. It takes decades, including the managed phase-out of aging and obsolete coal-fired power plants. Ideally, yes. Realistically, it’s painful. A transition of this scale requires not just technical planning but political will. Multisolving and stakeholder equity make it impossible without alignment across interest groups." "" "Indonesia’s high power distance may allow operational and policy-level alignment—but that does not guarantee unison in political will or follow-through. And even if political will emerges, whether the oligarchs agree remains unclear. Someone must still answer the hard, human question (as inhuman as it sounds): what’s in it for them? For their families? And for those they serve?" This signals a high level of perceived public sector corruption. With such an index, can we truly claim the moral ground for this transition—or for anything at all?" "" "This is not a matter of blame. It is a call to realism, discipline, and integrity. Environmental responsibility must not be reduced to slogans or pilot projects. It demands institutional clarity, long-term investment, and alignment of interest across all levels. The future must be cleaner, but also more honest. It can be done—if we plan, not just pronounce." 2025-03-31 Eid Mubarak from Indonesia. A moment to honor peace, renew gratitude, and strengthen the t...
Eid Mubarak from Indonesia. A moment to honor peace, renew gratitude, and strengthen the ties that move us forward—across faith, ventures, and shared purpose. May we build with heart, together." "" "Loren Eiseley once wrote:" "" "“The human brain is an imperfect instrument built up through long geological periods. Some of its levels of operation are more primitive and archaic than others. Our heads, modern man has learned, may contain weird and irrational shadows out of the subhuman past—shadows that under stress can sometimes elongate and fall darkly across the threshold of our rational lives. Man has lost the faith of the eighteenth century in the enlightening power of pure reason, for he has come to know that he is not a consistently reasoning animal. We have frightened ourselves with our own black nature and instead of thinking ‘We are men now, not beasts, and must live like men,’ we have eyed each other with wary suspicion and whispered in our hearts," "‘We will trust no one." "Man is evil. Man is an animal." "He has come from the dark wood and the caves.’”" "" "A Moslem friend once explained that Eid is a return to fitrah—to the original human nature: sincere, peaceful, and capable of compassion. After restraint and discipline, comes the call to begin again—not merely in ritual, but in how one lives and treats others." "" "For learners, for those building ventures, institutions, or ideas, this message offers something important. Suspicion, ego, and fear often dominate the systems people operate in. But there remains a choice: to build with conscience, to relate with respect, and to act not just from instinct, but from values." "" "May peace be with all. And may learners in every field remember the possibility of becoming more human, not less.

I learn humility—that’s conscious incompetence in the Dunning-Kruger diagram. It’s the same stage Mike Tyson stood in when he realized what he lacked, even at the top of the world." "" "When asked who punched harder—him or George Foreman—Tyson replied calmly: “He is. I can’t match somebody’s power who’s that big, with that much mass.” Then added, “The only thing that allowed me to be exciting was because I threw it faster than the other guys.”" "" "That’s conscious competence. He knew his edge. He didn’t copy power—he doubled down on speed. 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐲 𝐢𝐬 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐛𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐪𝐮𝐞—and Mike committed to that difference with discipline." "" "He had a great teacher who saw his gift before he did. That’s unconscious competence—raw potential shaped into precision." "" "But it didn’t begin there. Tyson was once unconsciously incompetent—a street kid full of rage, unaware of what he lacked. Structure, routine, and hard mentorship helped him see himself clearly." "" "After years of growth under Angelo Dundee—his father figure—Tyson rose. But after Dundee passed and Tyson faced chaos, he spiraled into unconscious incompetence again. He lost speed. He lost clarity—both in the ring and in life—despite fame and wealth." "" "So I bring his journey—and his short, honest answers—into the Dunning-Kruger framework." "" "In a recent interview, a teenage reporter asked him about legacy. Tyson replied:" "" "“I don’t believe in the word legacy. It’s just another word for ego. I’m just passing through. I’m gonna die and it’s going to be over. Who cares?”" "" "That’s not nihilism. That’s clarity. 𝐇𝐞 𝐧𝐨 𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐫 performs 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞. 𝐇𝐞 speaks 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐬𝐞𝐞𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧, but people listen. " "" "In boxing, Tyson now stands in conscious incompetence—he knows what he had, and what he lost. In life, perhaps he’s reached unconscious competence—not in speed or dominance, but in humility and presence." "" "𝐓𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐦𝐲 𝐬𝐭𝐮𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬—𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐠 𝐩𝐞𝐨𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐜𝐤 𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐬:" "🪬 Desire can’t be installed by a coach. A coach can guide, but the fire must come from within. It’s often shaped early—between ages 3 to 17—when memory, values, and identity are formed. A teacher can elicit it, but not inject it." "🪬 Don’t confuse visibility with value. Going viral doesn’t mean it’s meaningful. Tyson’s explosiveness wasn’t luck—it was built. Quietly. Over time." "🪬 Discipline lasts longer than talent. Fame fades. Process stays. Repetition becomes identity." "🪬 Many quit at conscious incompetence. That’s the hard stage—when flaws are visible, but mastery hasn’t arrived. Those who endure it go further than those who peak early and burn out." "🪬 Legacy is not the point. What matters is becoming present with who one is—not what others remember." "" "Where am I in this story?" "Like Tyson, I stand in conscious incompetence. I see what I lack. I learn. And I keep walking." "" "No shortcuts. Just process. That’s the only fight worth staying in.
2025-03-26 (5 of 5) Can We Return to Our Childhood? — Through the Shadows of Wayang"
(5 of 5) Can We Return to Our Childhood? — Through the Shadows of Wayang" "" "Wayang holds a unique place among the six traditional sources of knowledge. It is art—but also intuition, critique, and communal reflection. Around 1949, a figure known as Harsono Hadisuseno (sometimes referenced as Hadiharsono), then a government official, suggested that wayang could serve not only as entertainment but as a vehicle for national education. Some believe this marked the beginning of what would later be called Wayang Pancasila⁽*⁾—a symbolic retelling of the nation’s foundational values through familiar characters and classical form." "" "The power of Wayang is not in its realism, but in its reflection. Wayang has lived in the heart of Nusantara for around a millenia. More than performance, it is memory preserved in shadow — memory that bends with time, but does not fade. " "" "As written in the Kakawin Arjuna: “There are those who, on witnessing a Wayang play, are moved to tears and made melancholy and confused in spirit — even though they are all aware that what they see are but leather puppets, with only the illusion of speech and movement like people." "" "This anonymous composition may be part of that tradition." "" "A full Wayang Purwa structure, written in nine scenes — complete with Talu, Perang Kembang, and Sanggar Pamujan, where story, silence, and shadow all play their part." "" "Its story centers on a fictional kingdom where silence grows louder than command, where stillness replaces virtue, and where a throne erodes not by rebellion, but by forgetting. The tale names no figures. It does not claim prophecy." "" "Yet those familiar with the language of wayang—where meaning often rides behind metaphor—may sense something near." "" "This is Part 5 of the series exploring: Can we return to our childhood?" "" "Tradition answers through experience" "Science answered through laws." "Philosophy answered through frameworks." "Theology answered through longing." "Now, art answers — not with conclusions, but with echoes." "" "Let the Gending begin." "" "Click the article below for the complete scenes. " "" "⁽*⁾Brandon notes that the Wayang Pancasila genre “disappeared as quickly as new propaganda needs pushed it aside” (Brandon, 1997, p. 24). It used Pandawa characters to represent the five principles of Pancasila, combining mythic symbolism with national ideology. " "Brandon, J. R. (1997). On Thrones of Gold: Three Javanese Shadow Plays. Harvard University Press.

"" "In my search for answers, I’ve turned to four foundational forms of knowledge:" "🪬 Empirical science, where time, entropy, and irreversible systems challenge the idea of going back" "🪬 Philosophy, where frameworks like ontology, epistemology, and axiology confront the question of what is real, knowable, and valuable" "🪬 Tradition, which reminds us that memory is not just personal, but cultural and inherited" "" "Now: " "" "🪬 Theology, which invites us to consider whether our longing to return is not nostalgia — but a spiritual calling. This theological lens does not stand above the others — it stands alongside them." "" "Each tradition of knowledge reveals something the others cannot. Together, they form a fuller map of the human experience." "" "In this piece, I explore what "returning to childhood" means in a theological sense — across faiths thought — not as regression, but as restoration." "" "Not as sentimentality, but as spiritual clarity." "" "Maybe childhood isn’t a past we’ve lost — but a posture we’re called to rediscover." "" "Read the full article here
2025-03-26 (3 of 5 Part 2) It was proposed that philosophers, too, carry the longing to return to the...
(3 of 5 Part 2) It was proposed that philosophers, too, carry the longing to return to their childhood. This article explores how they attempt to answer that wish through their own philosophical frameworks. This article is an attempt to carry a desktop exercise for me wearing a hat of knowledge acquirer through philosophy. " "" "This is how a philosopher might respond to the wish to return to childhood: through frameworks of inquiry that do not seek literal return, but renewal — of perception, of meaning, of self." "" "I see this not as a desire to escape into innocence, but as a movement toward recovering the clarity of wonder — the kind of gaze that once asked without fear, noticed without bias, and stood before the world unguarded by doctrine or distraction." "" "For me, the philosophical response to the wish to return to childhood is not about regression, but renewal. It is an attempt to reawaken the original questions, to reclaim the freshness of perception, and to stay close to what once felt self-evident before language made it abstract.
2025-03-26 (3 of 5 Part 1) Can We Return to Childhood? A Philosophical Journey"
(3 of 5 Part 1) Can We Return to Childhood? A Philosophical Journey" "" "Motif: From a deep unease — a fear rooted in the current collapse of clarity, truth, and shared meaning. The falling Rupiah, the rise of authoritarian nostalgia, and a public sphere addicted to performance and spectacle have made me, once trained in engineering but now seeking grounding. Not out of naivety — but out of the need to reclaim something that feels lost. And so, I turned to philosophy. Not as abstract speculation, but as a tool for confronting the now." "" "Ontology — What Is Childhood? Heidegger reminds us that being is time-bound and always unfolding. Bergson would say we don’t "return" to moments; we carry their rhythm. Ontologically, childhood is not "back there" — it's a temporal mode of being we once inhabited and may still carry" "" "Epistemology — Can I Know My Childhood? Ricoeur reminds us that we don't remember the past directly; we narrate it. So the question becomes: What kind of knowledge is memory? It is emotional, embodied, and storied. To say "I know my childhood" is to say: I know what I need it to mean, now." "" "Axiology — Why Does It Matter? MacIntyre shows us modernity has fractured moral traditions. Childhood might represent a time when values were still whole. The desire to return is the desire for coherence, rootedness, and moral clarity." "" "Continental Philosophy — Language, Power, Trace Derrida says the "childhood" we seek is already a trace — never fully present, always shaped by the language we use to describe it. Foucault challenges our assumption of innocence: childhood may have been shaped by power and discipline. Ricoeur offers redemption: we construct self through narrative. " "" "Analytic Philosophy — Is the Question Coherent? Gilbert Ryle would warn against category errors — childhood is not a place you can travel to. Wittgenstein would ask: what language game are you playing? The analytic tradition doesn’t mock your longing, but it demands you clarify: are you speaking metaphorically or literally? Because if literal, the question collapses." "" "Virtue Ethics — What Kind of Person Desires This? Aristotle might say: the desire to return is the desire to flourish. MacIntyre hears mourning in your voice — mourning a broken moral world. C.S. Lewis sees hope: childhood as the place where virtue first stirs. " "" "Existentialism — What Does the Longing Reveal? Sartre says: you are fleeing your freedom. Kierkegaard says: you are in anxiety before becoming. Camus urges: revolt against absurdity. The longing to return is not naive; it is a crisis. One that demands you either freeze or choose. To return is impossible. But to become? That is still open." "" "Pragmatism — What Is the Use of This Longing? 2025-03-19 Hearing of the loss of Professor David Schmittlein brought back vivid memories of my inten...
Hearing of the loss of Professor David Schmittlein brought back vivid memories of my intensive travels between Singapore and Boston. From June 2016 to October 2017, I traveled back and forth, fully immersed in the MIT Sloan Executive Education ACE Program, that granted me an affiliated alumni status. Then, I took two additional courses in 2018. A few months after finishing these courses, I had the opportunity to meet him at an MIT reunion. If my memory serves me well, I may have encountered him previously at one of the school receptions." "" "This morning, as I looked at my certificates of accomplishment, when I saw his signature, something caught my attention, something harder to define. It wasn’t just the ink on the page or the formalities of certification. There was a pattern, a consistency in the way things worked, in how people carried themselves, in conversations that felt familiar even across different settings." "" "The confidence his team exuded, the way they empowered others, and the way conversations unfolded: it was clear this leadership culture wasn’t dictated, but absorbed. Professors weren’t just delivering content; they were pushing boundaries alongside students, questioning, refining, and co-creating knowledge. Each class felt like more than just a learning space. It was an expectation to engage, challenge, and extend knowledge beyond oneself. The classes didn’t encourage passive absorption, they mandated active sharing, questioning, and making others aware. There was an openness that wasn’t forced or performative. It was simply how things worked: automatic, part of their muscle memory." "" "Trying to make sense of this, I turned to the model for analyzing a workgroup¹: this culture apparently didn’t emerge by chance but reflected a deeper structure of how teams function under strong leadership. The framework highlights how leaders define corporate culture not through control but through recruitment choices, shared mental models, and the ability to mobilize unseen power. The kind that shapes behavior even without explicit directives. " "" "I recalled how collaboration weren’t enforced but ingrained, making me reflect on how leadership shapes entire group then individuals! Whether Schmittlein consciously designed it this way, I can’t say, but through this lens, I saw an embedded culture where alignment happened naturally, and expectations weren’t imposed but internalized. The structure or policies were tools to move idea, to make people work together safely, to flourish diversity. It is a leadership that quietly permeated lives! " "" "I may not have been a degree student, but I fit into that culture. I never felt like I was merely attending courses; I was immersed in something larger. Knowledge didn’t sit in silos. It moved across disciplines, across people, across ways of thinking, allowing it to flourish." "" "May he rest in peace." "⸻" "¹ McCaskey, M. B. (1983). A framework for analyzing work groups. Harvard Business School Teaching Note 9-476-053.

Are you being persecuted, oppressed and feel silenced? I am with you. Machiavelli’s silence was calculated. Nietzsche’s was defiant. Both were choices—pauses filled with purpose. But the silence of the oppressed is not chosen. It is forced. It does not empower; it erases." "" "When silence is imposed, it does not simply steal words—it takes identity. Every unheard cry is a piece of dignity torn away. Every voice stifled is a name forgotten. This silence is not empty. It is heavy. It lingers in the air, pressing down, swallowing those who endure it whole. And yet, even in the depths of erasure, something remains. A flicker. A breath. A waiting." "" "At first, the voice resists, clawing at the walls, searching for cracks, hoping to be heard. But the walls do not move. And then, for the first time, a scripture once distant takes shape in reality:" "" "“When you pray, pray in your closet.”" "" "This is not surrender. This is recognition. There is still a listener." "" "Where the world silences, something beyond it hears:" "Søren Kierkegaard spoke of the weight of an unheard truth. " "Simone Weil understood that suffering is not just pain—it is being stripped of expression." "Hannah Arendt warned that silence, when imposed, does not simply mute—it rewrites reality." "" "Yet what cannot be spoken does not disappear. It sinks deeper, where words become something else -" "" "A prayer. A thought. A defiance." "" "“I was mute and silent; I held my peace to no avail, and my distress grew worse.” (Psalm 39)" "" "Not all silence is absence." "Some are waiting to be answered." "" "Dedicated:" "" "For the oppressed and the persecuted." "For those who have waited—too long." "For those at the crossroads, trapped in the in-between." "For those in the terror tunnel, confined by threats, unseen." "For those who cannot walk high, who move in shadows, unheard." "" "For those cast aside, again and again—" "Rejected by companies, by families, by friends." "By schools that close their doors." "By Scopus Q1 indexed journals that play gods, deciding who is worthy of words." "" "For the unheard, the unseen, the ones the world forgets." "For those who carry silence, heavy as stone, waiting to be met." "" "==============================" "" "Niccolò Machiavelli – “It is a common fault not to anticipate storms when the sea is calm.”" "Friedrich Nietzsche – “The silence of the eternal spaces terrifies me.”" "Søren Kierkegaard – “The eternal truth is not noisy; it does not try to be noticed. It is content to be.”" "Simone Weil – “Even if, through his stammerings, he should utter a cry to pierce the soul, neither the magistrate nor the public will hear it. His cry is mute.”" "Hannah Arendt – “The sad truth is that most evil is done by people who never make up their minds to be good or evil—they simply go along, silently.”
2025-03-10 (2 of 3) Warranted Intimacy: The Speech of the Chosen - Disclaimer: This reflection is int...
(2 of 3) Warranted Intimacy: The Speech of the Chosen - Disclaimer: This reflection is intended for a limited audience and is a personal exploration of suffering, history, and human endurance. It is not meant to persuade, impose, or challenge any belief system. Readers are encouraged to engage at their discretion." "" "Throughout history, those with the deepest faith have also been those who dared to confront God. Faith, at its most profound, does not merely endure silence—it speaks into it, wrestles with it, demands justice from it." "" "In Warranted Intimacy: The Speech of the Chosen, I explored how figures in the Bible—Job, Jeremiah, David, Moses, Habakkuk, and even Jesus—engaged in raw, unfiltered conversations with the divine. They did not speak from rebellion but from relationship. Their bold challenges were not acts of doubt but of trust. Only those who truly belonged to God could speak so honestly with Him. Their grievances, their accusations, their cries of abandonment—these were not rejections of faith but rather the most sacred expressions of it." "" "Elie Wiesel stands in this lineage. His trial of God after Auschwitz, his refusal to accept divine silence passively, his protests against heaven—these are not signs of lost belief but of a faith that has been to the depths and still refuses to let go. Like Job, he asked questions that had no easy answers. Like Jeremiah, he accused God of injustice. Like Christ on the cross, he cried out in divine abandonment. And yet, in all this, he never renounced his faith." "" "His defiance was faith in its most wounded, yet most enduring, form." "" "In the same way that Moses dared to say, 'Show me Your glory,' and Abraham demanded, 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?', Wiesel stood before God and prosecuted Him—not from irreverence, but from a place of intimacy. He did what only those who truly know God can do: he held Him accountable." "" "In this article, I continue the exploration of this sacred paradox—how faith is not merely about obedience, but about the courage to demand answers, to insist on justice, to cry out into the silence. Wiesel’s story is not an exception to the biblical tradition of protest; it is a continuation of it." "" "The ANSWER in form of question remains, for those of us who have wrestled, who have lost, who have demanded justice from heaven: " "" "How can you not believe in God after Auschwitz?" Grateful that my research method chapter “Qual-Quant-Quant/Qual-Qual Mixed Method: Autoethnography in Building System Dynamics' Causal Loop Diagram” has been published in International Journal of Multiple Research Approaches, 2024, Vol 16, Issue 2, p132-154" "" "🔗 DOI: https://lnkd.in/gVKDGszb ($30—see the first comment for details)." "📖 Journal eISSN: 1834-0814 | ISSN: 1834-0806" "🔗 Journal link: https://lnkd.in/gnyCHyUb" "🔗 Citation: Tambun, A. R. Y., Yudoko, G., & Aldianto, L. (2024). Qual-Quant-Quant/Qual-Qual Mixed Method: Autoethnography in Building System Dynamics' Causal Loop Diagram. International Journal of Multiple Research Approaches, 16(2) https://lnkd.in/gHhHb9he" "" "Although the journal is not yet Scopus-indexed, I deeply appreciated the editorial and review process—one of the most rigorous I have encountered in terms of world-class academic writing standards." "" "I first submitted the manuscript on 30 August 2024 via the ScholarOne platform https://lnkd.in/gq9HTzZW . It was returned for review on 4 September, underwent extensive revisions, and after a thorough back-and-forth review process, I received the Letter of Acceptance on 28 November. The Copyright Agreement was signed on 4 February 2025, and now, it is officially published." "" "A special thanks to the esteemed Editor-in-Chief, Professor Anthony Onwuegbuzie and to the Managing Director, Professor Donggil Song for leading an exceptional editorial team. Their dedication and expertise made this an invaluable academic experience." "" "Abstract" "This article develops a novel mixed methods research framework to investigate the corporate-backed, university-based Indonesian innovation and entrepreneurial ecosystem. The framework integrates autoethnography and system dynamics, combining qualitative and quantitative research approaches to capture the dynamic interactions within the ecosystem. Autoethnography provides deep insights into entrepreneurs' lived experiences through personal narratives and observations, while system dynamics models complex interactions, identifying leverage points and evaluating policy impacts. This study contributes to the field of mixed methods research by demonstrating how the integration of interpretivist and constructivist approaches through autoethnography with the empirical rigor of system dynamics enhances the modeling of complex systems. The research offers a methodological innovation that addresses a gap in the mixed methods research literature, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding entrepreneurial ecosystems and for informing policy development in similar contexts. This approach exemplifies how mixed methods research can be leveraged to produce actionable insights, particularly in contexts requiring both rich qualitative data and robust quantitative modeling.

"" "To strengthen economic resilience, the government has introduced tax reforms, industrial incentives, sovereign wealth management, and public-private partnerships. "" "Globally, sovereign wealth funds have driven economic transformation. Norway’s $1.4 trillion GPFG provides stability through global investments, while Singapore’s $287 billion Temasek accelerates industrial and tech growth. Can Danantara achieve the same in Indonesia?" " " "𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗹𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆." "" "No policy measure, no matter how well-designed, can succeed without deeper cultural transformation." "" "Even the most skilled policymakers cannot implement lasting change without institutional and cultural reform. Policies like tax reforms, industrial strategies, and Danantara are only as effective as the system they operate in. "" "Without addressing these barriers, all rational economic efforts, including Danantara, will ultimately fail." "" "Wishing the best for the government in navigating these challenges. They have perhaps the best economic team since the Berkeley Team in the New Order Era. " "" "However, no economic strategy will create lasting impact without a fundamental cultural transformation." "" "A long-term cultural shift spanning 50–75 years (2–3 generations) is essential for meaningful transformation. 2025-03-01 Communication is more than just words—it carries layers of meaning shaped by culture, hier...
Communication is more than just words—it carries layers of meaning shaped by culture, hierarchy, and social etiquette. In Indonesian culture, responses to missed calls such as "Ada apa?" or "Kenapa, Pak?" may sound normal in some contexts but inappropriate in others. This distinction is not a generational change but rather a reflection of deeply rooted cultural norms regarding politeness, respect, and hierarchy. I take time to write the scientific reasons behind. " "" "In practice, when responding to a missed call, the choice of words subtly signals recognition of status and social norms." "" "1. Why “Ada Apa?” or “Kenapa, Pak?” Can Be Problematic" "For a student responding to a teacher or a younger person to an elder, saying "Ada apa, Pak?" or "Kenapa?" can feel abrupt. It assumes that the call was urgent and immediately demands an explanation, which can be perceived as lacking deference. " "" "A more appropriate response would be:" ""Maaf, saya tadi tidak sempat angkat. Ada yang bisa saya bantu, Pak?" (Thanks Shabrina Wahyu Mulyani)" ""Tadi Bapak menelepon saya?"" "" "These responses maintain politeness while showing attentiveness, without sounding demanding or impatient." "" "2. Why Higher-Ranked Individuals Rarely Say “Ada Apa?” because:" "🍇 Maintaining Social Harmony – Indonesian culture values rasa sungkan (a sense of deference) and tepa selira(mutual respect). Higher-ranked individuals tend to use softer, more open-ended responses." "🍇 Grace in Leadership – Politeness is an unspoken expectation for those in higher positions, reinforcing authority through measured and respectful communication." "🍇 Encouraging Voluntary Explanation – Rather than directly asking why someone called, they allow the other person to naturally state their reason for calling." "" "3. Why Some Still Say "Ada Apa?" Despite Their Age or Status" "" "While hierarchy influences communication, personal style and informality also play a role. Among peers, close colleagues, or friends, "Ada apa?" is common and generally not considered rude. However, tone and context matter—when said in a neutral or friendly tone, it may not come across as abrupt." "" "Language is not just about conveying messages but also about navigating relationships. Mastering culturally correct communication is a valuable skill that fosters respect and professionalism in any setting." "" "Thanks Adriel Tohonan Simamora Andersen Tan Fahimudin Tamash et al

Not all gatherings are eventful, but this one was—remarkably so. A dark room, secluded and private, where only invited guests could enter—whispering a password at the door. The scent of cigars lingered, mixing with the low hum of conversation. Dusk lights cast shadows, faces half-illuminated, words carried in careful tones. I had expected cold nights and small talk, distance in conversations that never quite reach beyond the surface. But after an intensive week of structured learning—12-hour days filled with problem-solving, execution, and the rigor of an entrepreneurial bootcamp—I was still in recovery mode. I wasn’t sure if my mind was ready for another deep engagement." "" "Yet, as the evening unfolded, something unexpected happened. Conversations moved effortlessly—from governance to sustainability, from business to social impact. No debates, no need to prove anything—just an exchange of perspectives that sharpened understanding. "𝘈𝘴 𝘪𝘳𝘰𝘯 𝘴𝘩𝘢𝘳𝘱𝘦𝘯𝘴 𝘪𝘳𝘰𝘯, 𝘴𝘰 𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘰𝘯 𝘴𝘩𝘢𝘳𝘱𝘦𝘯𝘴 𝘢𝘯𝘰𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳"⁽*⁾. That realization made the evening more than just a meeting of minds; it was a quiet confirmation that words and actions ripple beyond what is immediately visible." "" "For my young audience, meaningful growth rarely happens alone. The most valuable learning comes through engagement with those who challenge and expand thinking. This is where rebel talent thrives—authenticity, perspective, curiosity, novelty, and diversity all in motion. Not passive listening, but active questioning. Not just absorbing knowledge, but testing ideas in real time." "" "The contrast between the bootcamp and this gathering made one thing clear. Structured intensity builds discipline, but fluid conversations build depth. Both are necessary. One sharpens skills; the other sharpens vision. Together, they shape a way of thinking that is both grounded and adaptive." "" "On a lighter note, I had planned to reset with an 8km walk afterward, but safety concerns in Jakarta at midnight reduced it to 2.5km. Not enough to clear the system, but just enough to reflect on an evening that left much to think about." "" "Grateful for the opportunity to engage in such meaningful discussions, and to the Harvard Club of Indonesia for making this gathering possible. Out of respect for privacy, I won’t tag names." (6 of 7) TEACHING NOTE: DARVO: A Hidden Pattern in Corporate Crisis Communication" "" "When corporate scandals erupt, the response may follow a familiar script—denial, counterattacks, and an attempt to claim victimhood. This pattern aligns with a psychological framework known as DARVO (Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender). Originally studied in interpersonal misconduct cases, DARVO may also emerge in business and financial crises, often without those using it even realizing it." "" "Take the recent eFishery anticlimax as an example. Faced with allegations of financial misconduct, responses from both company leadership and investors may reflect DARVO tactics:" "" "𝗗𝗘𝗡𝗜𝗔𝗟: Emphasizing commitment to ethics rather than addressing specific allegations." "𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗔𝗖𝗞: Discrediting accusers or shifting focus to external pressures." "𝗥𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗦𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗩𝗜𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗠 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗢𝗙𝗙𝗘𝗡𝗗𝗘𝗥: Positioning themselves as the ones suffering harm rather than those responsible." "" "Most executives and organizations deploying DARVO may not consciously intend to use it—it is often an instinctive reaction to protect reputations and financial interests. But recognizing this pattern is crucial for investors, regulators, and the public to critically assess corporate responses in crisis situations." "" "🔍 What do you think? Have you seen DARVO tactics in corporate scandals before?" 🚨 University Reform in Indonesia: Ambition vs. Reality 🚨" "A recent policy address on higher education outlined bold aspirations—universities as engines of national development, research driving innovation, and a shift from bureaucracy to impact. Yet, history shows that policy statements alone do not transform institutions. " "" "The question remains: Can these reforms succeed when the underlying shared assumptions—hierarchical governance, shortcut mentality, and exclusive collectivism—remain intact?" "" "Every few years, policymakers introduce new programs, incentives, and KPIs to push Indonesian universities toward innovation and real-world impact. Yet, time and time again, these reforms fail to deliver meaningful change." "" "Why? Because cultural fit matters. You can’t impose a system that contradicts deeply ingrained shared assumptions and expect it to succeed." "" "In my latest article, I analyze:" "✅ Why past university reforms have struggled to shift cultural foundations" "✅ Lessons from South Korea, Japan, and Finland on what works (and what doesn’t)" "✅ Why simply introducing an "innovation engine" will fail unless deep-seated cultural norms evolve" "" "🚨No Reform Succeeds Unless Our Culture (READ: Shared Assumptions) Fits 🚨" "" "Indonesia’s deeply ingrained cultural traits—hierarchical decision-making, risk aversion, shortcut mentality, and exclusive collectivism—shape how universities operate. These are not just habits; they are shared assumptions that dictate institutional behavior. Policies must align with these realities before they can change them." "" "🚀 Start now by understanding and accepting t₀ of our culture." "" "Reform begins not by imposing change, but by recognizing our current cultural reality and working from there. Cultural transformation takes time—50 to 75 years, or two to three generations. The longer we wait, the harder it becomes to break free from institutional inertia." "" "I explore why education reform in Indonesia will remain surface-level unless cultural transformation is prioritized." "" "💡 Examples: " "📌 South Korea succeeded by gradually shifting incentives and breaking hierarchy in research." "📌 Japan struggled because cultural inertia blocked real change, despite strong policies." "📌 Finland is a rare case where shared assumptions changed first, leading to deep and lasting reform." "" "➡ For Indonesia, simply introducing new policies (like an innovation engine) will fail unless deeper cultural shifts occur." "➡ If corruption, shortcut mentality, and exclusive collectivism remain dominant, reform will be a surface-level exercise." "🔑 The most critical factor: Cultural Fit." "" "https://lnkd.in/gE8KcZ5q

Many students who have experienced learning with me know that I always assign at least one student—whom I observe has special needs or struggles to focus—to be the designated ChatGPT class operator. Meanwhile, the rest of the class is required to close their computers and phones for most of the session. This practice is based on a clear principle: allocating brain energy to active listening and deep processing rather than spreading attention across multiple apps and distractions. By doing so, students develop stronger cognitive discipline, sharpening their ability to engage in discussions without relying on external tools as a mental crutch." "" "The real distinction is not in AI itself but in the ability of individuals—both students and teachers—to use it wisely. Those who approach AI with curiosity, discipline, and a willingness to think critically will strengthen their cognitive abilities and stay ahead. In contrast, those who struggle with self-regulation, avoid challenges, or resist technological advancements will find themselves increasingly dependent, overwhelmed, or disconnected from meaningful learning. The future belongs to those who see AI not as a replacement for thinking but as a tool to push their intellectual boundaries." "" "Students and teachers alike interact with ChatGPT in ways that reflect their own capacity, mindset, and personal discipline. The tool itself does not shape learning outcomes—rather, it amplifies the abilities and limitations of those who use it." "" "This variation in how students engage with AI highlights a critical distinction: while some use ChatGPT to expand their learning and thinking, others become overly dependent on it, leading to cognitive stagnation. The same applies to teachers—those who adapt and integrate AI responsibly will enhance their intellectual capacity, while those who resist it may struggle to remain effective. A 4.0 GPA is just a number—many have achieved it, including my students. But for me, it is special, something to be grateful for and to cherish—not because of the number itself, but because of the grace that made it possible. I hold onto this moment, hoping to carry it with me all the way to graduation, knowing that it is not a guarantee, but a gift." "" "More than anything, it is a reminder to never take anything for granted. It wasn’t just about discipline or persistence—𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗱 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴. I don’t feel smarter, just deeply grateful—to my professors who guided me, to every moment that shaped me, and above all, to 𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲." "" "At this stage in life, every step in learning feels like a gift. Life has its way of throwing surprises—sometimes good, sometimes not. I’ve faced rejection, alienation, envy, even bullying (believe it or not). I’ve been deceived, betrayed, and caught off guard more times than I can count (perhaps simply because I never learned to see the world through a political lens). " "" "Through it all, my work ethic has never really changed actually. If anything, I was probably even more perfectionist in the past. "" "But life is "funny". Sometimes it rewards, sometimes it punishes—smart work doesn’t always lead to recognition. 2025-02-09 I was invited to watch a Barongsai and dragon dance performance. As the drums thundered, t...
I was invited to watch a Barongsai and dragon dance performance. As the drums thundered, the lion leaped, and the dragon weaved through the air with fluid grace, I felt something unfamiliar—an eerie mix of awe and displacement. It was my first time seeing this live." "" "For those alienated Indonesian Chinese descendants kids, despite their families having lived in Indonesia for five, six, or even seven generations since the 1800s, growing up between 1966 and the late 1990s meant never seeing this in real life. They grew up without the pulse of the drums, without the thrill of the lion’s playful agility or the dragon’s sweeping grandeur. Barongsai and Tari Naga existed only in stories, in faded photographs, in whispers of a culture that had been silenced. For decades, these symbols of strength, wisdom, and prosperity were erased from public life, leaving behind an emptiness too subtle to articulate, yet deeply felt." "" "Then, in 2000, President Gus Dur lifted the ban. What was once forbidden roared back to life—not just as a performance, but as a reclamation." "" "This afternoon, as I stood there watching, I realized this was more than a dance. It was history moving before my eyes, a culture returning to its rightful place." "" "Repression, persecution, alienation—those who endure them do not break. They emerge unshaken, like diamonds, gleaming in the light.

Read the full analysis here: https://lnkd.in/gTi67ted ²" "" "Temasek, SoftBank, Sequoia Capital India, and Northstar etc backed eFishery to unicorn status, but when financial misrepresentation unraveled, attention fell solely on the founders. Yet, investor biases may have played a role in letting the fraud persist since 2018." "" "🔹 Confirmation Bias – Investors accepted information that fit their expectations and ignored red flags." "🔹 Optimism Bias – They assumed financial missteps were just "growing pains" rather than signs of fraud." "🔹 Sunk Cost Fallacy – Instead of reassessing risks, they kept funding to justify prior investments." "🔹 Illusion of Control Bias – Some believed their influence could correct governance issues." "🔹 Halo Effect Bias – A founder’s past success was mistaken as proof they could scale a company." "🔹 Authority Bias – Investors deferred to influential backers and charismatic founders." "🔹 Hindsight Bias – After the fraud was exposed, many claimed the red flags had been obvious all along." "🔹 Status Quo Bias – Investors resisted stricter governance even after repeated startup failures." "" "Venture capital isn’t the problem—but without stronger due diligence, financial misrepresentation will continue." "" "Which biases do you think contributed most to the fraud going unnoticed for so long?" Have you ever wondered what type of company you work for in terms of its market reach, operational strategies, and degree of localization?" "" "Many professionals focus on job roles and career growth, but the company’s structure determines decision-making speed, operational flexibility, and cultural fit." "🔹 Is your company an international firm that exports its products with minimal local adaptation?" "🔹 Are you in a multinational company that tailors strategies for different markets?" "🔹 Does your employer operate as a transnational company, balancing global integration with strong regional autonomy?" "🔹 Is it a global company, where branding and operations are standardized worldwide?" "🔹 Or a regional company, focused on dominating a specific geographic area?" "" "📌 In my latest article, I explore how companies evolve between these structures. A case in point is SLB (formerly Schlumberger)—once a transnational firm with strong regional autonomy, now shifting toward a multinational model with centralized leadership." "👉 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐦𝐞𝐚𝐧 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐞𝐞𝐬?" "In the early 2000s, Schlumberger employees had significant regional autonomy—local decision-making, regional innovation centers, and flexibility in adapting to market conditions. Today, SLB operates under a centralized structure, with stronger global coordination and standardization." "" "No wonder, back then, we were told that our passport wasn’t green, red, or blue based on nationality—it was the Schlumberger Blue passport. Employees could be mobilized across borders within hours. That level of flexibility may no longer be the case today." "" "This shift is not unique to SLB—many companies that were transnational in the 1990s and early 2000s have moved toward more centralized multinational models due to globalization, digital transformation, and cost-efficiency strategies." "" "📌 𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐨 𝐲𝐨𝐮?" "If you’re considering a new job or trying to better understand your workplace, ask yourself:" "✅ How does your company make decisions—centrally or regionally?" "✅ How much flexibility do local teams have?" "✅ Does the company adapt to different markets or enforce uniform strategies globally?" "The answers shape your experience, expectations, and long-term career fit." 2025-02-05 The Beatitudes Series: 5th of 5 articles. Happiness had always been a mystery to me. It fe...
The Beatitudes Series: 5th of 5 articles. Happiness had always been a mystery to me. It felt like something just out of reach, something tied to the next achievement, the next possession, the next milestone. If only I had this, if only I accomplished that—then, maybe, I would be happy. The pattern was predictable: every time a goal was reached, a new one took its place. Satisfaction was fleeting, and happiness remained elusive. " "" "In hindsight, this was how I had understood happiness when I had the honor to deliver a commencement speech as the representative of my graduating class - IPMI (IPMI Institute) Full-Time February 2000. The first topic that came to mind was happiness. " "" "𝑾𝒉𝒂𝒕 𝒅𝒐𝒆𝒔 𝒊𝒕 𝒎𝒆𝒂𝒏 𝒕𝒐 𝒃𝒆 𝒕𝒓𝒖𝒍𝒚 𝒉𝒂𝒑𝒑𝒚? 𝑾𝒉𝒚 𝒅𝒐 𝒑𝒆𝒐𝒑𝒍𝒆 𝒄𝒐𝒏𝒔𝒕𝒂𝒏𝒕𝒍𝒚 𝒄𝒉𝒂𝒔𝒆 𝒂𝒇𝒕𝒆𝒓 𝒕𝒉𝒊𝒏𝒈𝒔 𝒕𝒉𝒆𝒚 𝒃𝒆𝒍𝒊𝒆𝒗𝒆 𝒘𝒊𝒍𝒍 𝒃𝒓𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒕𝒉𝒆𝒎 𝒉𝒂𝒑𝒑𝒊𝒏𝒆𝒔𝒔, 𝒐𝒏𝒍𝒚 𝒕𝒐 𝒇𝒊𝒏𝒅 𝒊𝒕 𝒔𝒍𝒊𝒑𝒑𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒂𝒘𝒂𝒚? " "" "These were questions I had pondered for years, and I knew I wanted to explore them in my speech. The process of writing that speech was an enlightenment of its own, and my thoughts have continued to evolve ever since. " "" "One book that came to mind right away was Robert H. Schuller’s The Be (Happy) Attitudes: 8 Positive Attitudes That Can Transform Your Life¹. I had first come across it during a work assignment in Mumbai (was Bombay) in 1997, when Schlumberger stationed me there for seismic services in Geco Sapphire for ONGC. One of my favorite pastimes in India was visiting bookstores, where books were not only abundant but also incredibly affordable. I had bought a handful of titles that day, including Schuller’s book, for Rs 55—a small price for something that would later leave a lasting impact on me. " "" "Though I had read the book back then, it was only in 2001, as I prepared my speech, that I revisited it with a new perspective. Schuller’s reflections on happiness, rooted in the Beatitudes, resonated deeply with the realizations I had come to over the years. His insights helped me frame what I wanted to share with my peers as we stood at the threshold of our next journey." "" "And so, my speech took shape. What follows is the original speech as I gave it that day March 15, 2001" "" "Paul Tambunan, Wikandaru, M. Sitepu, Budisantoso Tjong, Indra Kurniawan - my GFP Team" "" "¹ Schuller, R. H. (1986). The be (happy) attitudes: 8 positive attitudes that can transform your life. Bantam Books." 𝘋𝘐𝘚𝘊𝘓𝘈𝘐𝘔𝘌𝘙: This article engages with Luke 16 as a literary and historical text within an academic framework. It is not intended to promote any religious belief. If you do not engage with biblical literature in this context, you may wish to refrain from reading further." "" "Many claim to stand for justice and integrity, yet when corruption prevails, their true allegiance is revealed—not to principles (no to the ultimate God in Sila Pertama), but to wealth and power. Ancient wisdom warns that when material gain takes precedence over honesty, institutions crumble, and societies decay." "" "If a nation cannot be trusted in small matters, how can it uphold justice? When leaders exploit power for personal gain, governance collapses, and citizens lose faith in reform. Bribery, nepotism, and embezzlement drain resources meant for the vulnerable, deepening inequality." "" "And when corruption becomes second nature, the disease infects not just individuals, but the entire system. Corruption is so deeply entrenched, ingrained in reflexes, systems, and mental models" "" "𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐫𝐮𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧—𝐚𝐧 𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐢𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞! 𝐈𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞, 𝐮𝐧𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐮𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲." "" "A cancer so advanced it resembles a Stage 4 or Stage 5. No medicine. No radiology. No chemical treatments. Khalas! (!خلاص). Greed has not simply gone astray—it has decayed, rotted, and reeks beyond isolation. The stench cannot be contained. The body itself must perish for the sickness to be eradicated." "" "But does it have to be this way?" "" "I wrote about this in "Beyond Shame: Ethical Dimensions of Mindsets in Corruption", published by The Jakarta Post. https://lnkd.in/gUU3dNNy and https://lnkd.in/g9jR_GBP). It explores the contrast between shame-based (𝐤𝐨𝐫𝐮𝐩𝐬𝐢 𝐣𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐮𝐬 𝐚𝐬𝐚𝐥 𝐠𝐚𝐤 𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐡𝐮𝐚𝐧, 𝐚𝐬𝐚𝐥 𝐛𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐠-𝐛𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐠) and guilt-based cultures in shaping corruption." "" "But corruption will not end overnight. Reversing corruption takes two to three generations—50 to 75 years—because it is not just a policy issue. It is a system-1 mental model, a nation’s muscle memory, deeply embedded over time. " "" "Real change happens when people stop tolerating corruption and start demanding justice. A society where wrongdoing goes unpunished cannot sustain fairness or progress." "" "If reform does not begin now, when will it?" "" "A fundamental truth remains: “if you cannot be trusted (𝐴𝑀𝐼𝑁𝐴*) with unrighteous Mammon, who will entrust (𝑌𝐴𝑇𝑀𝐼𝑁*) you with true riches (𝐴𝑀𝐼𝑁*)?" "" "History shows that societies built on deception collapse from within. Where corruption thrives, moral integrity disappears, inequality deepens, and trust erodes. It is a breach to the "Kemanusiaan yang Adil dan Beradab"" "" "* in Aramaic" "" "This article is continuation of the first part https://lnkd.in/gnckDma4 explaining Luke 16:1-7 "(1 of 2) Parables of the Shrewd Manager: a childlike trust in the unqualified mercy of God as their only hope for salvation"" "

NOTE from Thich Nhat Han's Session" "" "🙏 Mindfulness in talking and listening, as well as mindful consumption." "🙏Mindfulness is full awareness of one's surroundings." "🙏Mindful breathing is a form of communication." "🙏The more you continue to talk, the more you get caught up in your words." "🙏You have to return to yourself to listen to both your happiness and the pain in your body." "🙏Your body is an essential part of your home." "🙏Breathing in, I am aware of my body; breathing out, I send away the sorrow." "🙏Breathing connects your body, mind, and feelings." "🙏Home is the here and now." "🙏Recover yourself and reconnect with yourself with every step you take." "🙏Acknowledging our feelings without pushing them away or judging them is an act of homecoming." "🙏Understanding suffering brings compassion." "🙏Loving yourself is the foundation of compassion." "🙏Self-understanding is important for understanding others." "🙏Self-love is essential to loving others." "🙏When you truly come home to yourself, you understand your suffering and become able to cultivate happiness." "🙏What we consume with our eyes, ears, and minds is also food." "🙏Communication is both nutrition and nourishment." "🙏What you read and write can heal you. Everything you write down can heal both you and those who read it." "🙏Conversation is a form of nourishment. Mindfulness in speaking and listening is important." "🙏When you read or listen to something, be mindful of toxic communication." "🙏Mindfulness is like skin that protects us from toxic communication." "🙏Home is the place where loneliness disappears." "🙏With each in-breath and out-breath, we pave our way home." "🙏Home is within us. Mindful breathing is a form of communication." "🙏Freedom is the foundation of happiness. You can attain freedom by connecting your mind and feelings." "🙏Stop thinking and talking, and listen to your body. Mindfulness allows us to recognize and take care of our suffering." "🙏Take time to sit and pause as a practice of mindfulness." "When you sit and breathe mindfully, your mind and body can reunite." "🙏To bring awareness to your body: Breathing in, I am aware of my body; breathing out, I send away my sorrow." "🙏When you walk, stop thinking about other things and focus on your steps. With each step, say to yourself, "I am home." Feel the connection in every step with the earth." "🙏When we bring mindfulness to our steps, we become aware of the existence of both our body and the earth." "🙏Deep listening must come first; it has the power to heal suffering." "🙏What you say and write can nourish your body and those around you." "🙏Speak truthfully, gently, lovingly, and protectively. Be true to yourself." "🙏Tell the truth. Don't exaggerate, manipulate, or use hateful language—speak peacefully." "🙏Our compassion brings happiness and peace.
2025-02-02 (4 of 7) Poverty Breeds Corruption—Wealth Exploits It Corruption is often seen as a tool o...
(4 of 7) 𝗣𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘁𝘆 𝗕𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗱𝘀 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗿𝘂𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻—𝗪𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗼𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗜𝘁 Corruption is often seen as a tool of the powerful, but poverty is an even stronger driver of unethical behavior. Economic hardship forces individuals into survival mode, where corruption becomes a necessity rather than a choice. At the same time, wealth does not eliminate corruption—it refines it. The poor engage in corruption out of desperation, while the rich use it to maintain power. However, poverty remains the stronger predictor of corrupt acts." "" "𝗣𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘁𝘆: 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗿𝘂𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝘀 𝗦𝘂𝗿𝘃𝗶𝘃𝗮𝗹" "Growing up in deprivation normalizes corruption. Liu and Peng (2015) found that bribery in schools teaches children that unethical shortcuts are necessary for advancement. Transparency International (2023) highlights how early exposure to corruption—whether paying off officials or securing jobs through nepotism—makes it seem like a survival strategy rather than a moral failure. The scarcity mindset (Sheehy-Skeffington & Rea, 2017) further reinforces corruption, forcing individuals to prioritize immediate survival over ethics. Worlu et al. (2023) found that economic hardship weakens family structures, reducing moral reinforcement. Fergusson et al. (2004) linked poverty to higher crime rates, emphasizing that structural failures push the disadvantaged toward corruption." "" "𝗪𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵: 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗿𝘂𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝘀 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹" "Affluence doesn’t eliminate corruption—it transforms it. You and Khagram (2005) argue that wealth enables bribery, regulatory manipulation, and influence-peddling. The elite engage in corruption not out of necessity, but as a calculated tool to consolidate power. Wealth can provide a moral buffer. Worlu et al. (2023) found that children in stable, affluent families were less prone to corruption. However, in weak institutional settings, the rich still manipulate systems for personal gain, proving that corruption in affluence is about entitlement, not need." "" "𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗣𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘁𝘆" "Both rich and poor engage in corruption, but the poor are more vulnerable. Poverty forces people to justify corruption for survival, while the rich corrupt systems to stay in control. Addressing corruption requires more than economic growth—it demands strong institutions, ethical education, and transparency to break the cycle that keeps the disadvantaged trapped and the elite untouchable." 2025-01-31 (2 of 7) The recent fraud saga by an Indonesian unicorn startup1 has not only shaken Indon...
(2 of 7) The recent fraud saga by an Indonesian unicorn startup¹ has not only shaken Indonesia's start-up ecosystem but also raised critical questions about corporate governance and ethical accountability. As reported by The Jakarta Post, eFishery inflated its revenue by nearly $600 million for 3 quarters in 2024 and exaggerated its operations, tarnishing Indonesia's wannabee image reputation as a thriving hub for innovation.²" "" "But this isn't just about one company. It's about the cognitive biases and environmental pressures that lead founders down unethical paths. Many start-up founders (not only eFishery or individual person) fall victim to overconfidence bias, believing that small ethical compromises won't have long-term consequences. The fear of failure and the pressure to impress Venture Capitals (read: investors) can exacerbate these biases, leading to decisions that prioritize short-term gains over long-term integrity." "" "The key paradox more fascinating—and concerning— is that ethical resilience is RARELY built in adulthood, its roots lie in early childhood. Neuroscience research shows that the synaptic pruning and myelination processes during formative years play a crucial role in developing moral reasoning. Children who grow up observing ethical behavior and are encouraged to think critically are more likely to resist unethical pressures later in life." "" "Their perception of life, that create "sparkling moment" or "dark moment", such as growing up in penury can instill a scarcity mindset, where immediate survival takes precedence over long-term consequences. On the other hand, affluence can lead to a sense of entitlement, increasing the likelihood of unethical behavior." "" "Let's expose the children to integrity and no compromise culture. Say yes when yes, no when no. Never succumb to any pressure to quick rich scheme, instill discipline and long-term thinking and system dynamics mental model. " "" "Let's not let the actions of this particular startup (of a few) overshadow the hard work of many good citizens who are striving to build a reputable and innovative ecosystem. It's time to address these biases head-on and foster a culture of transparency and accountability since early childhood. " "" "#StartUpEthics #CognitiveBiases #CorporateGovernance #Innovation #eFisheryScandal #EthicalLeadership #Neuroscience #IndonesiaStartUps" "" "¹ 100% not 98% https://lnkd.in/gj6kAx65" "² eFishery reportedly inflated revenue by millions of dollars https://lnkd.in/gkmpkcPR" "" "For more complete background research please visit https://lnkd.in/gUGbJf27 " "" "📰 Published in The Jakarta Post , February 1, 2025 https://lnkd.in/ga9wCCqM

2025-01-30 Cloned Journal! How Cognitive Bias Led to it - (apparently no PhD students are interested)...
Cloned Journal! How Cognitive Bias Led to it - (apparently no PhD students are interested). Publishing in a Scopus-indexed journal is a challenge. After 16 rejections, my close friend was eager—perhaps too eager—to finally get an acceptance. And then it came. But something was wrong." "" "A personal email address from a former USSR country-based contact despite being a Venezuelan-based journal publishing both Spanish and Portuguese articles, poorly English written, a questionable website, quick turnover of review —all clear red flags. Yet, he overlooked them." "" "Why? Because cognitive biases clouded his judgment. Those are:" "" "1️⃣ Desperation Bias (Scarcity Heuristic) – The urgent need to publish made him susceptible to seizing any opportunity, even one that didn’t fully check out (he included this desperation in his new year prayer list)" "2️⃣ Confirmation Bias – After so many rejections, he wanted this to be real, so he focused on the acceptance and ignored the inconsistencies." "3️⃣ Optimism Bias – he assumed that this time, things would work out, despite the growing list of warning signs." "4️⃣ Authority Bias – The journal mimicked a legitimate one, and its claim of being Scopus-indexed created a false sense of credibility, it exists in the Scopus wall." "5️⃣ Commitment and Consistency Bias – Having invested so much effort in writing and revising, he felt compelled to move forward rather than reassess the situation." "6️⃣ Anchoring Bias – Seeing “Scopus-indexed” on their site anchored his expectations, making him less critical of other details." "7️⃣ Cognitive Exhaustion (Decision Fatigue) – After multiple rejections and resubmissions, his ability to critically evaluate this journal was weakened." "8️⃣ Sunk Cost Fallacy – The time and effort he had already spent made him more willing to ignore red flags instead of starting over." "9️⃣ Affect Heuristic – The emotional relief of being accepted made him favor intuition over rational verification." "1️⃣ 0️⃣ Survivorship Bias – he focused on the fact that some researchers publish in indexed journals, overlooking the many who fall for fraudulent ones." "1️⃣1️⃣ Cognitive Miserliness – Instead of expending additional mental effort to verify the journal’s legitimacy, he relied on surface-level cues. The journal appeared indexed, so he didn't check ScimagoJR or review previously published papers. Had he done so, the cloning would have been obvious. This bias made him prioritize efficiency over thorough scrutiny, leading to a critical oversight." "" "" "" "https://lnkd.in/grDHtiMF

" "" "Last semester I raised a concern of mental health of teachers in the article "Unseen Tolls: Mental Health Challenges Facing Lecturers"² having seen them being victims of bullying by students and elaborated it in not yet published journal but been disseminated through linkedin article and went viral "(2 of 2) What About Teachers' Mental Health: Anybody Cares? ³" "" "The article in Nature provide an alternative view on seemingly “the nature of PhD education” - harsh criticism that deteriorate spirit! The research tasks will still be prolific of course, the quality must not be uphold, but the relationships among the "players" must be so conducive to allow so called (I say) "fearless psychological environment"." "" "Bullying is in nature somehow, but are we going to succumb to the reptile brain? 2025-01-23 Attending ART SG 2025 last week in Singapore was a vivid reminder of how art thrives when ...
Attending ART SG 2025 last week in Singapore was a vivid reminder of how art thrives when supported by a robust ecosystem of collaboration, cultural authenticity, and long-term strategy. With 105 galleries showcasing works that combined tradition and modernity, this event echoed the principles I outlined my article “𝘼𝙧𝙩𝙞𝙨𝙩𝙧𝙮 𝙖𝙣𝙙 𝙚𝙣𝙩𝙚𝙧𝙥𝙧𝙞𝙨𝙚: 𝙃𝙖𝙧𝙢𝙤𝙣𝙞𝙯𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙘𝙧𝙚𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙫𝙞𝙩𝙮 𝙬𝙞𝙩𝙝 𝙘𝙤𝙢𝙢𝙚𝙧𝙘𝙞𝙖𝙡 𝙨𝙪𝙘𝙘𝙚𝙨𝙨” https://lnkd.in/g7KUsGFh published by The Jakarta Post " "" "𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗮 𝘁𝗼 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝗴𝗹𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗲, 𝘄𝗲 𝗺𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗱𝗱𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀—𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘁-𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗺 𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗲𝘁𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀—𝗮𝘀 𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝘆 𝗛𝗼𝗳𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱𝗲. 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝘁𝗼 𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗲𝘁𝗲." "" "What can we learn from events like ART SG aligned with my article?" "" "🏕️Balancing Artistic Depth with Commercialization: The dual-track principle respects the timelines of creativity and commercialization, ensuring sustainable growth without compromising artistic quality." "🏕️Strengthening Local Ecosystems: Creating spaces for collaboration among artists, communities, businesses, and policymakers is essential for fostering innovation and resilience." "🏕️Preserving Cultural Authenticity: Traditional practices, like gamelan or wayang, must remain central while integrating modern platforms to amplify their global relevance." "🏕️Prioritizing Long-Term Orientation: Shifting from short-term gains to sustainable strategies allows for scalability and resilience in the creative industry." "🏕️Collaborating Across Stakeholders: Artists need partners—marketers, operational experts, and businesses—to bridge the gap between creation and commercialization." "🏕️Community Engagement: Festivals, guided cultural tours, and local art events strengthen cultural identities and attract diverse audiences." "🏕️Competitiveness through Innovation: Overcoming cultural barriers by adopting a risk-taking mindset and fostering global competitiveness is crucial for Indonesia’s creative industry." "🏕️Modern Integration: Combining traditional art forms with technology like AR can create immersive experiences, making heritage more engaging for contemporary audiences." "🏕️Commercialization as Value Creation: Commercialization is not about monetizing art alone but capturing value in ways that sustain livelihoods and ensure long-term viability." "🏕️Sustainability in Art: The ultimate goal is a creative ecosystem where artists can thrive economically, healthily, and independently, ensuring innovation across generations." "" "ART SG demonstrated how integrating traditional culture with modern approaches creates an ecosystem where art and innovation coexist sustainably." "" "#ARTSG2025 #CreativeEconomy #CulturalAuthenticity #SustainableArt #IndonesiaInnovation
2025-01-20 I hope my under represented students can compete in this broken meritocracy: As a co-learn...
I hope my under represented students can compete in this broken meritocracy: As a co-learner, I witness firsthand how the erosion of meritocracy is quietly stealing the dreams of many students." "" "🔍 In 2023, Indonesia’s Constitutional Court lowered the minimum age for presidential and vice-presidential candidates from 40 to 35¹. Now, in 2025, the consequences are becoming painfully clear—especially in the classroom." "📉 This decision wasn’t just a legal adjustment. It symbolized how elite influence now overshadows competence and experience, damaging the belief that hard work and ideas lead to success." "" "📸 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗰𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀, 𝘀𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗼 act to reach their 𝗱𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺." "📸 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝘁 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀, 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗮𝗺𝗯𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗲𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝘀𝗶𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱." "" "🔴 𝗣𝗼𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝗻 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘀𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗲𝘁𝘆." "Who knows who, who trusted who, nepotism, favoritism are human traits. But, in democratic society when meritocracy collapses, even political meritocracy and cultural meritocracy are destroyed:" "🍇 𝗣𝗼𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗰𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆—which should reward leadership based on competence—is replaced by favoritism and power consolidation." "🍇 𝗖𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗰𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆—which should honor wisdom and genuine contributions—is overtaken by privilege and inherited status." "" "🔴 𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲’𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜 𝘀𝗲𝗲 𝗮𝗺𝗼𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀:" "🥵 Many now believe that connections matter more than ideas or effort." "🥵 Some feel that leadership and success are out of reach without privilege." "🥵 𝗧𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗹𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 when they see doors closed to those without influence." "" "This is not just a political issue—it’s a cultural crisis that limits Indonesia’s future." "" "💡𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗮 𝗺𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗮 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝘂𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗮𝘀, 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗶𝘀𝗱𝗼𝗺—𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗶𝗻𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗹𝗲𝗴𝗲." "" "📢 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝘄𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝗮 𝘀𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗲𝘁𝘆 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗲𝗲𝗹𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗮 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗿 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘄, 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗱, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗯𝘂𝘁𝗲?" Early in my career, I faced crossroads that tested my aspirations, my values, and my ability to take calculated risks. Decisions that seemed straightforward on the surface were often layered with questions like:" "" "🍇 How to assess the capital (whether it is cultural or/$ economic or/& social or/and symbolic capitals) you’ve built and its alignment with your goals." "🍇Why timing and calculated risks are critical in career transitions." "🍇The role of relationships and storytelling in building a meaningful career." "" "In this article (my 3rd of 3 articles on Bourdieu's Capital Framework), I try to provide a structured framework for making pivotal career choices. Whether you’re an early-career professional or reflecting on decades of work, this perspective helps evaluate decisions not just for their immediate impact, but for how they align with your raison d’être." 2025-01-20 Why run a marathon? Because it mirrors life’s biggest challenges—whether starting a career...
My 3rd non-competitive marathon wasn’t about speed or competition; it was about persistence, self-discipline, and learning to embrace every phase of the journey. Why run a marathon? Because it mirrors life’s biggest challenges—whether starting a career, navigating change, waiting for opportunities, or finding purpose after retirement." "" "The first 20 km felt like life at its best—filled with excitement, optimism, and momentum. The early kilometers, full of energy and anticipation, mirrored the enthusiasm of starting something new. By 8.5 km, the rain poured, soaking me completely, but instead of holding me back, it felt like a tailwind, adding strength and joy to the experience. These moments reminded me how, in the early stages of a career or life chapter, everything seems possible, and even unexpected events can fuel progress." "" "From 20–30 km, the tone shifted, much like searching for meaning after 20 years in a career. The effort began to feel heavier, and doubts started creeping in: Can I complete this marathon? Is it worth doing? The soreness and endless pain became harder to ignore, testing my perseverance and forcing me to confront the bigger questions. This phase required slowing down, rethinking strategies, and finding a deeper purpose to keep going." "" "From 30–36 km, the journey transitioned into something larger than myself. My body slowed, and the effort became monumental, but my mind stayed focused. It reminded me of people entering retirement, realizing that life’s purpose is no longer about personal achievements but about contributing to others—becoming mentors, philanthropists, or leaving a meaningful legacy. This phase taught me the importance of shifting focus from individual goals to serving a greater purpose." "" "By 39 km, joy and anticipation took over. Seeing the finish line on the horizon made me forget the struggles and pain of the journey. The pleasure of nearing the end erased the labor it took to get there, filling me with gratitude for every step and every lesson learned along the way." "" "Crossing 42.195 km was a moment of pseudo triumph—a climax of emotions, wisdom, and fulfillment. Chemically, it is when the dopamine bursts in the brain. It wasn’t just an end but a feeling of renewal, as if life was giving me the opportunity to start all over again, victoriously and wiser. The effort, pain, and perseverance culminated in a sense of accomplishment so profound that it inspired the desire to face new beginnings with greater clarity and strength." "" "Adding 2 extra kilometers beyond the finish line wasn’t just about celebrating the victory—it was about taking time to reflect on the journey, savor every step, and acknowledge the lessons learned." "" "Marathons teach us to embrace challenges, respect the process, and find fulfillment in every phase of the journey." "" "In your life—whether starting, waiting, transitioning, or redefining—how do you pace yourself to cross the finish line with purpose and fulfillment?

Yesterday, I spent hours in deep discussion with some of my former students (from STEI ITB and School of Business and Management ITB ) — now climbing their corporation career. They are the crème de la crème in their fields, yet they still remember their "old teacher." Moments like this remind me why I dedicated my life to co-learning. " "" "We discussed many things, but one idea stood out: “Tandur”—the Javanese practice of planting while moving backward. Farmers step backward to ensure every seed is planted in a straight line. It’s a powerful lesson: true progress requires reflection. As Søren Kierkegaard said:" "" ""𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐨𝐧𝐥𝐲 𝐛𝐞 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐨𝐝 𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐬; 𝐛𝐮𝐭 𝐢𝐭 𝐦𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐛𝐞 𝐥𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐬."" "" "In today’s fast-moving world, many chase quick rewards without thinking about the long-term impact. But success comes from slowing down, reflecting, and moving forward with intention—doing things right the first time. Like the farmer, each step we take should align with our larger goals. Success is built carefully, not through shortcuts." "" "To my former students—now my teachers—thank you for reminding me that learning and growth never stop. Thanks to Dr. Haryono Budi Santosa who inspired "Tandur". " "" "And to everyone reading this: Pause. Reflect. Plant your seeds with care. The harvest will come when the work today is done with purpose." "" "Except from the article " ""The sky is still pale when the farmer steps barefoot into the paddy field. The cool mud squeezes between his toes, grounding him in the land he’s known all his life. He bends forward, hands steady, carefully dropping seeds into the damp soil. But then, he does something unexpected—he begins to move backward." "" "Slow, deliberate steps. Eyes fixed on the straight line of seeds behind him. His hands work with practiced precision, planting each seed as if it were a promise. He does not glance ahead. The unknown stretches before him, but it doesn’t concern him. His focus is on the work already done, making sure each step now aligns perfectly with the last." "" "He will not rush. He will not correct mistakes later. There is no later. The line must be straight now. He moves back until his heel touches the boundary between his field and his neighbor's—a silent marker of responsibility and respect." "" "The farmer cannot control the rain. He cannot stop the pests or predict the market price of rice. But this, this process of planting, is entirely his. And he will do it right."" 2024-12-28 (D-3 End of Year Reflection) “Linear Thinking? Considering System Dynamics for Complex, In...
(D-3 End of Year Reflection) “Linear Thinking? Considering System Dynamics for Complex, Interconnected Problems”. Prof. John Sterman’s 14-minute masterclass at the 2024 MIT Sustainability Summit (see my uploaded YouTube: https://lnkd.in/gNP_MPZF) on how well-intentioned policies often fall victim to policy resistance, where the very structure of systems undermines interventions and exacerbates problems. For instance, building more roads to ease traffic often leads to worse congestion. Overusing pesticides accelerates resistance in pests, creating a vicious cycle. Even economic growth in affluent societies has paradoxically decreased well-being. These examples highlight the limitations of conventional approaches in a world where nothing is truly linear—feedback, delays, interconnections, complexity, and policy resistance shape every system." "" "This is where system dynamics becomes indispensable. Unlike conventional, linear thinking—which often focuses on symptoms and leads to short-sighted interventions—system dynamics examines feedback loops, delays, and the interconnected nature of systems. It provides actionable insights by addressing root causes and redesigning systems for lasting, meaningful change." "" "Sterman illustrates these ideas with compelling metaphors, such as the Slinky experiment, showing how behavior emerges from a system’s internal structure, and the bicycle inner tube, which captures the tension between the world we aspire to and the reality we face. These examples highlight the shortcomings of short-sighted thinking and the power of systems thinking to create sustainable solutions." "" "His speech is also a call to action. Confronting complexity often leaves people overwhelmed or resigned to simplistic solutions. But Sterman argues that we must strengthen our emotional, moral, and intellectual resilience, refuse to erode our goals, and work tirelessly to accelerate positive feedback loops like renewable energy adoption and public acceptance. Recognizing opposition is vital, but so is holding fast to aspirations and embracing the hard fight for systems change." "" "Sterman’s masterclass highlights why system dynamics is essential for addressing the world’s most pressing challenges. His insights inspire a shift from reactive problem-solving to designing systems that enable meaningful and lasting change. Explore the full article to understand how this powerful approach can transform complex issues into opportunities for sustainable progress and collaboration. Let this serve as a call to action as we embrace the new year with renewed purpose and resolve." "" "https://lnkd.in/gi3RUHPE
